# Part 3 source records: works selected from the self-improvement survey (arXiv 2607.13104) and its project page, 2026-09-30

**Date:** 2026-09-30 · generated by `tools/evidence-check/build_part3_files.py` from the verified store; not edited by hand.

Each work was saved as full text and read by one agent, which locked every item to a line of the saved text with a short verbatim anchor. A script checked that each anchor occurs in the saved text and that the numbers of the item stand within three lines of it. A second agent, which did not write the record, then tried to refute each item against the text. Items shown here passed both checks. Where the auditor corrected an item, the corrected wording is shown and the Audit column says so. The verbatim anchors and the saved texts are kept outside the repository; this file gives the location of every item instead. Only works that are eligible under the source rule (2026-09-29, D313; citation priority restated on 2026-09-30) are listed; the others are in the evidence ledger, section 1b.

Columns: # = item index (the reference is <record id>#<index>); Field = what the item is about; Line = line in the saved text of the version read. Full references: evidence ledger, References.

| 2 | definition | Eq. (2) decomposes the scaffold as Sigma_t := (p_t, m_t, T_t, g_t): p_t = structured prompts or system instructions; m_t = memory mechanisms together with their retrieval and update policies; T_t = the set of external tools with their invocation interfaces; g_t = additional control logic such as routing, scheduling or safety constraints. theta_t and Sigma_t together determine how the agent reasons, plans and acts (lines 366-369). The Notation table glosses g_t slightly differently, as control, routing, or verification logic (line 4964). | - | Definition (no measurement). | §3.1, Eq. | 3 | definition | Separate from the intrinsic configuration, the agent keeps an ephemeral execution state X_t (e.g., key-value caches, intermediate plans, short-term working memory); behaviour is the induced policy pi_{theta_t,Sigma_t}(A_t / X_t) (Eq. 3), with A_t (roman, distinct from the calligraphic configuration symbol) the action produced at time step t. X_t is typically discarded or reset once an immediate goal is reached or an external task boundary is crossed, and is not part of the agent's intrinsic configuration; a standard agent that adapts only X_t (e.g., in-context examples) keeps its underlying capabilities bounded by its fixed initial setup (line 375). Caveat: the Notation table defines X_t instead as input, observation, or task context (line 4976). | - | Definition (no measurement). | §3.1, Eq. (3) (lines 370-375) | 370 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | definition | Self-improvement (SI-FMA) is formalized as a self-induced operator U split into an execution phase and an update phase: A_{t+1} = U(A_{1:t}, E(pi_{theta_t,Sigma_t}; Sigma_t, C_t)) (Eq. 4). E is an agent-executed procedure that produces a learning signal (interaction trajectories, reflections, critiques or proposed edits) by running the induced policy against a task context C_t (a task distribution, a user interaction stream or a self-play environment); Sigma_t is an explicit argument of E so the agent can inspect its own scaffold; A_{1:t} is the configuration history. U commits durable changes to theta or Sigma, unlike the transient evolution of X_t; the updates are not strictly irreversible and may be undone (line 387). | - | Definition (no measurement). | §3.2 'Self-improvement as a self-induced operator', Eq. (4) (lines 381-387) | 386 | primary | supported |
| 5 | loop_cost | Foundation-model improvement (Eq. 5): theta_{t+1} = U_theta(theta_{1:t}, E(pi_{theta_t,Sigma_t}; Sigma_t, C_t)) with Sigma_{t+1} = Sigma_t; E yields rewards, preference comparisons, synthetic labels, critiques or verification outcomes, and U_theta is a parameter-learning procedure (policy-gradient, offline or online RL, preference optimization). The authors state this pathway typically runs on longer time scales, incurs substantial computational cost and produces stable, global changes to the agent's capabilities. | - | Qualitative statement about the cost of the update loop (parameter training); no number, unit or budget given. | §3.2 'Foundation model improvement', Eq. (5) (lines 396-400) | 400 | primary | supported |
| 6 | definition | Scaffolding improvement (Eq. 6): Sigma_{t+1} = U_Sigma(Sigma_{1:t}, E(pi_{theta_t,Sigma_t}; Sigma_t, C_t)) with theta_{t+1} = theta_t. E (possibly under a meta-objective) generates update artifacts such as prompt edits, memory reorganizations, tool-interface changes or new control routines, and U_Sigma commits them as structural updates meant to outlast individual task boundaries (line 408). These updates reshape (i) the conditioning context given to the model, (ii) the effective action space via admissibility constraints and tool schemas, and (iii) the execution semantics that ground token sequences into environment actions; compared with model improvement, scaffolding improvement is described as typically faster, more reversible and more context-dependent. | - | Definition (no measurement). | §3.2 'Scaffolding improvement', Eq. (6) (lines 403-409) | 409 | primary | supported |
| 7 | definition | A skill is modelled as a reusable, named instance of the update operator U, serialized into one substrate of A_t: a tool and its calling convention (T), an instruction or workflow (p), a memory entry (m), consolidated weights (theta) or control logic (g) (line 411). An object-level skill acts on the task or world state by running a (typically multi-step) routine through E, which the survey likens to a temporally extended option in hierarchical RL; the U step lies in acquiring it, not in invoking it. A meta-level skill instead edits the agent's own configuration (writing a tool, refactoring a prompt, consolidating memory, patching the scaffold). | - | Definition (no measurement). | §3.2 'Skill as a reusable update' (lines 411-414) | 413 | primary | supported |
| 8 | taxonomy | Section 4 writes a generic procedure IMPROVE_target(.; S_t), where S_t is an update signal produced through the agent's own execution (trajectories, critiques, preferences or other self-generated artifacts). Works are sorted first by update target (model parameters theta vs scaffold Sigma), then by signal form, and scaffold methods also by component. Model-side signal forms: intrinsic generative demonstrations D_t, intrinsic evaluative feedback e_t (scalar rewards, preference pairs, critiques) and extrinsic exploratory experience tau_t (lines 447-459). Scaffold components with the works cited for each (lines 470-489; names from the survey's own later sections, calc. cross-reference): prompt optimization p (TextGrad, EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder, APE); memory evolution m (Mem0, Wang et al. 2025i, Zhang et al. 2025e, MemoryBank); tool governance T (ATLASS, ToolGen, Tool-Star, AgentOrchestra); full scaffolding update Sigma (ADAS, Darwin Goedel Machine, AlphaEvolve, Live-SWE-agent). | - | Classification scheme (no measurement). | §4 intro, §4.1 'Classification by signal form', §4.2 'Classification by scaffold component' (lines 438-489) | 438 | primary | supported |

| 22 | limitation | Web synthesis: page layouts and interaction flows change over time (non-stationarity, weak observability), which can quickly erode gains measured on static snapshots. | 31 | eval_protocol | Judge pitfalls: when Phi_judge produces m_t, the protocol should disclose the judge model version, prompt, rubric kappa and the evidence shown to it, and should isolate the judging budget from the agent's execution budget b_t, because judge reliability varies with its resources (context limits, multi-agent debates, tool-use steps) and unreported judge overhead hides whether the agent improved or the evaluator became more exhaustive (line 1992). If the same judge drives updates and reports results, the system will likely over-optimize to its latent biases; rigorous protocols should enforce evaluator independence with a distinct judge configuration for final reporting (e.g., a more capable model or an orthogonal rubric), and reliability can be supported by repeated runs with variance estimates, aggregation across multiple judge instances, and calibration against a verifiable subset using Phi_metric or targeted human review (line 1994). | - | Reporting recommendation; judging cost is to be accounted separately from agent execution cost; no number. | §8.1.2 'Specify the judge and the judging budget' and 'Prevent over-optimization to the judge' (lines 1992-1994) | 1992 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 35 | recommendation | Deployment strategy from the fast/slow asymmetry: when environmental feedback is noisy, it is better to confine updates to the scaffold and validate them by rigorous execution tests; parametric consolidation (distillation or fine-tuning) can be deferred until the new behaviour has proven stable. Consolidation is called lossy: distilling complex trajectories into weights biases the model toward average-case execution and often discards rare but crucial error-recovery strategies discovered during exploration; as a result any theta update invalidates prior safety bounds and needs renewed adversarial testing (line 2029). | - | Design recommendation; no measurement. Citations given (AgentDistill, Qiu et al. 2025a; Lyu et al. 2026) not verified. | §9.1 'From Fast Exploration to Slow Consolidation' (line 2029) | 2029 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 36 | selection_rule | The critic as governed infrastructure: a critic inside the loop is an attack surface; the agent's capability ceiling is usually bottlenecked by the critic's exploit-resistance. If one component both proposes and accepts updates the loop becomes self-confirming, so critics can be decoupled from generators; critic evolution must not be under the agent's unconstrained control and should be limited to monotone changes (e.g., purely additive test generation) gated by human audit trails. | - | Design recommendation; no measurement. | §9.1 'The Critic as Governed Infrastructure' (line 2031) | 2031 | primary | supported |
| 37 | safety | Safety through layered gating: risks are highest under full-scaffold self-improvement, where one-off exploits (e.g., a prompt injection) can become persistent vulnerabilities once poisoned memories or hijacked tool logic are committed. | 0 | problem_definition | Definition 1 (Exogenous-Context MDP, EC-MDP) is the tuple <S, M, A, P_exo, P_endo, R, gamma>. S = exogenous state space, the set of all tasks, with next task drawn as P_exo(s_{t+1}) = rho(s_{t+1}) independent of the agent's actions or memory; M = endogenous state space, the memory store, a finite subset of the universe M_inf of all possible experiences (footnote, line 112); A(M) = {A subset of M : /A/ <= k}, retrieval subsets of at most k memories; P_endo(M_{t+1} / s_t, M_t, A_t) = sum over trajectories tau of pi_LLM(tau / s_t, A_t) * 1[M_{t+1} = M_t union {Build(s_t, tau)}], i.e. the frozen LLM pi_LLM produces trajectory tau and Build turns task plus trajectory into one new memory (line 114); R(s_t, A_t) = expected r(tau) under pi_LLM (line 116); gamma in [0,1] = discount factor. The retrieval policy pi_ret(A / s, M) is the agent's sole optimized policy while pi_LLM stays frozen (line 116). The joint kernel factors as P_exo(s_{t+1}) * P_endo(M_{t+1} / s_t, M_t, A_t) (Eq. 1, line 121). | - | Formal problem definition; not a measurement. | §3 Problem Formulation, Definition 1 and Eq. 1 | 110 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Objective: maximize over pi_ret the initial state value V^{pi_ret}(M_0), where V^{pi_ret}(M_t) = expected sum over k of gamma^k r(tau_{t+k}) with tasks s_k ~ rho, retrievals A_k ~ pi_ret, trajectories tau_k ~ pi_LLM (lines 132-136). The set-level action value Q(s, A; M) = E_tau[r(tau) + gamma V^{pi_ret}(M')], M' = M union {m_new(tau)}, is approximated, assuming retrieved memories contribute independently, by the first-order decomposition Q(s, A; M) ~ (1//A/) * sum over m_i in A of Q(m_i) (Eq. 3, lines 138-140). Each scalar Q(m) is a provenance value, the memory's marginal contribution to future rewards along causal generation chains, satisfying the structural Bellman equation Q(m) = E[r(tau) + gamma Q(m_new) / m in A] with m_new = Build(s, tau): the temporal bootstrap gamma V(M') is replaced by the downstream memory's value gamma Q(m_new). | - | Learning objective and value decomposition; not a measurement. | §3 Value functions and learning objective, Eq. 3 | 143 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | What changes is the external episodic memory store and its per-entry values, not the model: each memory is a tuple m_i = (c_i, e_i, Q_i) where c_i is natural-language text encoding a past experience, e_i = phi(c_i) is an embedding from a frozen encoder phi, and Q_i is a scalar Q-value (lines 208-212). New entries are added after every task and Q-values are updated by TD learning; the LLM pi_LLM stays frozen and the retrieval policy pi_ret (which reads the Q-values) is the only optimized policy (line 116). Section 3 opens with a frozen LLM agent that cannot learn via gradient updates and relies on a growing episodic memory store (line 106). | - | Description of the modified component (memory entries and their Q-values); not a measurement. | §4.1 Procedural Construction of Q-Augmented Memory | 212 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | After each interaction the system builds a new memory from the sampled trajectory by proceduralization: an LLM distills trajectory tau into an abstract 3 to 5 step script, and both the script and the raw trajectory are stored as memory content; successful trajectories are stored directly, while on failure an LLM generates a reflection (an analysis of what went wrong) stored as a separate memory. The new memory's initial Q-value is the average Q of the retrieved memories that contributed to it, or random if nothing was retrieved (line 217); its retrieval key is derived from the task description that generated it (line 217). | 3 to 5 step script | Description of what is stored per episode; not a measurement. | §4.1 Procedural Construction of Q-Augmented Memory | 213 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Credit assignment over the agent's own history: for each new memory MemQ records parents(m_new) = A, the retrieved set, which induces a provenance DAG (line 147). For task s_j with retrieved set A_j, reward R_j and new memory m_new,j, the per-memory TD error is delta(m_i, j) = R_j + gamma Q(m_new,j) - Q(m_i) for every m_i in A_j (Eq. 5, line 243); gamma = 0 reduces this to MemRL-style single-step EMA (line 246). A backward BFS from each retrieved memory m_0 adds alpha * (gamma*lambda)^{d(m, m_0)} * delta(m_0, j) to every reachable ancestor m, with d the shortest DAG path length (Eq. 6, lines 248-253). The BFS stops at maximum depth D (D = 4 in Table 3, lines 939-941) or when (gamma*lambda)^d < 10^-12; increments are buffered within an epoch with update counts N_i and flushed at epoch end as Q(m_i) += clip(DeltaQ(m_i)/N_i, -eps_clip, eps_clip) (lines 253-257). | discount floor (gamma*lambda)^d < 10^-12 | Update rule; the numbers are algorithm settings, not measurements. | §4.3 Provenance-Based Credit Assignment, Eqs. 5-6; Algorithm 1 lines 21-28 | 253 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Memories are selected at retrieval time, not accepted or rejected at write time. Locality filtering keeps candidates with cosine similarity >= theta_sim (the 'radius of competence'); if none qualify the task is treated as novel and the agent falls back to zero-shot (line 221). Candidates are scored by w_s * sim(s, m_i) + w_q * Q(m_i), with both terms normalized to [0,1] (lines 223-225), and chosen epsilon-greedy: top-k by score with probability 1 - epsilon, a uniform sample of k candidates with probability epsilon (lines 227-230). Every built memory is kept: the store grows monotonically with no consolidation or deletion (line 124; limitation, line 491). Appendix D sets epsilon = 0.0 for MemQ on LiveCodeBench, MMMU Pro and ERQA and 0.01 on LLAB, BFCL and GPQA (Tables 4-9). | - | Retrieval rule (threshold, weighted score, epsilon-greedy top-k); not a measurement. | §4.2 Q-integrated Retrieval Policy within Local Consistency | 227 | primary | supported |

| 0 | problem_definition | AEL formalizes the task as an episode stream {e_t}, t = 1..T, handled on two episode-based timescales: fast windows W^fast_k of N episodes update selection preferences, and slow windows W^slow_j of M >> N episodes aggregate evidence for reflection and memory consolidation (line 232). At each episode t the agent selects a harness configuration c_t = (p_t, z_t, m_t), where p_t is the planner, z_t the tool set and m_t the memory-retrieval policy, and then observes an outcome score s_t in [-1, 1]. In the default configuration p_t and z_t are fixed and a Thompson Sampling bandit chooses only m_t (line 234). Section 3.1 writes no separate objective equation beyond this per-episode outcome score. | - | Problem formalization; not a measurement. For the portfolio benchmark the text describes the training signal as episode-level return normalized by volatility (line 523) and lists the reward as per-bar portfolio return (Table 17, line 1698); the exact mapping from return to s_t in [-1, 1] is not given. | §3.1 Overview and Design Rationale | 233 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The backbone LLM stays frozen and the harness around it is learned. By default AEL learns three things online (lines 239-242): a Beta posterior per memory-retrieval policy via Thompson Sampling; a reflection insight regenerated each slow window and injected into the planner prompt; and procedural rules promoted from recurring semantic patterns. The planner identity, the 12-tool set and all tool implementations stay fixed (line 243). The memory-policy pool can grow when reflection adds a new LLM-designed retrieval policy as a bandit arm (§3.4, line 291). Planner selection (LinUCB), per-tool Thompson Sampling, cold-start initialization and skill extraction are supported but switched off by default; the authors state that the Table 3 ablation shows they degrade performance 'in this short-horizon regime' (line 244). Table 3 has rows for cold-start, planner evolution, per-tool selection and skill extraction, but no separate row for LinUCB planner selection (lines 573-589). | 12 tools fixed | Description of what the loop modifies (memory-policy posteriors, memory-policy pool, prompt insight, procedural rules) and what it keeps fixed (LLM weights, planner, tools); not a measurement. The reason for switching extensions off is scoped by the authors to the short-horizon (208-episode) portfolio setting (lines 244, 553). | §3.1, 'Which parts of the harness are learned' | 243 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | The fast-timescale signal is each episode's scalar outcome s_t in [-1, 1], converted into r~_t = clip((s_t + 1)/2, 0, 1) and used directly to update the memory-policy bandit posterior (and, in the full EAEL variant, the tool and planner bandits) (§3.6, line 302; Algorithm 1, line 327). Appendix G instead writes the module-specific reward as clip(lambda r_t + (1 - lambda) g_t^(m), 0, 1) with lambda = 0.5 and, under the main uniform-credit configuration, g_t^(m) = 1/3 for all modules (lines 1488, 1497-1502); this does not match 'used directly' in §3.6. At the slow timescale, reflection consumes aggregated trajectories to decide when structural evolution is needed (line 304). The outcomes come from the environment: the portfolio reward is per-bar portfolio return (Table 17, line 1698), and support routing is scored by accuracy against a deterministic gold route (line 1326); for the support stream the text only says the no-LLM hyperparameter sweep uses 'the same reward and reflection-injection logic' (line 2149). A Claude Opus 4.7 judge is used only in the post-hoc reflection-faithfulness analysis (Appendix A.2, line 1093; Appendix T, line 2063). In the non-default LLM-FCC credit variant, an LLM assigns per-module credit scores in [-1, +1] from the ground-truth bar return inside the loop (Appendix P.1, lines 1960-1961). | - | Definition of the training signal; not a measurement. §3.6 and Algorithm 1 define r~_t = clip((s_t+1)/2, 0, 1) (lines 302, 327). Appendix G defines uniform credit as g_t^(m) = 1/3 for all modules and blends it with the normalized outcome at lambda = 0.5 (lines 1488, 1502), giving 0.5 r_t + 1/6 for every module (calc.). The two descriptions conflict and the text does not say which one the reported runs used. | §3.6 Learning Signal | 302 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | What is stored: episodic memory records each episode's raw outcome (tools used, signals they produced, whether each signal was correct, and overall prediction quality). Semantic memory aggregates episodic records into cross-episode patterns and is distilled every 10 episodes. Procedural memory promotes high-confidence semantic patterns into executable rules that are injected directly into planner prompts and need no retrieval at query time (lines 262-267). How it is reused: the bandit-chosen retrieval policy sets which tiers are visible, how many entries are retrieved and in what format. Within that policy, entries are ranked by r(q,e) = f_match x (0.5 + 0.5 q_e) x (0.3 + 0.7 e^(-0.01 Delta)) x b_tau, and the top-k (default k = 5) entries above a quality threshold are returned (lines 269-276). | semantic distillation every 10 episodes | Description of the mechanism; not a measurement. Symbols in the relevance score (line 275): q is the query and e a memory entry; f_match sums feature-match bonuses (ticker, sector, tool); q_e is the entry's quality score; Delta is the number of episodes since the entry was written; b_tau is the tier boost, 1.0 / 1.2 / 1.5 for episodic / semantic / procedural. | §3.3 Three-Tier Evolving Memory | 262 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | After each slow window the LLM receives four inputs: (i) per-ticker episode summaries (planner used, score, directional accuracy); (ii) per-tool accuracy statistics over the window; (iii) market side information (sector returns, volatility regime, cross-correlation) computed from cached price data but not given to the predictor; and (iv) the last three reflections. It outputs a causal insight, a regime label and a confidence score. The insight is injected into the allocator's prompt at the next episode rather than written into the memory store, and module selection stays with the bandit (lines 285-287). | - | Description of the mechanism (the slow reflection loop over aggregated trajectories); not a measurement. | §3.4 LLM-Driven Reflection and Code Evolution, 'Slow-window reflection' | 284 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | In the portfolio setting described in §3.4, memory-policy evolution fires every 5 slow windows, starting after window 10, and only when the average Thompson Sampling reward across all policies falls below 0.4, i.e. when the whole pool is underperforming (line 290). The LLM then designs a new retrieval policy (tier visibility, retrieval depth, formatting strategy), which is added as a new bandit arm (line 291) with uninformative priors (lines 297, 1038). Appendix P.2 states that the generated retrieval policy was validated by AST parsing (line 2005). After training, the best posteriors are selected on the validation split and frozen for the test split (Algorithm 1, line 349). The other benchmarks use different triggers: the synthetic bandit checks every 13 episodes and injects when the trailing 25-episode mean reward is below 0.42 (line 2128), and the support-ticket stream default is every 40 episodes, window 120, threshold .58 (Table 24, line 2158). Appendix S describes the seed-42 running-case injection as following an under-threshold loss at episode 83, with the new arm introduced by the episode-84 reflection (line 2061). | every 5 slow windows after window 10; mean TS reward < 0.4 | Trigger and admission rule for new memory policies; not a measurement. Thresholds and cadences are benchmark-specific: 0.4 portfolio (line 290), 0.42 synthetic (line 2128), .58 support stream (line 2158). | §3.4 LLM-Driven Reflection and Code Evolution | 290 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## s003 — Metis: Bridging Text and Code Memory for Self-Evolving Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.24151v1 · version read: arXiv 2606.24151v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; only version listed) · v1: 2026-06-23
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper formalizes a training-free execute-reflect-reuse loop rather than an optimization objective. The agent faces a stream of tasks q^(1), q^(2), ... and keeps a memory M that starts empty (M_0 = empty set). For task q^(k), entries are retrieved from the current memory M_(k-1), usually by similarity-based vector search and LLM-based filtering, and put into the interaction context. The frozen LLM policy pi then acts as a_t ~ pi(. / c_t; M_(k-1)), where c_t is the interaction context at step t (c_1 holds the query q and a system prompt), a_t is the action (a code block or a tool call), o_t is the environment observation and c_(t+1) = c_t (+) (a_t, o_t) (line 100). The rollout stops at step T (a terminal action or a step budget) and yields the trajectory tau^(k) = (q, (a_1,o_1), ..., (a_T,o_T)) (line 101). One or more reflector modules then write back M_k = Reflect(M_(k-1), tau^(k)). Metis instantiates this as S_i = Select(q_i, M_(i-1)), tau_i ~ pi(. / q_i, S_i), M_i = Reflect(M_(i-1), tau_i) (lines 139-144). No single objective combining accuracy and cost is written; §4.1 reports accuracy, execution cost and memory-construction cost as separate metrics (lines 278-281). | - | Formal problem statement (loop definition); not a measurement. | §2.2 Self-Evolving Agent Systems (with §2.1 and §3.2 'Memory Schema') | 104 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Only an external memory is changed: Metis maintains M = (M_text, M_code), a structured text memory store plus a code memory library. Selected text memories are injected into the executor's context as natural-language guidance, while selected tools are compiled in the environment and exposed to the executor through their docstrings (line 119), so the code library adds callable actions. The paper places itself in the training-free paradigm in which experience is kept as an explicit, model-agnostic memory artifact that conditions a frozen policy during inference (line 103); model weights are not updated. | - | Description of the modified component (memory outside the model); not a measurement. | §3.1 System Overview | 111 | primary | supported |
| 2 | environment_knowledge | One of the three text-memory categories is environment facts (M_env), which capture task-independent properties of the execution environment and its constraints (line 131); the other two are common pitfalls (M_pit), stored as (trigger, mistake, consequence) tuples distilled from failed or inefficient executions (line 132), and execution plans (M_plan), reusable templates for recurring sub-routines and the only category eligible for promotion to code (line 133). For failed tasks the reflector probes the environment to find the cause and typically proposes a corrective pitfall or a warning environment fact (line 148). Each entry is m = (body, kappa, v): natural-language body, category label kappa in {env, pit, plan}, invalidation bit v in {0,1} (lines 135-136). Environment facts and pitfalls stay in textual form and are never promoted to code (line 88); code tools are built with sandbox inspection and execution testing and are grounded in the actual environment (lines 171-172), so they carry procedural API usage, but the paper does not describe them as environment knowledge. The saved text gives no worked example of an environment fact and no explicit state or transition model. | - | Description of what kind of environment knowledge is stored; not a measurement. | §3.2 Differentiated Text Reflection, 'Memory Schema' | 131 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | The text reflector is itself an agent (a bounded reasoning loop) with access to the same environment, tools and documentation as the executor (line 147). For failed tasks it probes the environment to identify the underlying cause and proposes a corrective pitfall or a warning environment fact; for successful tasks it continues to inspect the trajectory for inefficiencies, such as erroneous retries or unnecessary environment exploration, and proposes efficiency-oriented entries that would eliminate them. To keep plans general it is also conditioned on the queries of the most recent N tasks (line 149; N is not given). It reads trajectories through progressive disclosure: a compact per-step view keeping action type, tool name and head/tail-truncated action and observation (lines 237-246), with on-demand expansion of single steps, step ranges or tool implementations (line 249). Selected entries are later prepended to the executor's context as advice the executor may weigh, partially apply or ignore (line 154). | - | Description of how trajectories and environment interaction are turned into stored memory; not a measurement. How a task is determined to have failed or succeeded for the reflector is not stated in the text. | §3.2 'Agentic Reflection' (with §3.5 'Progressive Disclosure', §3.2 'Memory Reuse') | 148 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Code memory is grown by promoting recurring execution plans. Each plan p carries a candidate buffer B(p) of recent tasks that selected it, a related-task history R(p) bounded by budget beta, and D(p), the admitted tools implementing it (line 163). Whenever p is selected for task i, i is added to B(p) whether or not the task succeeded (lines 167-169); codification is triggered once /B(p)/ >= theta, a configurable reuse threshold (line 170). The codifier then receives the plan body, the candidate queries Q_B(p), the related queries Q_R(p), the current tool library as signatures and docstrings, and sandbox access for inspection and execution testing; candidate trajectories are deliberately excluded (line 172). Admitted tools are added to M_code and registered in D(p), and B(p) is folded into R(p) and emptied (Algorithm 1, lines 201-207); later text reflection may revise the plan to reference the tools (line 210). At reuse time, embedding-based top-k retrieval over text entries and tools is followed by a lightweight LLM Memory Manager that jointly selects text memories and tools; selecting a codified plan makes its tools eligible, and a static dependency closure adds all helper functions the selected tools call (lines 213-229). Values of theta, beta and k are not given in the saved text. | - | Description of the text-to-code promotion loop and reuse path; not a measurement. | §3.3 'Recurrence-Based Promotion', Algorithm 1; §3.4; §3.5 'Dependency Closure' | 171 | primary | supported |
| 5 | signal | The text states no rule that accepts memory on the basis of a benchmark score or test result during construction. The signal for promoting a plan to code is recurrence: the number of tasks that selected a non-invalidated plan since its last codification (B(p) is emptied after admission; lines 179, 207), explicitly not proof that the plan caused task success (a failed rollout also counts, lines 165, 169). The signal for admitting a tool is the harness's dependency-closure and compilation check in the executor's sandbox (lines 231-235). The signal for finalizing a text entry is the reflector's own judgment of generality plus validation gates for non-redundancy, mechanistic grounding and correct scope (line 149); the reflector (Claude Sonnet 4.6, line 264) probes the environment on failed tasks and inspects successful trajectories for inefficiencies (line 148). The text does not say how a training task is labelled failed or successful for the reflector (for example, whether AppWorld's evaluation-test outcome is passed to it). TGC (programmatic state-based evaluation tests, line 278) is the evaluation metric reported in §4. | - | Description of the feedback signals used inside the loop; not a measurement. Source of the reflector's failed/successful label is not stated in the text. | §3.3 'Recurrence-Based Promotion' | 165 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | A candidate text entry is finalized only if the reflector judges it sufficiently general and it passes the remaining validation gates for non-redundancy, mechanistic grounding and correct scope. Maintenance uses merge and update: several narrow entries capturing the same pattern are merged into one more general entry, and an inaccurate, biased or superseded entry is revised (line 151). Both follow invalidate-and-replace: the superseded entry's invalidation bit flips from 0 to 1 and the new entry is appended as a new record, so obsolete entries are excluded from future retrieval (line 152). The text does not say whether the validation gates are LLM judgments or programmatic checks. | - | Acceptance and replacement rule for text-memory entries; not a measurement. | §3.2 'Agentic Reflection' and 'Memory Maintenance' | 149 | primary | supported |
| 7 | selection_rule | Tool admission: the codifier is instructed to write small composable helpers rather than end-to-end solvers, each supported by at least two structurally distinct queries from Q_B(p) union Q_R(p), with task-varying elements (entities, time ranges, filters, API options) exposed as parameters rather than hard-coded (line 174). The harness statically scans the candidate for calls to existing library tools, injects all dependencies through the closure procedure and validates it in the executor's sandbox; formally Compile(impl(t), Close(empty set, {t})) = 1 (lines 231-233). If compilation fails, the codifier gets the error message and one corrective round; a second failure rejects the candidate and the tool is not added. The stated admission condition is compilation with dependency closure; no admission test against expected task outputs is stated. | - | Acceptance rule for generated tools; not a measurement. | §3.5 'Tool Admission Guard' (with §3.3 'Tool Admission') | 235 | primary | supported |
| 8 | setting | AppWorld: 9 simulated applications exposing 457 APIs; each task is a natural-language instruction requiring the agent to inspect the environment, compose actions and change sandbox state to satisfy programmatic evaluation tests. Executor: GPT-4o with ReAct, AppWorld's official agent implementation (lines 257, 265). Reflector: Claude Sonnet 4.6 for all memory-based methods, used only in the offline training phase (line 264). Embeddings: text-embedding-3-large (line 266); the Memory Manager is described only as a lightweight LLM (line 213). Baselines: No Memory, ACE (text context evolution), SkillX (skill artifacts), adapted to the same executor, task order and sandbox interface (lines 257-262). Protocol: each method consumes the training tasks in one fixed-order pass, then the memory is frozen and evaluated on held-out test tasks (lines 269-270). Splits: Official (original train / test-normal, scenario-disjoint, distribution-shifted) and Resampled (pooled and redrawn at task level with a fixed random seed, same sizes; a recurring workload) (lines 273-274); test-challenge excluded (line 271). Ablations: memory built on the official train split, evaluated on the dev split (line 419). Profiling study: AppWorld train split, 90 tasks (line 565). Split sizes for test-normal, the resampled test set and dev are not given in the saved text. | 9 applications; 457 APIs | Benchmark and model configuration; not a result. | §4.1 Experimental Setup (Benchmark, Baselines, Models, Protocol) | 253 | primary | supported |

| 0 | problem_definition | The loop is formalized around two memories. Asset Memory M_A = B_agt ∪ B_tool (Eq. 1), where B_agt is the Agent Bank of expert agents and B_tool the Tool Bank of executable tools. An agent entry m_agt = <ρ, ε, σ, T_avail> (Eq. 2): ρ is the role specifying the agent's identity, ε the agent's expertise and domain knowledge, σ suggestions that guide its behavior strategies, and T_avail ⊆ B_tool the set of tools it may use. A tool entry m_tool = <n, d_func, c_impl, ω_doc> (Eq. 3): n is the tool name, d_func a functional description, c_impl the implementation code, ω_doc input/output documentation; tools are stored in Model Context Protocol (MCP) format (line 282). The paper states no scalar objective or loss; the loop is defined by these stores plus the forward-inference / backward-evolution procedure (line 262). | - | Formal definition of the stored assets (Eq. 1-3); not a measurement. | §3.1.1 Asset Memory, Eq. 1-3 (lines 264-289) | 280 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | For each sub-task s_i (the planner LLM π_θ first decomposes task q_t into S = {s_1, ..., s_k}, line 304), the Recruitment Function Γ(s_i) (Eq. 5) returns a stored asset m* when sim(s_i, M_A) ≥ δ and otherwise calls Create(s_i / M_E, Web); sim measures the similarity between the sub-task and the stored assets, δ is a confidence threshold, M_E is Experience Memory and Web is web search. The authors say this test decides whether the sub-task lies beyond the agent's current capability boundary. Appendix A.5 specifies sim as cosine similarity between the sub-task embedding and asset keys (agent: role ⊕ expertise ⊕ suggestions; tool: name ⊕ functional description), taking the top-1 agent above δ (Eq. 12) and the top-K tools above δ (Eq. 13). The saved text gives no value for δ or K and does not name the embedding model. | - | Decision rule for reuse versus creation (Eq. 5, 12, 13); not a measurement. | §3.2.2 Asset Recruitment, Eq. 5 (lines 306-315); Appendix A.5 (lines 1092-1103) | 313 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | What changes over time are two external stores, not the model: new expert agents and new executable tools are added to Asset Memory, and distilled memory items are added to Experience Memory M_E = E_agt ∪ E_tool. Each item e = <h_title, d_desc, U_case, κ_content> (Eq. 4): h_title is the title, d_desc describes the context, U_case lists applicable use cases, κ_content stores the distilled knowledge. For agent experience κ_content holds strategic insights from trajectory reflections (line 298); for tool experience it holds implementation guidelines distilled from tool creation and debugging (line 300). The backbone is GPT-5-chat used through prompts; the saved text describes no training or weight update (reader's absence check). | - | Definition of the experience store (Eq. 4) and of what the loop modifies; not a measurement. | §3.1.2 Experience Memory, Eq. 4 (lines 290-300) | 296 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | The feedback signal is an LLM-as-a-Judge, not ground truth: given task q_t, execution trajectory tau_t and answer a_t, the Judge returns r_t in {0,1} (success or failure) and critique comments c_t naming strengths and weaknesses (Eq. 7). The authors assume ground-truth labels are inaccessible during backward evolution to simulate the real world, and add that such supervision could further help when available. The saved text does not name the judge model and does not say whether the judge is the GPT-5-chat backbone or a different model. | - | Signal definition: binary judge verdict r_t plus free-text critique c_t per task; no labels used during evolution. | §3.3.1 Trajectory Evaluation, Eq. 7 and footnote 3 (lines 327-335) | 330 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | After every task the system reflects on the trajectory and the judge output, e_new = Reflection(τ_t, r_t, c_t) (Eq. 10). When r_t = 1 (success generalization) it abstracts high-level guidelines: for agents, strategic advice and coordination patterns for specific roles; for tools, effective implementation patterns and usage recipes. When r_t = 0 or c_t indicates substantial debugging (failure diagnosis), the new item encodes anti-patterns and failure-fix pairs. Items are merged by union, M_E ← M_E ∪ {e_new} (Eq. 11). Reuse: at execution each sub-task's recruited agent is augmented with experiences retrieved from E_agt (line 324), and tool creation retrieves from E_tool (Eq. 6). | - | Description of how trajectories become stored memory items and how they are reused; not a measurement. | §3.3.3 Experience Memory Evolution, Eq. 10-11 (lines 546-561); §3.2.3 (line 324) | 556 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Missing capabilities are created, not searched: a new tool is sampled from the LLM conditioned on the sub-task, relevant tool experiences retrieved from E_tool, and web search results, m_tool^new ~ π_θ(s_i / Retrieve(s_i, E_tool), Web(s_i)) (Eq. 6); a new expert agent is synthesized by prompting π_θ with requirements derived from s_i (line 322). Appendix A.4 describes tool creation in three stages: a formal tool specification (name, description, input parameters, output format, step-wise core logic); grounding via web search of external documentation (GitHub tool descriptions, Stack Overflow debugging discussions) plus an Experience Memory query using the specification; then implementation as an MCP-compliant tool. | - | Description of the asset-creation step; not a measurement. | §3.2.2 Creation, Eq. 6 (lines 316-322); Appendix A.4 (lines 1030-1090) | 317 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Keep-or-repair rule for each newly created asset m_new (Eq. 8): it is kept unchanged only if r_t = 1 and Valid(m_new, c_t) holds; otherwise, including when the judge scored the task r_t = 0, Improve(m_new, c_t) runs a self-correction loop that revises the asset from the critique and test failures and regenerates tests until validation passes; the finalized asset is then added, M_A <- M_A U {m_final} (Eq. 9). The prose says this phase 'determines which newly created assets should be preserved' (line 337) and that backward evolution retains 'high-quality' assets (lines 245, 326), but Eq. 8-9 contain no discard branch and the saved text states no iteration cap or what happens if validation never passes; the text is therefore internally inconsistent on whether any created asset is rejected. Experience items have no stated acceptance filter; every distilled item is merged into M_E (Eq. 11, line 557). | - | Acceptance rule for assets as written in Eq. 8-9: pass all LLM-generated tests (and judge success) or iterate repairs until they pass; no discard rule or cap is specified, although lines 245, 326 and 337 describe selective retention. Not a measurement. | §3.3.2 Asset Memory Evolution, Eq. 8-9 (lines 336-350) | 346 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | data_generation | Validation tests are generated, not given: Valid(m_new, c_t) has the LLM synthesize test cases from the judge's critique c_t and executes the new asset against them; an asset passes only if it clears all tests. The tests therefore derive from an LLM critique, with no ground-truth labels (line 330); the saved text does not state how many tests are generated or their form. | - | Source of the generated tests: LLM-synthesized from the judge critique; pass criterion = all tests pass. Not a measurement. | §3.3.2 Asset Memory Evolution, after Eq. 8 (line 345) | 345 | primary | supported |
| 8 | result | Using the GPT-5-chat backbone for every baseline the authors ran (the OpenAI Deep Research row is copied from its paper and covers GAIA only), Mem2Evolve reaches an average Pass@1 of 70.24% over the eight benchmarks. That is ahead of the strongest capability-centric baseline Alita (63.78), the strongest experience-centric baseline AFLOW (58.44) and the best naive LLM setting, GPT-5-Chat CoT (51.71) (Table 2). The paper prints the margins 6.46 / 11.80 / 18.53 as percentages, but they are absolute differences in average score points (calc. from Table 2). The GAIA 'Total' column is not aggregated the same way across rows. Mem2Evolve's 76.31 is the unweighted mean of L1-L3, while Alita's 72.73 equals the question-weighted total over 53/86/26 questions (calc.). The printed +6.46 margin over Alita therefore mixes two aggregations; either consistent aggregation gives about +7.0 (unweighted +7.10; question-weighted +6.99, calc.). Each Table 2 run starts with no memory apart from the web search tool (line 652). That memory then accumulates on the scored test tasks is a reader's inference from lines 326, 579 and 652, which the text does not state outright. The number of runs is not stated. | 70.24% avg; +6.46 vs Alita; +11.80 vs AFLOW; +18.53 vs naive LLM | Table 2 'Avg.' recomputes (calc.) as the unweighted mean of the eight per-benchmark scores, within 0.02 of every printed value. The eight scores are GAIA Total, ALFWorld success rate, HotpotQA EM, 2WikiMultihopQA EM, AIME24/25 Pass@1, TravelPlanner average of five sub-metrics and WebShop success rate (Table 5, lines 1158-1194). The text itself does not define 'Avg.'. The caption labels every column Pass@1 (line 545). GAIA Total is an unweighted level mean for Mem2Evolve but question-weighted for Alita (calc.). Margins are absolute points. | §4.2 Main Results (line 577); Table 2 (lines 351-545) | 577 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## s005 — Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2305.16291v2 · version read: arXiv 2305.16291v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v2 text also saved, used only for the author-affiliation title block) · v1: 2023-05-25
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), March 2024, journal paper (ISSN 2835-8856); certifications J2C (Journal to Conference) with event certification iclr.cc/ICLR/2025/Journal_Track
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper gives no formula for its objective. It poses open-ended lifelong learning in Minecraft, a game with no predefined end goal (line 96), and drives it with a GPT-4 automatic curriculum whose overarching goal is 'discovering as many diverse things as possible'; the curriculum proposes progressively harder tasks from the exploration progress and the agent's state, and the authors describe this as an in-context form of novelty search. | - | Problem framing, not a measurement; the saved text contains no objective function, so there are no symbols to define. | §1 Introduction | 104 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Nothing inside the model changes: Voyager queries a black-box GPT-4 through prompting and in-context learning, without parameter access or gradient-based training or fine-tuning. What grows is outside the model: a skill library of executable action programs (line 105) and the curriculum's lists of completed and failed tasks (line 123; pseudocode lines 972-976), both of which are fed back into later prompts. | - | Description of the modified components (external skill library and task lists; model weights fixed); not a measurement. | §1 Introduction | 103 | primary | supported |
| 2 | mechanism | Each skill that GPT-4 generates and that passes verification is added to a vector database whose key is the embedding of a GPT-3.5-generated description of the program and whose value is the program code itself. For a new curriculum task, GPT-3.5 first writes a general suggestion for solving it, which is combined with environment feedback as the query context, and the top-5 relevant skills are retrieved into the code-generation prompt. | top-5 retrieved skills | Design of what is stored (key = embedding of a program description, value = the program) and how many skills are retrieved per query; not a measurement. Embeddings come from text-embedding-ada-002 (line 158). | §2.2 Skill Library, Figure 4 caption | 129 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Task success is judged by a second GPT-4 instance acting as a critic (self-verification) instead of manually coded success checkers: given Voyager's current state and the task (plus task context, line 1722), it says whether the program achieved the task and, if not, gives a critique suggesting how to complete it. Environment feedback (the chat log produced by bot.chat() calls inside the control primitive APIs and in the generated code, lines 148, 1281) and interpreter execution errors (line 150) are the other two feedback types. The refinement loop repeats until self-verification validates completion, but it is capped: if the agent is still stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, the curriculum is queried for another task (line 153; pseudocode lines 949-976). | - | Signal = the GPT-4 critic's boolean success judgment plus a text critique when the task fails, computed from the agent state (Appendix A.5.1 excludes recently seen blocks and nearby entities, line 1718), the task, the task context and few-shot examples (lines 1716-1726); an LLM judge, not an environment-provided reward (Table A.2 lists Voyager's rewards as None, line 1867) or ground truth. | §2.3 Iterative Prompting Mechanism | 152 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | Within a task, each round of code generation executes the generated program; the resulting environment feedback and code-interpreter execution errors are put into GPT-4's prompt for the next round of code refinement, together with the previous round's code and the critic's critique (§2.2 item 3, line 137). The code-generation prompt asks GPT-4 to first explain why the last round's code failed, then plan step by step, then write code (line 1293). | - | Within-task refinement loop (what is carried from one round to the next); not a measurement. | §2.3 Iterative Prompting Mechanism | 153 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | A program is kept as a skill only when self-verification validates task completion; it is then added to the skill library and the curriculum is asked for a new objective. If the agent is still stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, the curriculum is queried for another task; the pseudocode records such a task as failed (line 976), the failed-task list is part of the curriculum prompt (line 123), and the curriculum can reattempt the task later (line 272). | 4 rounds of code generation per task (cap) | Acceptance rule as described: a candidate program is committed if and only if the GPT-4 critic returns success within at most 4 code-generation rounds (pseudocode lines 949-976); not a measurement. | §2.3 Iterative Prompting Mechanism; Appendix A.1 Pseudocode 1 | 153 | primary | supported |
| 6 | data_generation | During lifelong exploration, tasks are proposed one at a time by the GPT-4 automatic curriculum rather than drawn from a fixed set (the zero-shot generalization test instead uses four fixed unseen tasks, lines 208 and 214-217, and the manual and random curriculum ablations use fixed lists, lines 1997-1999). The curriculum system prompt instructs GPT-4 to avoid tasks that need information beyond the player's status to verify (examples: 'Placing 4 torches' and 'Dig a 2x1x2 hole', which require visual confirmation from the screen) and to avoid all placing, building, planting and trading tasks; this is a prompt instruction, not an enforced filter, and the authors report that the curriculum still occasionally proposes unachievable tasks (line 275). Completion of each generated task is judged by the GPT-4 self-verification critic rather than a hand-coded checker (line 152). | - | Instruction in the curriculum system prompt (Prompt 1, criterion 8, line 1112); the directives are meant to keep proposed tasks achievable and verifiable (line 991); compliance with the instruction is not measured in the text; not a measurement. | Appendix A.3.4, Prompt 1, criterion 8 | 1112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | environment_knowledge | Environment knowledge enters the curriculum as 'additional context': GPT-3.5 asks itself questions about the current state and progress, each paired with a concept used to retrieve the most relevant document from a Minecraft wiki knowledge base, and answers them using that document. The authors say the wiki is optional in practice because GPT-3.5 already understands Minecraft game mechanics, and that it becomes useful when the model was not pre-trained on the domain. | - | Design description of an external knowledge source (retrieved documents plus model prior knowledge), not something learned from interaction; the warm-up schedule adds this context only after 15 completed tasks (Table A.1, lines 1076-1078); not a measurement. | Appendix A.3.2 Additional Context | 1021 | primary | supported |
| 8 | setting | Models: OpenAI gpt-4-0314 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 for text completion and text-embedding-ada-002 for embeddings; all temperatures 0 except the automatic curriculum, which uses 0.1 for task diversity. Environment: MineDojo with Mineflayer JavaScript APIs for motor control, so actions are code over high-level APIs rather than screen pixels and low-level controls (line 164). Baselines ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT, designed for NLP tasks, were re-interpreted by the authors to run in MineDojo (line 160). | temperature 0; curriculum 0.1 | Experimental configuration; not a measurement. GPT-4 is used for the curriculum, code generation and self-verification; GPT-3.5 for self-asked questions and answers and for skill descriptions (lines 125, 129, 152). | §3.1 Experimental Setup | 158 | primary | supported |
| 9 | result | In the lifelong exploration run, Voyager discovers 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations, stated as 3.3x as many novel items as its counterparts; AutoGPT lags and ReAct and Reflexion make little progress. Three trials were run per method (line 2015). The per-trial item lists in Appendix B.4.1 contain 63, 58 and 67 items for Voyager and 11, 22 and 25 for AutoGPT (calc. count), so 63 matches trial 1 and roughly the three-trial mean of 62.7 (calc.), and 3.3x roughly equals 63 divided by the AutoGPT mean of 19.3 (calc.); the text does not say which aggregate is used. | 63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations; 3.3× | Count of distinct Minecraft items obtained during the learning run itself (up to 160 prompting iterations; no held-out split), GPT-4 agent, compared with baselines. | 12 | result | Removing self-verification lowers the discovered-item count by 73%; the authors call self-verification the most important of the feedback types and say it decides when to move on to a new task or reattempt a previously unsuccessful one (the drops for the w/o environment feedback and w/o execution errors ablations are shown only in Fig. 9, not stated in the text). | 0 | problem_definition | The paper formalizes prompt optimization for an LM program as Phi* = argmax over V->S of (1//D/) * sum over (x, x') in D of mu(Phi_{V->S}(x), x'). Symbols: Phi is an LM program of m modules, each module i defined by a prompt template p_i that contains variables (open slots) v; V is the set of all variables used by the prompt templates of Phi; V->S is a total assignment of those variables to strings S; Phi_{V->S} is the program run under that assignment; mu is the metric; D is the trainset, with inputs X and optional metadata X' (such as labels); (x, x') is one input with its metadata; /D/ is the number of training examples. The objective is thus the mean task metric of the whole program over the trainset. | - | Formal objective (section 2, symbol definitions on lines 144-147, equation on line 149); not a measurement. Line 151 adds that mu supervises only the entire task, so every variable in V is latent, and that designers generally have small datasets and small budgets of LM calls. | §2 Problem Statement (lines 144-149) | 146 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The optimized variables are, for each module's prompt, one variable over free-form instructions and a set of K variables over demonstrations (few-shot examples); all other variables of Phi are set to constant values. The setting assumes no access to LM weights, log-probabilities, or handwritten metrics or labels for intermediate stages (line 106), so the change is to prompt text outside the models. | - | Description of the search space (what a candidate may modify); not a measurement. | §2 Problem Statement; §1 Introduction (line 106) | 152 | primary | supported |

Table 1 is at lines 200-248. | §1 Introduction; Table 1 | 106 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | Demonstrations are bootstrapped by running the program on training data: an input-output pair (x, x') is sampled from D, Phi(x) is run to produce a full trace tau, and if mu(Phi(x), x') >= lambda the trace is assumed correct and the inputs/outputs of each module in the trace become candidate few-shot examples; this repeats until N sets of K examples per module exist. MIPRO's Step 1 uses the same process (Figure 4 caption, line 191). The bootstrapping runs use a teacher model: Llama-3-8B (the task model) by default, but GPT-4o for ScoNe and HoVer (line 264), so on those two tasks the demonstrations are GPT-4o traces rather than the task model's own trajectories. | - | Stored item = per-module input/output pairs from traces whose final output scores at or above threshold lambda (§4.1 line 180; Appendix F.1 line 1128 states the test as the output being 'equivalent to y'); traces generated by the teacher LM named on line 264; reused as few-shot demonstrations in module prompts; not a measurement. | §4.1 Bootstrap Random Search (Initialize); §3.1 Bootstrapping Demonstrations | 180 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | setting | Evaluation runs on CybORG CAGE-2, a cyber-defense gym modelled as a POMDP: a blue defender protects a 13-host enterprise network against an automated red attacker (B_line) over a 30-step horizon. Public 30-step B_line reference points quoted by the authors: CardiffUni PPO -3.47 (DRL top score), rule-based heuristic -58.83, random action -154.06, no-action -218.65; the authors call a return below -100 a major failure and below -150 a catastrophic failure. The four LLM families are Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite (primary), Grok-4-Fast, Llama-4-Maverick and Qwen3-235B (Table 2, line 286); all agents and learning agents in one run use the same LLM (lines 130, 132). | 13 hosts; 30 steps; -3.47 / -58.83 / -154.06 / -218.65 | Environment description plus external reference returns (episode return = sum of per-step rewards, <= 0, closer to 0 is better). The four reference points are cited by the authors from Kiely et al. 2023 and the CardiffUni repository, not measured by them. | §4 Experimental Setup, 'Evaluation Task and Environment: CybORG CAGE-2' | 333 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The objective is an episode return as close to zero as possible. The per-step reward r_step <= 0 penalizes both ongoing compromise and the operational cost of the defender's actions; the evaluation return is R = sum of r_step (Table 2, line 322), written in Appendix F as R = sum_{t=1..30} r_t over the T = 30 steps of an episode (line 2228). The defender sees only host-level indicators (processes, connections, files) and must infer the attacker's latent state. Per step it picks one action: Monitor, Analyse h, Remove h, Restore h or Decoy h, where h is a host (lines 777-785). | - | Definition of the reward/return used as objective. Symbols: r_step (= r_t) = scalar per-step reward at step t, non-positive; R = episode return; T = 30 = episode length in steps; h = target host. Not a measurement. | Appendix B, 'Partial Observability and Reward' (with Table 2 Metrics, line 322; Appendix F, line 2228) | 787 | primary | supported |
| 2 | problem_definition | FORGE runs N copies ('instances') of the Planner-Analyst-ActionChooser hierarchy in parallel. Instance i in {1..N} keeps memory M_i = (M_i^P, M_i^A, M_i^C), one part each for the Planner (P), Analyst (A) and ActionChooser (C). Persistent memory holds user-set instructions and knowledge (only the ActionChooser and the learning agents get the environment action reference table; the Planner gets no action knowledge, so its strategy is attributable to learned artifacts); dynamic memory starts empty and accumulates learned knowledge artifacts. The representation is the experimental variable: Rules (ordered conditional heuristics), Examples (ReAct-style demonstrations: thought, tool, observation, answer) or Mixed (both, generated separately over the same context). Algorithm 2 adds S stages, k_A attempts per stage, graduation threshold theta and failure trigger tau; the settings used are N = 10, S = 6, k_A = 3, tau = -1.1 (per-step reward) and theta = -15 (episode return) (Table 2, lines 314 and 318). | - | Formal setup of the protocol state; symbols as listed in the claim. Not a measurement. | §3.1 Agent Architecture (with Table 2, Protocol Params and Hyperparameters) | 156 | primary | supported |
| 3 | what_is_changed | Only the prompt-injected dynamic memory changes: no weight updates, and no external oracle or stronger model (the same LLM generates actions and synthesizes memory, line 130). Memory is stored on disk and re-injected into each agent's system prompt at every attempt, with a fixed capacity to prevent unbounded context growth. Rules enter via a <reflection_knowledge> section and Examples via a <TOOL_USE_EXAMPLES> section (Appendix C, lines 791 and 812); in the released artifact the dynamic memory lives in YAML files such as reflection_knowledge.yaml and reflection_examples.yaml, updated during training (lines 734-737). | - | Description of the modified component; not a measurement. The capacity value is not printed in the saved text (the word 'capacity' occurs only on this line). | §3.1 Agent Architecture; Appendix C; Appendix A.1 | 157 | primary | supported |
| 4 | signal | CAGE-2 gives only a scalar per-step reward with no natural-language feedback, so the agent must infer from numerical signals alone what went wrong. FORGE uses this reward twice: a per-step reward below the failure trigger tau aborts the episode and starts reflection (tau = -1.1, line 318), and after each stage a frozen checkpoint return R_i decides graduation and champion selection (Algorithm 2, lines 185-195). The authors state that tau = -1.1 is derived from the environment's reward structure (line 492). | - | Description of the feedback signal. tau is compared with each per-step reward r_step; R_i is the return of a frozen single-episode checkpoint probe per instance (line 494). Not a measurement. | §1 Introduction, property (3) of CAGE-2 | 110 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Inner loop (Algorithm 1): the agent acts until episode end or until a per-step reward drops below tau; on failure the episode is aborted and the full trajectory captured (snapshot = trajectories, M_i, metadata, environment state; line 145). A learning agent on the same LLM (Reflector for Rules, Exemplifier for Examples, both for Mixed) analyzes the trajectory up to the failure point together with the environment state and synthesizes a knowledge artifact: a conditional heuristic or a structured interaction demonstration. The artifact is appended to memory and the episode restarts from step 0, up to k_A attempts per stage. Run in isolation, this loop is the Reflexion baseline (line 162). | - | Description of how failed trajectories become stored memory; not a measurement. | §3.2 Inner Loop: Failure-Triggered Reflexion (Algorithm 1) | 161 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | After each stage a frozen checkpoint evaluation gives a return R_i per active instance; the active (non-graduated) instance with the highest checkpoint return is the champion, and its complete memory state replaces the memory of every other active instance. The replacement is destructive and full, not an interpolation of rule sets (line 269), and favors convergence over population diversity. The checkpoint is a frozen single-episode probe used during training for graduation and champion selection; the main results come from a separate post-session evaluation of frozen instances (lines 494, 502), except where the paper explicitly reports checkpoint values (the -3.60 peak, line 505; checkpoint-score volatility in Figure 5B, line 511; per-stage checkpoint returns in Tables 19-20, line 3248). | - | Acceptance rule for memory: argmax of single-episode checkpoint return among active instances, then full broadcast (Algorithm 2 lines 195-199); not a measurement. Because checkpoint values are also reported, every number taken from this paper must be labelled checkpoint (single episode, selection signal) or post-session evaluation. | §3.3 Outer Loop, 'Champion Broadcast' (Algorithm 2 lines 15-17) | 273 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | selection_rule | Instances whose checkpoint return exceeds the graduation threshold theta are graduated: their memory is frozen and they are excluded from all subsequent stages (theta = -15 episode return, line 318, which the authors equate with roughly 10x better than a random agent, line 492). Graduation is meant to lock strong solutions before the next broadcast can overwrite them and to save compute. After all stages every instance, graduated or not, gets a final frozen evaluation; with broadcast disabled the protocol reduces to parallel independent Reflexion (line 276). | - | Freezing rule: checkpoint return R_i > theta; not a measurement. | §3.3 Outer Loop, 'Graduation and Early Stopping' (Algorithm 2 lines 12-13) | 275 | primary | supported |
| 8 | result | Post-session evaluation, FORGE vs zero-shot, best representation per model: Gemini -189.6 -> -24.5 (Examples, 7.7x), Qwen -103.3 -> -24.3 (Examples, 4.3x), Llama -113.1 -> -28.3 (Examples, 4.0x), Grok -58.4 -> -33.7 (Rules, 1.7x). FORGE beats Reflexion in all 12 model-representation conditions. The best single checkpoint return was -3.60 (Gemini Rules), near the DRL top score of -3.47, while post-session means stay lower. | -189.6 -> -24.5 (7.7x); -103.3 -> -24.3 (4.3x); -113.1 -> -28.3 (4.0x); -58.4 -> -33.7 (1.7x); best checkpoint -3.60 | Mean episode return (sum of 30 per-step rewards, <= 0, closer to 0 is better) of frozen instances in post-session evaluation; factor = zero-shot mean / FORGE mean (calc. check 189.6/24.5 = 7.74). Runs: Gemini 7 FORGE sessions per representation with 1-2 evaluations per instance; other models 3-4 sessions with >= 2 evaluations per instance (line 494); N = 10 instances per session. Evolve vs held-out: training stages and evaluation both use the CAGE-2 B_line 30-step scenario (stages use uniquely seeded environments, line 175); no other attacker or environment is evaluated (line 528). | §5.1 'Performance over Zero-Shot and Reflexion' (Table 3) | 505 | primary | supported |
| 9 | result | FORGE improves post-session evaluation return by 29-72% over Reflexion in all 12 model-representation conditions; the no-graduation variant also beats Reflexion in all 12, which the authors read as confirming that champion broadcast is the essential mechanism. Reflexion instances stay volatile across stages while FORGE steadily compresses score variance (Figure 5B). | 29-72%; 12 of 12 conditions | Delta Refl column of Table 3: relative improvement of FORGE's mean post-session return over the Reflexion baseline mean under the same model, representation and training budget (calc. check, Gemini Rules: (62.7 - 30.6)/62.7 = 51%, matching the printed 51%). Reflexion instances per condition: 30-70 (Table 1/Table 8). | §5.1 'Population Broadcast vs. Isolated Reflexion' | 517 | primary | supported |
| 10 | result | The authors state that the share of evaluation episodes below -100 falls from about 90% under zero-shot to about 1% under the strongest configurations, read from Figure 7A (all models pooled; lines 521, 525). The ~90% zero-shot figure is not reproducible from the paper's tables: Table 12's listed zero-shot scores fall below -100 for 10/10 Gemini, 1/20 Grok, 7/10 Llama and 3/10 Qwen rows (calc. pooled 21/50 = 42%), and Grok's zero-shot mean of -58.4 over 100 episodes caps the pooled share at about 84% (calc.); only Gemini alone matches ~90%. The authors attribute FORGE's effect to four mechanisms: removing the heavy tail of low zero-shot returns, compressing variance, population-level distillation via champion broadcast, and graduation-based early stopping to reduce compute. | ~90% -> ~1% of episodes below -100 | Tail-risk metric: frequency of episodes with return < -100 (Table 2, line 331, where it is called 'catastrophic'; line 333 calls < -100 'major' and < -150 'catastrophic'). ~90% and ~1% are author readings of a figure, not table values; '~1%' holds for the strongest configurations only, not the mean over all FORGE conditions; the ~90% zero-shot value conflicts with Tables 1, 3 and 12 (calc.). For comparison, Reflexion failure rates in Table 8 range from 17% to 50% by model and representation (lines 1357-1428). | §6 Discussion | 525 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 11 | cost_time | In the replicated Gemini study the authors read from Figure 4 Panel B that Rules consumed ~106M total tokens vs ~177M for Examples and ~188M for Mixed, which they call a ~40% cost reduction (Rules vs Examples, line 507), attributed to shorter prompts and fewer active instances due to faster graduation. The paper's own tables show a much smaller gap: Table 11 per-instance adaptation tokens for Gemini FORGE are Rules 7.3M, Examples 8.4M and Mixed 10.2M (calc. Rules 13% below Examples), the same means as Table 9; the text does not reconcile these with the figure. No-graduation variants are stated to use more tokens in every representation because all 10 instances stay active for all 6 stages, which the authors take as confirming that graduation's primary contribution is compute savings. | ~106M / ~177M / ~188M total tokens; ~40% | Token Cost = total prompt + completion tokens over training + evaluation (Table 2, line 328), Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite FORGE study; ~106M/~177M/~188M are approximate readings of Figure 4B, with the aggregation unit (per session or summed over 7 sessions) not stated. Calc.: the Table 5 τ-sweep totals are 98-113M per run, the same scale as ~106M, which suggests but does not prove a per-session figure. This is the cost of the improvement process plus its evaluation, compared across memory representations; it is not a FORGE-vs-baseline saving and not the per-episode inference cost of the improved agent. ~40% = Rules vs Examples (calc.: 1 - 106/177 = 40%; vs Mixed 1 - 106/188 = 44%). Tables 9/11 adaptation tokens give about 13% (calc.). Tokens only; no dollars or time. | §5.1 'Token Cost Analysis' (Figure 4B) | 509 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 12 | cost_time | Without graduation all 10 instances stay active through all 6 stages and, per the authors' reading of Figure 6B (all models pooled), consume roughly twice the adaptation tokens per instance by S6. | 0 | problem_definition | Given an initial prompt p_0 and i.i.d. training data D_tr = {(x_1,y_1),...,(x_n,y_n)} of input/output text pairs (line 66), with every prompt p drawn from the space L of coherent natural language (line 67) and a black-box API LLM_p(x) that returns a likely text continuation y of the concatenation of p and x (line 68), the algorithm iteratively refines p_0 into p-hat, an approximation of the optimal prompt p* = argmax over p in L of m(p, D_te), where m(.) is some metric function and D_te is in-domain test or development data. | - | Formal objective; not a measurement. In the experiments the metric m is F1 score (line 199). | §2 Discrete Prompt Optimization with Nonparametric 'Gradient Descent' (lines 66-69) | 69 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Only the prompt text is edited: the authors say the algorithm optimizes the language of prompts rather than selecting few-shot examples, and in the §3.4 experiments a randomly selected pair of few-shot examples was held constant while the other parts of the prompt were optimized. The LLM is used only through a black-box API (line 68), and the conclusion says the method improves prompts with no hyperparameter tuning or model training (line 326). | - | Description of the optimized component; not a measurement. | §3.2 Setup | 200 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The same metric function m, F1 score, is the optimization target for all tasks; the authors report that scoring prompts by the model's log-likelihood did not help in preliminary experiments and that APIs like ChatGPT and GPT4 did not provide log likelihoods at the time. The gradient step is driven by the prompt's errors on a minibatch, i.e. examples with LLM_p(x_i) != y_i (Algorithm 2 step 2, line 123). | - | Optimization target = F1 of the prompt's predictions against the dataset labels; test results are reported as binary F1 (line 196). Not a measurement. | §3.2 Setup; Algorithm 2 | 199 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | In Related Work the authors contrast RL prompt editors, which are tied to numerical reward functions, with their own scoring function, which they say could be anything, even a text comment from a user, adding the parenthetical 'we use GPT itself for this'. The sentence does not say which step GPT scores; §3.2 names F1 as the optimization metric (line 199). | - | Authors' description of the admissible scoring signal; not a measurement. | §4 Related Work | 323 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Expansion step: sample a minibatch, run the current prompt on it and collect the errors; plug the errors into template Nabla, which asks the LLM to describe problems with the prompt that could have led to these mistakes (the natural-language 'gradients'); give the gradients to prompt delta, which asks the LLM to edit the current prompt to fix the described problems (line 115); then make extra candidates with a paraphrasing LLM_mc that rewords candidates while keeping their meaning (line 116). Between iterations Algorithm 1 carries only the beam: B_{i+1} is Select_b over the union C of all expansions of the prompts in B_i (lines 90-102). | - | Algorithm description (Algorithms 1 and 2); not a measurement. | §2.2.1 Expansion Step; Algorithm 2 (lines 117-131) | 114 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Nabla must consider the current prompt p_0 plus p_0's behaviour on a minibatch (particularly the errors) and generate a natural-language summary of p_0's flaws, which becomes the gradient g; the text gradients represent directions in a semantic space that make the prompt worse. The same Nabla and delta prompts are used for all tasks (footnote 2); the Appendix A.1 Nabla template asks for {num_feedbacks} reasons why the prompt could have gotten the listed examples wrong (lines 459-466). Step size is 'adaptive': the LLM decides the edit size (footnote 3, line 81). | - | Algorithm description; not a measurement. | §2.1 Gradient descent with Prompts; Appendix A.1 | 78 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Selection keeps the b most promising candidates on the beam (line 133). Because evaluating each candidate on the entire training set is expensive, the authors map selection to best arm identification: the n arms are the n prompt candidates, an arm's hidden value is the prompt's performance on the underlying dataset, and pulling an arm means evaluating the prompt on a randomly chosen data point; the goal is to find the b best arms with as few pulls as possible (line 135). | - | Selection framing; not a measurement. | §2.2.2 Selection Step | 134 | primary | supported |
| 7 | selection_rule | UCB selection samples prompts from a proposal distribution of prompt performance, evaluates them on a random data subset, updates the distribution, and at the end keeps the b prompts with the highest weight (Algorithm 3); UCB-E favours exploration (line 162). Successive Rejects runs n-1 phases and drops the lowest-scoring prompt in each phase (lines 163-165); Successive Halving drops the bottom half per phase (line 189). The exploration parameter c was set to 2.0 for all experiments (line 238). After the last step Algorithm 1 returns p-hat as the argmax of m over the final beam B_r (line 106). | - | Acceptance rule: candidates survive on estimated metric m from sampled training data (Algorithms 3 and 4); not a measurement. | §2.2.2 Selection Step; Algorithms 1, 3, 4 | 136 | primary | supported |
| 8 | setting | Four classification tasks with Yes/No labels (lines 193-194; binary F1 per line 196): Jailbreak, a novel task whose dataset has 452 multilingual examples with human-annotated jailbreak labels; Ethos, 997 English online comments with hate-speech labels; Liar, 4000 English statements with context and lie labels; Sarcasm, 10,000 Arabic online comments with sarcasm labels. For each task 50 examples are randomly sampled for development and 150 for test; the reported results average 3 trials (Appendix C instead uses 12 replicates, line 535); test-set binary F1 is reported 'based on maxpooling over the final beam of candidates'. Unless otherwise stated the model is a January 2023 gpt-3.5-turbo via the Azure OpenAI API, temperature 0.0 during few-shot classification and 1.0 in all other contexts. | 452 / 997 / 4000 / 10,000 examples; 50 dev / 150 test; 3 trials; temperature 0.0 / 1.0 | Dataset sizes as printed; evaluation = test-set binary F1 averaged over 3 trials, 'based on maxpooling over the final beam of candidates' (line 196). ## s010 — How to Correctly do Semantic Backpropagation on Language-based Agentic Systems

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.03624v1 · version read: arXiv 2412.03624v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v1 text 2412.03624-pdf.txt consulted for the title block, the running header and the Implementation boxes) · v1: 2024-12-04
