| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | GASO (Graph-based Agentic System Optimization) is posed on a directed acyclic computational graph (V,E,H,Theta): V = nodes, each a variable of the system; E = directed edges; H = forward functions attached to nodes; Theta, a subset of V = the optimizable parameters (line 110). A node without predecessors holds either a user query Q or a parameter theta; every other node v = h_v(Predecessors(v)) (Eq. 1). The objective is to find Theta* minimizing the expected loss E_{Q~D}[l(Q, A(Q,Theta*))], where D = distribution of queries, A(Q,Theta) = the final response produced by the output node (the node with no successors), and l = a loss per query-response pair (e.g. negative utility). In addition a semantic alphanumeric feedback F(Q,A) is provided as an extra optimization signal; Q, A, Theta and node outputs are free-form strings. | - | Formal problem statement; not a measurement. | §2.1 The Graph-based Agentic System Optimization Problem | 119 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The semantic gradient of l(Q, A(Q,Theta)) with respect to a variable v, written nabla_v l_Q, is defined as directional information on how altering v can improve system performance for query Q. Semantic backpropagation starts from nabla_A l_Q (typically derived from the answer feedback F(Q,A)) and visits variables in reverse topological order (lines 138-139); for each successor w of v a backward function hat-h_w^v maps (Predecessors(w), w, nabla_w l_Q) to a direction nabla_v^w l_Q, the analogue of derivative times Jacobian in reverse-mode autodiff (line 144), and an aggregation function A_v, which generalizes the RMAD sum, combines these directions into nabla_v l_Q (line 147; Algorithm 1). | - | Definition of the credit-assignment quantity; not a measurement. | §3 Methods; §3.1 Semantic Backpropagation, Algorithm 1 | 137 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | Only the optimizable parameters Theta are changed: the paper restricts GASO to the special case with fixed edges (footnote 2), and the components are frozen large models with auxiliary optimizable parameters (line 87). In practice theta is a natural-language instruction, often a prompt prefix or suffix (line 124). In the question-answering experiments the graph has seven variables of which three are optimizable instructions, initialized identically across tasks to generic strings (line 271); the LIAR graph has 13 variables with six optimizable instructions (line 343). | - | Description of the search space; not a measurement. | §2.1, footnote 2 (also §1 line 87, §5.1 line 271, §5.2 line 343) | 112 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | The output feedback F(Q,A) is the fixed string 'The answer should be {desire}.', where {desire} is the target output given by the dataset (line 568); it is a template filled with the dataset target, not an LLM-generated judgment. On LIAR the loss is tied to correctness: Table 2 defines classification accuracy as the negative loss plus one (line 366); the text does not define the loss for GSM8K, BBH or BigCodeBench. Semantic gradients are computed only for queries whose loss exceeds the threshold, set to 0.5 with batch size two in all semantic-gradient-descent experiments (line 527). | - | Definition of the feedback string, the LIAR loss-accuracy relation and the loss threshold; not a measurement. Loss definitions for GSM8K, BBH and BCB are not given in the text. | Appendix C.1 Prompt templates (also Table 2 caption, Appendix B) | 568 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | The backward functions are implemented by querying an LLM that sees all inputs of h_w (i.e. all predecessors of w, so neighbouring nodes that share the successor) together with the semantic gradient of w; for an optimizable parameter theta, nabla_theta l_Q aggregates, over all successors w of theta, their semantic gradients and the other predecessors of h_w. The backward prompts (Figures 4 and 6) show the task, question or context, all hints, the output and the feedback, and ask how each hint should be changed, one line per hint (lines 639-641, 718). The no-neighbour variant used to emulate TextGrad shows only a single hint (Figure 7, lines 724-739). | - | Implementation of the credit-assignment step; not a measurement. | §3.1 Semantic Backpropagation (also Appendix C.1 Figures 4, 6, 7) | 160 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Semantic gradient descent (Algorithm 2) learns from the system's own forward runs on training queries: it repeatedly samples Q from D (the uniform distribution on the training set, line 287), runs the graph, and only when l(Q,A) exceeds threshold tau computes semantic gradients and adds them to G_v; once b such above-threshold queries are collected, the optimizer phi (an LLM, line 166) rewrites each theta conditioned on G_theta. What is stored is the per-iteration batch of gradients; for a parameter theta each gradient is a string with 'Input' (the other inputs of the node theta feeds, i.e. Predecessors(w) without theta), 'My output' (that node's output w) and 'Feedback received on my output' (the semantic gradient of w), concatenated over successors (line 160; Figure 8, lines 743-757). It is reused only as 'examples that it did not answer well' in the optimizer prompt (line 792), which forbids the keyword 'feedback' and example-specific content (line 810). Algorithm 2 resets G_v to the empty set at the start of every iteration (line 186). | - | Description of the learning loop and of what is stored and reused; not a measurement. | §3.2.2 The Optimization Procedure, Algorithm 2 (also Appendix C.1 Figures 8, 10) | 171 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | An update gate accepts the jointly proposed new parameter set {phi(theta,G_theta)} only if it performs better than the current set on a validation set, with L_Val(Theta) = sum over Q in Val of l(Q, A(Q,Theta)) (lines 175-177). The text words it as strict improvement ('outperform', line 175; 'performs better', line 345) and Algorithm 2 uses a strict < (line 194), while the displayed condition on line 180 uses <=. In the question-answering experiments the gate is computed on the training samples (line 286); on LIAR the same 50 training samples serve as both D and the validation set (line 348). An iteration is counted whenever a new parameter set is proposed, accepted or not (line 284); footnote 3 says TextGrad does not include such a gate but its official implementation does (line 175). | - | Acceptance rule: sum of per-query loss over the validation set (here the training samples), new vs current parameters; strict vs non-strict comparison is inconsistent in the text (lines 175, 180, 194, 345); not a measurement. | §3.2.2 The Optimization Procedure, footnote 3, Algorithm 2 (also §5.1 line 286, §5.2 line 348) | 175 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## s011 — Trace is the Next AutoDiff: Generative Optimization with Rich Feedback, Execution Traces, and LLMs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.16218v2 · version read: arXiv 2406.16218v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2024-06-23
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024), Main Conference Track, poster; DOI 10.52202/079017-2287

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | OPTO (Optimization with Trace Oracle) is defined by a tuple (Theta, omega, T): Theta is the parameter space, omega is the context of the problem, and T is the Trace Oracle. In each iteration the optimizer selects a parameter theta in Theta (which may be heterogeneous); T returns trace feedback tau = (f, g), where g is the execution trace represented as a DAG whose root nodes contain the parameter and f is the feedback given to exactly one output node of g; the optimizer then uses tau to update the parameter according to omega. omega is fixed per instance and carries invariant information to interpret f plus side-information such as desired properties of the parameters, while f may change with theta and g (lines 210-211). No scalar objective is required; Appendix F (Axiom 1, line 872) defines a solution as a theta that a verification oracle (a human, an ML model or a polynomial-time algorithm) accepts given (theta, omega, f). | - | Formal problem setup; not a measurement. | §2.1 Problem Definition of OPTO | 208 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Parameters are declared with two primitives: node wraps a Python object and can be set trainable, making it an OPTO parameter, optionally with natural-language constraints (line 234); bundle turns a Python method into an operator whose docstring and source code are recorded, and a trainable bundle makes the method's code itself a parameter (line 236). Parameters changed in the experiments include the numerical input x (§5.1, lines 353, 1167), two integer green-light durations in [15,90] for traffic control (line 356), a DSPy program's prompt_template plus its create_prompt and extract_answer functions (line 369), the Meta-World controller code (line 1495), the Battleship reason/act functions (Fig. 2), and in the TextGrad comparison the solutions or prompts of TextGrad's Solution- and Prompt-optimization tasks (line 438). Appendix A states OptoPrime has difficulty with parameters that cannot be compactly represented in text, which prevents it from optimizing neural network weights (line 804). | - | Description of the editable surface (what a parameter update may modify); not a measurement. | §3.1 Design of Trace | 236 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | In OPTO the output feedback f is generic: scores, gradients, natural-language hints or explanations, and console messages. Execution errors inside bundle-decorated methods are also turned into feedback through an exception node that ends the graph (lines 243, 855). The experiments use automatically generated feedback (line 796): a larger/smaller direction message for numerical optimization (line 353), an estimated vehicle-delay loss for traffic (line 357), a binary hit reward in text for Battleship (line 167), a text success flag plus return for Meta-World (line 1494), and template correct/wrong messages for BBH (line 1471). | - | Type of feedback signal passed to the optimizer; not a measurement. | §2.1 Problem Definition of OPTO | 209 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | For BBH training of Trace and Trace-CoT the feedback is template-based: the positive message is 'The answer is correct! No need to change anything.', and the negative message states the expected answer ('We expect the output of your answer to be {ANSWER}') and asks to modify the prompt and relevant parts of the program (line 1471). Every incorrectly answered training example therefore reveals its ground-truth answer to the optimizer; a correct one only confirms that the output matched it. The evaluation function is deliberately simple (extracting a segment or exact string matching), leaving the workflow to produce the expected format (line 1470). | - | Training feedback for the BBH prompt-and-code optimization (Trace and Trace-CoT), per training example (15 training examples per task, line 1471); the Fig. A.7 example code uses shorter answer-free strings and is illustrative only; not a measurement. | Appendix I.5 BigBench-Hard | 1471 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | As the decorated workflow runs, Trace records a DAG (line 242), extracts the minimal subgraph connecting the parameters and the output, and sends tau = (f, g) to the optimizer (line 243). OptoPrime renders this subgraph as a pseudo-algorithm problem: a code-execution report listing operator calls, operator descriptions from docstrings, input, intermediate and output values, the trainable variables with their constraints, and the feedback (Fig. 4; template sections in Fig. A.2, lines 929-945). It then sends one ReAct-CoT style LLM query asking for reasoning and suggested new values of the variables (line 343). | - | Description of how trace and feedback are turned into a parameter update; not a measurement. | §4 Design of the First OPTO Optimizer, Subgraph Representation | 338 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Because a single feedback may be uninformative (e.g. rewards without a description of how they are generated, line 345), OptoPrime has a basic memory module that stores past parameter-feedback pairs and reuses them as in-context examples; per the Fig. A.5 template each memory entry lists variable values and the feedback received (line 1015). Meta-World used a memory of size 10 (line 1496), and the authors find memory crucial on the traffic task (line 361). | - | Description of what is stored across iterations and how it is reused; not a measurement. | §4 Design of the First OPTO Optimizer, Optimization Memory | 346 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Section 4 states the update condition as whether a suggestion can be extracted from the LLM's response; the output prompt lets the LLM answer TERMINATE when no change or answer is needed (line 987). | 0 | problem_definition | The paper models a multi-agent system (MAS) as a directed graph G=(V,E), where /V/=N is the number of agents and E ⊆ V×V are the communication channels. For a user query Q the system runs T synchronous epochs; in epoch t agents act in a topological order π, and agent C_i outputs r_i^(t) = C_i(P_sys^(t), Q, {r_j^(t): C_j ∈ N^-(C_i)}), where P_sys^(t) comprises the global instructions (the text says 'including each agent's R_i', a symbol it does not define, presumably the role) and N^-(C_i) are the in-neighbours whose outputs are its context; an aggregation operator A fuses r_1^(t)..r_N^(t) into an interim solution a^(t), and epochs repeat until a preset limit or an early-stopping criterion, giving the final response a^(T) (lines 123-138). | 1 | what_is_changed | G-Memory acts on each agent's memory state Mem_i: an operator Φ(I^S, {sparsified interaction graphs}; Role_i, Q) evaluates the utility and relevance of each retrieved insight and sparsified interaction graph for the agent's role and the task, and initializes Mem_i with filtered insights, interaction snippets and summaries before the MAS reasoning epochs (Eq. 8). In the authors' implementation G-Memory is invoked once, at the onset of solving query Q; per-round or per-agent invocation is described as an option. The abstract states the gains come without any modifications to the original MAS frameworks (line 84). | - | Description of the intervention point; not a measurement. | §4.2 Bi-directional Memory Traversal, Eq. 8 | 191 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | After the memory-augmented MAS finishes a query it yields a^(T) and receives environmental feedback: execution status Ψ ∈ {Failed, Resolved}, token usage and other performance metrics. | 3 | mechanism | Retrieval and reuse for a new query Q: (1) coarse top-k retrieval over the query graph by cosine similarity of query embeddings v(·) (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, line 227) (Eq. 4); (2) expansion with the 1-hop neighbours of those queries on the query graph (Eq. 5); (3) upward traversal: every insight node whose supporting-query set Ω_k intersects the expanded set is retrieved (Eq. 6); (4) downward traversal: an LLM scorer R_LLM rates the relevance of each candidate historical query to Q, the top-M are kept, and an LLM graph sparsifier S_LLM builds a sparsified interaction graph for each by retaining dialogue elements (Eq. 7); implementations are in Appendix C. | - | Description of the retrieval procedure (what is read back from memory and how); not a measurement. | §4.1 Coarse-grained Memory Retrieval and §4.2 Bi-directional Memory Traversal, Eqs. 4-7 | 185 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | What is stored and how it grows. The interaction graph for a query has utterance nodes u_i=(A_i, m_i) (speaking agent, text) and edges (u_j, u_k) when u_j is transmitted to and inspires u_k; a query node is q_i=(Q_i, Ψ_i, G_inter^(Q_i)); an insight node is ι_k=(κ_k, Ω_k), insight text plus supporting queries, with hyperedges (ι_m, ι_n, q_j) (Eqs. 2-3, lines 141-156). After each task G-Memory traces each agent's utterances into the interaction graph and stores it; adds q_new=(Q, Ψ, G_inter^(Q)) with edges from the top-M relevant queries of Eq. 7 and from the supporting queries of the insights used (Eq. 9); creates a new insight ι_new=(J(G_inter^(Q), Ψ), {q_new}) via an LLM summarization function and links it to the utilized insights (Eq. 10); and adds q_new to Ω_k of every utilized insight (Eq. 11). | - | Description of the memory update from the system's own trajectories; not a measurement. | §4.3 Hierarchy Memory Update, Eqs. 9-11 (structures in §3, Eqs. 2-3) | 194 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | As written in the main-text Eqs. 9-11, the memory update does not branch on outcome: every completed query, resolved or failed, becomes a query node that carries its status Ψ (Eq. 9); Eq. 10 creates a new insight node from J(G_inter^(Q), Ψ) (the prose calls these 'possible new insights', line 201); and each utilized insight is re-inserted with q_new added to its supporting set, 'reflecting their relevance to this successful (or failed) application' (line 207). The equations only add nodes and edges or extend Ω_k; the filters described in the main text act at retrieval time (top-k similarity with k in {1,2}, 1-hop expansion, top-M LLM relevance with M in {2,3,4,5}, lines 227 and 464, and the role-specific utility filter Φ, line 191). ## s013 — From Knowledge to Noise: CTIM-Rover and the Pitfalls of Episodic Memory in Software Engineering Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.23422v1 · version read: arXiv 2505.23422v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; v1 is the only version) · v1: 2025-05-29
- Source class: institutional supplement · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the 1st Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models (REALM 2025), Vienna, July 2025, pages 411-427; Anthology ID 2025.realm-1.30; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.realm-1.30. This is an ACL 202…
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper states no formal objective or loss. Its research question is whether cross-task-instance memory (CTIM, the authors' name for memory made of knowledge extracted with experiential learning from past task instances, line 80) generalizes from ExpeL's domains to software engineering. The stated rationale is that experiential learning should help uncover a repository's structure and so reduce the number of turns spent exploring the codebase. The only formula in the text is the CTIM size cap c(n) = ceil(sqrt(n)) (line 181; see selection_rule). | - | Research question and motivation; not a measurement. | §1 Introduction (lines 80-82) | 82 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The agent's prompt context is changed; no weight update is described (the CTIM is provided for in-context learning, lines 184 and 324). AutoCodeRover, which splits the task into bug localization and patch generation (line 89), is augmented with a general CTIM and a repository-level CTIM. The full CTIM is placed in the user prompt at the start of the trajectory, not as a subset at each turn (line 91). Optionally the most task-similar past successful trajectory is added as an in-context exemplar (line 184). To collect training trajectories, AutoCodeRover is also extended with Reflexion-style retries (up to three attempts with self-reflection; §3.1 line 100; Figure 1 caption point A, line 83); the text does not state whether these retries are also used in the evaluation runs. | - | Description of the modified component (context/memory, not weights); not a measurement. | §2.3 Concurrent Work (line 91); Figure 1 caption (line 83) | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | The signal that selects experience is task success on SWE-bench. Only trajectories in which the agent solved the instance count as past successful trajectories. Failed attempts enter only as the failing half of success-failure tuples from the same instance (line 179), whose Reflexion self-reflections informed the next retry (line 100). The add/edit/upvote/downvote operations on CTIM items are issued by the distilling LLM (o1), which is restricted to modifying only the current repository's knowledge base in the repository-level phase (line 407). The text describes no per-item test or benchmark check before an item is kept. | - | Success = the agent solved the SWE-bench instance; the saved text does not define the resolution check further. Not a measurement. | §3.1 Systematic Collection of Past Successful Trajectories | 99 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | Experience collection: AutoCodeRover is extended with Reflexion, so an instance is retried up to three times with self-reflections informing each subsequent attempt. During training, AutoCodeRover's own patch-generation retries are cut from three to two. On the 401-instance train split this yields 183 successfully solved trajectories (calc.: 183/401 = 45.6%). These are supplemented with 53 successful AutoCodeRover trajectories from SWE-bench Lite, giving 236 past successful trajectories from which the CTIM is built. The Lite trajectories are experiences sourced from outside the system (Figure 1 caption, point B, line 83). | 183; 53; 236 | Counts of successful trajectories (instances solved) used as CTIM source material; 183 from CTIM-Rover's Reflexion-augmented runs on the train split with GPT-4o, 53 from prior AutoCodeRover runs on SWE-bench Lite. | §3.1 Systematic Collection of Past Successful Trajectories | 100 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Distillation reuses ExpeL's two settings. The first is sets of successful trajectories from distinct instances; the second is tuples of successful and failing attempts in the same instance. It also reuses ExpeL's item operations: add, edit, upvote and downvote, and an item whose importance falls below 0 is removed (footnote 4, line 181). Phase 1 builds a general CTIM. Phase 2 builds a repository-level CTIM by showing the distilling LLM (o1, line 175) only instances from one repository, with the general knowledge in the prompt as a reference; the LLM may modify only that repository's knowledge base (line 407). Stored items are natural-language knowledge items (called 'rules' in the prompts, line 408). Because source trajectories skew to django and sympy, the general 'sets' setting oversamples all non-django repositories to balance django against the rest (line 405). | - | Description of the knowledge-distillation procedure and what is stored; not a measurement. | §4.1 Repository-Level Knowledge Distillation (lines 179-181); Appendix D.1-D.2 (lines 405-408) | 179 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Exemplar reuse: the authors build a Milvus index of problem-statement embeddings using CodeT5 base. During evaluation, the most task-similar past successful trajectory is retrieved by cosine similarity with a 90% threshold, so an exemplar is shown only when a relevant one exists (about 62% of samples). | 90%; ≈62% | 90% = cosine-similarity threshold between problem-statement embeddings; ≈62% = share of test samples for which an exemplar passes the threshold. | §4.2 Exemplar retrieval | 184 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | CTIM items are kept or discarded by ExpeL-style importance counts: upvote/downvote change an item's importance, and an item below 0 is removed (footnote 4). CTIM-Rover doubles the initial importance of items, expecting longer intervals between instances where an item applies. It also caps the CTIM at c(n) = ceil(sqrt(n)), where c(n) is the maximum size of the CTIM and n is the number of available successful trajectories for constructing that CTIM. The stated aim is a concise set of high-quality insights that avoids degrading performance with noisy knowledge. calc.: if size counts items and n = 236 for the general CTIM, the cap is ceil(15.36) = 16 items; the text does not print the resulting CTIM sizes. | c(n)=⌈√n⌉; initial importance doubled | Retention rule for memory items (importance threshold 0, doubled initial importance, size cap); not a measurement. | §4.1 Repository-Level Knowledge Distillation | 181 | primary | supported |
| 7 | environment_knowledge | The repository-level CTIM is the environment knowledge. The authors state that it may provide insights on (1) the structure of the project, (2) entry points or data flow and architectural patterns, (3) coding conventions encountered, (4) common failure modes of the software's application domain (e.g., image processing in OpenCV), or (5) common bugs the agent encountered in the past, and they expect the agent to explore its environment more efficiently by reusing knowledge about previously explored areas (line 182). The repository-level distillation prompt explicitly targets repository structure, data-flow patterns and localized characteristics (line 407). The train/test partition mostly maintains repository overlap, which the authors call 'a critical prerequisite for the cross-repository knowledge transfer of repository-level knowledge' (line 304). The knowledge is held as text items; the text describes no explicit state model. In the evaluation, the repo-level-only configuration scored 31% vs 42% for the baseline (Table 1). | - | Categories of repository knowledge the distillation is meant to capture; not a measurement. | §4.1 Repository-Level Knowledge Distillation | 182 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 8 | result | On the authors' 45-instance test split of SWE-bench Verified (GPT-4o agent, line 175), full CTIM-Rover (by the Table 1 ablation rows: CTIM plus exemplar) resolves 40%, versus 42% for AutoCodeRover (Table 1, lines 127 and 136). | 0 | problem_definition | The paper defines a sparse sequential task scenario. The agent is continuously given tasks {tau_n}_{n=1}^{inf} (tau_n = the n-th task, an open-ended stream) as text instructions (e.g. 'Obtain water bucket') from the environment or as subgoal plans from an LLM. Task-relevant resources (e.g. water, cow) are assumed rare and sparsely distributed, so novel events from visited places must be memorized for future tasks. At every time step t the agent receives X_t = {i_t, l_t, t}: i_t in R^{H x W x C} is the first-person pixel view (H height, W width, C channels); l_t = (coord_x, coord_y, coord_z, yaw, pitch) in R^5 is the agent's 3D position and camera angles relative to its initial position l_0; t is the time step. | - | Problem statement in prose with observation notation (no optimization objective is written as a formula in §3); not a measurement. | §3 Method, 'Problem Setting' | 99 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The naive baseline is Steve-1, an instruction-following policy pi_Inst(a_t / h_t, tau_n) that outputs low-level mouse and keyboard controls a_t given h_t, the past pixel observation sequence i_{t-128:t}, and task tau_n. Its Transformer-XL is ineffective at recalling observations from a few thousand steps ago and quadratic complexity makes processing thousands of observations inefficient, so it cannot recall visited places or task-relevant resources seen in the past. §1 (lines 86-87) adds that this span is only the last 128 hidden states, a few seconds of gameplay at Minecraft's 20 Hz simulation, and that the agent then reverts to inefficient random exploration for each new task. | 128 (h_t = i_{t-128:t}) | Context window of the baseline policy, in past pixel frames (128 steps); not a performance measurement. | §3 Method, 'Instruction Following Policy' | 100 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | MrSteve keeps Steve-1 as the executor pi_Inst and wraps it with a Memory Module, the Place Event Memory M_t that stores novel events from visited places, and a Solver Module (Mode Selector, a count-based high-level goal selector pi_H-Nav and a low-level navigator pi_L-Nav called VPT-Nav). Per Algorithm 1 / §3 (line 121) the loop reads memory for the task; if candidates exist it navigates to the stored location and executes tau_n with Steve-1, otherwise it explores; the loop repeats every fixed step or when a new task is given. | - | Architecture description (which components are added around the controller); not a measurement. | §3 Method (Figure 2, Algorithm 1) | 101 | primary | supported |
| 3 | what_is_changed | The navigator is a trained component: VPT (initial model 'rl-from-foundation-2x', Table 5) is the starting policy; a goal embedding G_psi(l_t, g_t) (goal encoder = 4-layer MLP, line 1034) is added to the output of VPT's Transformer-XL, and PPO fine-tunes the goal encoder, LoRA parameters, policy pi_psi and value v_psi with a reward based on the distance to the goal (line 138). Appendix L.1 (line 1034): the reward is the increase or decrease in Euclidean distance between the goal and the agent, plus an additional reward of 100 when the agent reaches the goal within 3 blocks. Reading compares the task embedding tau_hat_n = Enc_t(tau_n) (MineCLIP text encoder) with stored e_t by cosine similarity. The simplest variant is a FIFO memory of capacity N that drops the oldest frame; the paper notes its read cost grows linearly with memory size and that it loses task-relevant frames from visited places. | H=16 | Definition of the stored record (video embedding, position, time); H = number of past frames encoded; not a measurement. | §3.1 Memory Module | 125 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Retention rule of Place Event Memory: each place cluster M_k (frames grouped by top-down location and yaw) is subdivided into event clusters E_i^k with center embeddings; after the place cluster accumulates a set number of new frames, DP-Means over their MineCLIP embeddings forms candidate event clusters, and a new cluster whose center has cosine similarity above threshold c with an existing cluster is merged into it (the two are 'indistinct'); otherwise it is kept as a new event. When capacity is exceeded, the oldest frame in the largest event cluster is removed, so memory retains diverse places and distinct events within each place. Table 2 (lines 823-835) sets place cluster size 6, update frequency 100, top-K 30, MineCLIP threshold c 73.5, task threshold h 22.74. | - | Keep/merge/evict rule for stored frames; hyperparameter values quoted from Table 2 (Appendix E.4), not measurements. | §3.1 'Place Event Memory'; Appendix E.1 Algorithm 3 | 130 | primary | supported |

| 0 | problem_definition | §3 formalizes a multi-agent system: X = {x_1..x_J} is the task set and A = {a_1..a_M} the agent set; each agent a_m = (Base_m, Role_m, M_m, Tool_m), where Base_m is the underlying LLM, Role_m its functional role or persona, M_m = {z_1..z_j} its memory space and Tool_m its accessible tools. Each memory piece z_i = (xi_i, r*_i) pairs a context prototype xi_i with an action prototype r*_i (line 139). A task runs through stages T = {t_1..t_N} (each one collaborative step such as decomposition, reasoning, verification or integration); at stage t the active agents A^(t) each see a local context c_m^(t) = (x, phi_m^(t), rho_m^(t)), where phi is information from previous actions of neighbouring or predecessor agents and rho is memory retrieved from M_m, produce v_m^(t) = pi_m(c_m^(t)) with policy pi_m, and the outputs are aggregated as s^(t) = Agg({v_m^(t)}) (lines 136-153). | - | Formal setup (notation); not a measurement. | §3 Preliminary | 138 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | §5.1 casts self-evolution as cumulative-regret minimization: Regret(X) = sum over tasks x in X of (R*_x - E[R_x(tau(x), y_hat(x))]) and Objective = min over the agent policies {pi_m} of Regret(X), where tau(x) is the joint trajectory of all active agents over stages t = 1..N, R_x is the task reward that evaluates both the collaborative process and the final output, R*_x = max over (tau, y_hat) of R_x is the optimal achievable reward, and y_hat(x) is not defined separately beyond appearing as the reward's output argument (lines 250-256). For the router, §5.3 defines r(alpha) = alpha r_E(alpha) + (1 - alpha) r_X(alpha) with r_E, r_X the expected rewards of the E-pool and X-pool under routing probability alpha, and R(T) = sum over t of (r(alpha*) - E[r(alpha_t)]); the O(log T) regret theorem rests on Assumption 1 that r on [0.5, 1] is strictly concave with a unique maximizer alpha* in (0.5, 1) (lines 287-298). | - | Objective definition (reward/regret only; no token, time or cost term appears in it); not a measurement. | §5.1 Problem Formulation (and §5.3, Assumption 1, Theorem 2) | 252 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | The component that changes is each agent's private memory M_m, split into an exploitation pool (E-pool) holding consolidated experience from previous tasks for retrieval, and an exploration pool (X-pool) that serves as a temporary buffer for the current task and generates novel experiences (lines 166-172), plus a per-agent router weight w_E (lines 187-231). The backbone LLMs run unchanged; the paper describes no weight update, and the models are served locally via Ollama (Qwen3) and Hugging Face Transformers (Gemma4) (line 318). | - | Description of what the method modifies (external memory and routing weights, per agent); not a measurement. | §4.1 Dual-Memory Pools, Eq. 1 | 171 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | What is stored from the system's own trajectories: each E-pool piece is z = (xi, r*) with r* = (r_trajectory, r_comment), where r_trajectory holds the specific action (e.g. task decomposition or direct answering) together with the cooperation trajectory passed to the next-stage agents, and r_comment is the agent's action-level self-commentary including its rationale; the authors say a piece records how the task was solved and who executed each sub-task (line 181), and a retrieved piece with a compatible collaboration trajectory can have its historical allocation reused as a coordination prior for the next stage (line 206). | - | Description of the stored memory record and how it is reused; not a measurement. | §4.1 Dual-Memory Pools (memory-piece definition); §4.2 | 180 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Reuse at run time: when agent a_m meets sub-task x^(t), its router picks the E-pool with probability alpha_E = w_E / (w_E + w_X) (Eq. 2); on the E-pool it retrieves the Top-K pieces by similarity between embeddings e(x^(t)) and e(xi_z), subject to a similarity threshold tau (Eq. 3), and if no piece is similar enough it falls back to the X-pool, which instantiates an exploratory memory piece z_new; either the retrieved set or z_new is passed with x^(t) and phi to the LLM to generate the action (Eq. 4). The saved text gives no values for K or tau and does not name the embedding model. | - | Description of the retrieval and routing procedure; not a measurement. | §4.2 Memory Retrieval for New Tasks, Eqs. 2-4 | 198 | primary | supported |
| 5 | signal | The signal for updating memory routing is an LLM evaluator that scores the full solution trajectory stage by stage (not only the final answer) on correctness, allocation quality, intermediate coherence and final integration; the binary reward is Delta_t = 1 if the current stage's score q_curr exceeds the previous stage's score q_prev, else 0 (lines 214-217; no rule is given for the first stage). Line 161 calls it an external LLM-as-a-judge; the saved text does not name the judge model. §4.3 describes no ground-truth answer or benchmark score entering the update; however, in the AutoGen configuration the trajectory that is judged includes a Ground Truth Agent that 'identifies potential errors against a reference standard' (line 1406), which the text does not specify, so reference information inside the judged trajectory cannot be excluded for the AutoGen cells. | - | Update signal = stage-to-stage improvement indicator from LLM-judge stage scores; benchmark accuracy appears only in reported results; in AutoGen runs an unspecified 'reference standard' is used by the Ground Truth Agent inside the judged trajectory (line 1406). Not a measurement. | §4.3 Dual-Memory Update | 215 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | Router update with alpha = 0.5 (additive step) and beta = 0.5 (decay factor): if the E-pool was used at stage t, w_E increases by 0.5 when Delta_t = 1 and otherwise becomes max(1.0, 0.5 w_E) (Eq. 6); if the X-pool was used, the update is reversed, so a successful exploration step decays w_E and an unsuccessful one raises it (Eq. 7); w_X stays fixed at 1.0 (line 231). Appendix A.2 notes that the E-pool selection probability therefore lies in [0.5, 1) (line 1270). | alpha = 0.5, beta = 0.5, floor 1.0; w_X = 1.0 | Update rule for the per-agent routing weight (hyperparameter values as printed); not a measurement. | §4.3 Dual-Memory Update, Eqs. 6-7 | 219 | primary | supported |
| 7 | selection_rule | After each task, all memory pieces in the X-pool are merged into the E-pool and the X-pool is emptied (Eq. 8). Baselines: MetaGPT, ChatDev and G-Memory memory designs plus no memory (line 309). | - | Experimental setting; not a measurement. | §6.1 Experimental Setup; Appendix B.2 | 316 | primary | supported |

| 0 | problem_definition | The saved text states no objective or loss; its formal definitions are of trajectories, cases and the graph. Eq. 1 (lines 114-116) writes a trajectory for task τ as T_τ = {(s_t, a_t, o_t)} for t = 1..T, where s_t is the agent's internal state or prompt context at step t, a_t the action taken, o_t the observed outcome or feedback from the environment (such as execution results or correctness signals), and the trajectory ends after a finite number of steps T when a solution is produced or a failure condition is reached. Eq. 2 abstracts the k-th attempt on task τ into a case c_τ^(k) = (τ, x_τ, y_τ^(k), r_τ^(k), σ_τ^(k)): τ the task, x_τ the task input, y_τ^(k) the agent's final output for that attempt, r_τ^(k) ∈ {0,1} whether the attempt succeeded, and σ_τ^(k) salient execution signals extracted from the trajectory (error messages, failure types, corrective feedback). Cases with r = 1 are 'golden', cases with r = 0 'warning' (line 124). Eq. 3 defines the experience graph G = (V, E) with heterogeneous node types V and typed relations E (lines 131-133). | - | Formal definitions (Eqs. 1-3); not a measurement. | §2.1 Trajectories and Case Abstraction, Eqs. 1-2 | 123 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What changes is an external experience graph and the experience hints built from it and injected into the agent's prompt; the agent model's parameters are not modified. Cases written during online execution become available to subsequent tasks. The graph can be attached as a plug-and-play experience layer to existing self-evolving agents (here Reflexion and SE-Agent) without changes to the underlying language model or task-specific solving procedures (line 270). | - | Description of the modified component (external memory + prompt context); not a measurement. | §3.1 Online Self-Evolution | 261 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | After each attempt the provisional case is finalized with the generated output, a correctness signal and extracted execution signatures. The binary outcome r (Eq. 2) decides whether the case is stored as a golden (success) or warning (failure) case, and a corrective attempt after an earlier failure on the same task is linked by a fixed_by edge (line 259). The saved text does not say what produces the correctness signal at run time (for example the benchmark's hidden unit tests or gold answers); for HumanEval it describes hidden unit tests as the benchmark's automatic evaluation (line 1038). No LLM judge or human feedback is described as the signal. | - | Signal = binary per-attempt success r ∈ {0,1} plus execution signatures σ (error messages, failure types, corrective feedback); not a measurement. | §3.1 Online Self-Evolution | 256 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | Online loop: for each incoming task the agent creates a provisional case (task input and context, no output or outcome yet), queries the graph with retrieval and reranking, turns the reranked cases into structured experience hints injected into the prompt, executes, then finalizes the case and inserts it: a new case node joined to the task anchor node by a contain edge, a directed fixed_by edge when the case is a corrective attempt following an earlier failure on the same task, and similar_to edges to existing cases by semantic affinity (lines 252-260). The graph therefore stores every attempt as a golden or warning case node under a per-task anchor node, with typed contain, similar_to and fixed_by edges (lines 136-143); reuse is by retrieving these cases as fixed-by, warning and golden hints for later tasks (line 238). | - | Description of the store-and-reuse loop; not a measurement. | §3.1 Online Self-Evolution | 259 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Retrieval (Algorithm 1, Eqs. 4-8) pools the cases attached to the current task's anchor, the one-hop similar_to neighbourhood of the semantic seeds (query-side seeds plus bridge seeds reached from warning-prioritized anchor cases), and the fixed_by targets of cases in that neighbourhood, then deduplicates and caps the pool. In the experimental protocol (§4.1.2), the query-side seeds are the top K_s = 10 cases by dense similarity of MiniLM sentence embeddings in a FAISS index (lines 277-278), expanded one hop over similarity edges with fanout F_sim = 5; at most one case is selected from the task anchor, followed by similarity-based bridge expansion with fanout F_bridge = 5; after merging and deduplication the pool is capped at K_c = 30, relevance combines prompt-level and failure-aware similarity with alpha = 0.8, and at most H = 5 experience hints are injected into the prompt (line 279). | K_s = 10; F_sim = 5; F_bridge = 5; K_c = 30; α = 0.8; H = 5 | Retrieval and hint hyperparameters stated once in the experimental protocol (§4.1.2, lines 277-279); the text does not say they hold unchanged in every experiment (the ablations change retrieval and hint composition, lines 596-604; the offline protocol states five hints plus five insights, line 587); not a measurement. | §4.1.2 Experimental Protocol and Hyperparameters | 279 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | selection_rule | No acceptance test is applied to stored experience: in the online setting every finalized case, golden (r = 1) or warning (r = 0), is incorporated into the graph (lines 124, 257); in the offline setting the graph is frozen and no new cases or edges are added during evaluation (line 265). Selection happens only when experience is read: at retrieval, Select() prioritizes warning cases among the task-anchor cases as bridge seeds (line 156) and the pool is deduplicated and capped (Eq. 8); candidates are then sorted by relevance rho (Eq. 10) and hints are assembled in that order under a limited budget, with fixed-by hints first, then warning hints, then golden hints (§2.4, lines 240-241). Algorithm 2 (Appendix A, lines 961-1035) implements the fixed-by priority by first selecting warning cases that have an outgoing fixed_by edge (up to a configured limit), optionally adding their corrected counterparts, and then filling the remaining hint budget M from the ranked list in relevance order; it has no separate warning-before-golden step. | - | Rule for what is kept (everything) and what is injected (priority order under a hint budget); not a measurement. | §2.4 Experience Reranking, Hint assembly | 241 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | Ranking score. | 0 | problem_definition | Eq. 1 gives the probability of trial i's action sequence as a product over steps k = 1..j of p_B(a_{i,k} / S_{i,k}, P, S_{i,k-1}, a_{i,k-1}, e_{i,k-1}, ..., S_{i,1}, a_{i,1}, e_{i,1}); Eq. 2 defines the target as P* = argmax over P in A of the sum over i in U of R(p_B([a_{i,1}, ..., a_{i,j}])). Symbols: B = the base LLM; T = the target task; P = the natural-language prompt (task description, scoring rules, safety constraints); S_{i,k} = the environment state at step k of trial i rendered as a text string; a_{i,k} = the action at that step; e_{i,k} = the environment feedback; i = index of a testing trial; j = number of actions in the trial; k = step index; R = human-designed score rules or functions applied to the executed action sequence; A = the space of all natural-language prompts; U = the set of all testing trials of the task; P* = the optimal prompt. | - | Formal objective (sum of per-trial scores over the task's testing trials); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation, Eqs. 1-2 (lines 84-103) | 103 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Only the natural-language prompt given to the acting LLM (TaskLLM) is rewritten; the paper gives a task description, scoring rules and safety constraints as example components (line 84). No model parameters are used or changed: the paper motivates discrete prompt search by the lack of parameter access for black-box LLMs (line 72), and Algorithm 1 changes only prompts, although one tested model, Mixtral-8x7B, is open (line 132). The only trained component is an auxiliary task-specific Longformer-base (148M) score predictor that filters which generated candidates are evaluated (lines 106-107, Eq. 3); it does not act in the environment. PROMST optimizes the prompt offline across tests with one execution trial per test, unlike Reflexion's per-test online memory (line 81). | - | Description of the optimized object; not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | The scalar signal is a human-designed score function. In the experiments it is the task progress score S = num(sub-goal_success) / num(sub-goal_all), i.e. the share of sub-goals or sub-steps completed (Eq. 4). A candidate prompt's score is the average over multiple trials whose initial environment state (e.g. number of objects or agents) is varied (line 105). The authors did not use the task completion score as the metric because it is sparser; Appendix F (Table 9) reports the two as positively correlated, e.g. BoxLift progress 0.90 vs completion 0.31 at levels 5-6 (lines 1085-1098). | - | S = completed sub-goals / all sub-goals of a trial (Eq. 4), averaged over a task's trials; the number of trials per task is not stated in the saved text. | §4.3 Experimental Setups, Eq. 4 | 131 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Error feedback comes from human-designed rules written a priori (line 74), not from a human in the loop or an LLM critic. When the TaskLLM hits an error, the trial terminates (line 105). A rule-matched template then produces feedback text that includes the incorrect TaskLLM output (Appendix H, line 1129). The error types (Table 6, lines 731-773) are: syntactic error, stuck in the loop, failure over query time limit, invalid action, collision, move out of the grid, wrong picking up order and wrong object action; the first three are listed for all 11 tasks. The authors' statements of per-task design effort disagree and are not measured: line 114 says humans need to design 2 to 4 new error types per task, Appendix H (line 1125) says a few (3-5) templates for a novel task, and Table 6 lists 0 to 3 types beyond the three shared ones (none for BoxNet1 and BoxLift, three for Gridworld2). | - | Qualitative description of the feedback channel (rule-triggered text on errors in the agent's own trials); not a measurement. | §3.2 PROMST Framework, 'Human-Designed Feedback Rules'; Appendix A Table 6 | 113 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | New candidates come from a parent prompt in two LLM steps. First, up to 10 feedback instances are sampled at random from the parent's recorded feedback and grouped by error type, and SumLLM summarizes each type. Then GenLLM writes a new prompt from the parent, those summaries and the trajectory of ancestor prompts (Algorithm 3, lines 848-866). All results are stored in a dictionary D that records each prompt's score, human feedback and ancestor prompts (Algorithm 1, line 778). D is reused for parent selection and for score-model training. The authors say random sampling of feedback encourages diverse candidates and likely promotes the more frequent errors. | 10 | Number of feedback instances sampled per candidate generation (min(10, available), Algorithm 3 line 854); not a result. | §3.2 PROMST Framework, 'Candidate Prompt Generator'; Appendix B Algorithms 1 and 3 | 117 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Each candidate evaluation needs one TaskLLM query per action over multiple trials (line 106). To limit this, PROMST trains a score predictor online and uses it to choose which generated candidates to evaluate. The predictor is a task-specific bidirectional Longformer-base (148M) fine-tuned on prompt-score pairs collected in early generations. It is first applied at generation sd and updated with new pairs every generation. Five models are fine-tuned on random 4:1 train/test splits to obtain the mean, variance and test error of the predictions. Few-shot GPT-4 as a predictor did not improve with more examples, and fine-tuning surpassed it once there were more than 40 data points (line 458). | 148M; five models on random 4:1 train/test splits | Predictor size (parameters) and the resampling scheme used to estimate its uncertainty; not a result. | §3.2 PROMST Framework, 'Score Prediction Model' | 107 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | There are two gates. (i) From generation sd onward (Algorithm 2, 'if i >= sd', line 815), a generated candidate p' is evaluated only if E[M_k(p')] + Var[M_k(p')] + E[error_k] >= hyper_M x max(D.score()) (Eq. 3, lines 109-112). The first two terms are the mean and variance of the five models' predicted scores, E[error_k] is their average test error, and max(D.score()) is the best score found so far; adding variance and error keeps the filter conservative. For each parent, generation continues until n candidates pass or 3n attempts are made (Algorithm 2, line 823). Before generation sd, all n candidates generated per parent are evaluated without filtering (Algorithm 2, lines 839-843). (ii) The top k prompts by score in D become parents for the next level (Algorithm 1, line 798), and the output is the highest-scoring prompt (line 804). Settings: n = 20 kid prompts per parent in the first level and 8 afterwards; k = 5; hyper_M = 0.8; sd = 4. Search stops when the last three levels bring no score improvement. All methods explore the same number of candidates (line 448). | n = 20 (first level) / 8 (later levels); k = 5; hyper_M = 0.8; sd = 4 | Hyperparameters of the search and of the score-model filter; the acceptance criterion is the task progress score averaged over trials; not a result. | §4.3 Experimental Setups, 'Hyperparameters'; §3.2 Eq. 3; Appendix B Algorithms 1-2 | 448 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

It returns fine-grained feedback f_k, which attributes note utility to trajectory decisions (line 1040), and a utility mode u_k in {Unsatisfactory, Satisfactory, Excellent}. The mode routes the episode to failure-avoidance, improvement-oriented or success-reuse memories (line 180). Per the Limitations, human-written notes are used for benchmarking and the motivating analysis, while memory is distilled from agent-generated episodes (line 557). The Evolver abstracts away instance-specific details that cannot be reused directly, such as URLs, query paths and post wording (line 1046). It stores phase-specific guidance rather than full trajectories or generic reflections (line 1055). The paper's example: a mishandled statistic-based claim yields an evidence-acquisition memory that triggers on similar numerical claims and recommends checking the original source, denominator and context (line 200). | - | Description of what is stored (memory item schema) and how it is produced; not a measurement. | §4.3 Actionable Memory Evolution (also App. B.2) | 198 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Reuse happens at two points. First, the Claim Analyzer summarizes the post into a query q_C and retrieves the top-n memories whose Phase is claim analysis and whose Trigger has the highest lexical overlap with the query. It uses their ActionStrategy fields to write a verification brief c_{k+1} (lines 205-219). Second, before each action step t, the Note Writer summarizes its decision state into a query q_A^t. The state covers search history, collected evidence, remaining uncertainties and the current phase p_t in {EvidenceAcquisition, NoteWriting}. It then retrieves the top-n phase-matched memories by lexical overlap (lines 222-228). In the implementation, retrieval selects the top k=4 entries by lexical overlap, and the dataset is processed with batch size 4 for memory updates (lines 1216-1217). | - | Description of retrieval (lexical overlap on Trigger, filtered by Phase); not a measurement. | §4.4 Memory-Guided Note Generation, Claim Analysis (also App. E.2) | 206 | primary | supported |

M is the frozen target model, h the harness, x a task; running h(M, x, s) yields a trajectory tau and a scalar score r(s) in [0,1] (Eq. 1). Given train, selection and test splits D_tr, D_sel, D_test, the method generates a candidate set C(D_tr) from D_tr, selects s*_sel = argmax over s in C(D_tr) of the mean of r(s) over the /D_sel/ selection tasks (Eq. 2), and reports Test(s*_sel) = mean of r(s*_sel) over the /D_test/ test tasks (Eq. 3). | 3 | mechanism | A separate optimizer model separates failed from successful trajectories and partitions each group into reflection minibatches, so that recurring procedural errors (wrong source searched, wrong answer format, tool result not verified) rather than single anecdotes drive edits. Failure minibatches propose missing or corrective rules; success minibatches preserve behaviors that already work; in the default patch mode each reflection returns structured add/delete/replace edits (in the alternative rewrite mode, a small set of rewrite suggestions). Failure-driven and success-driven proposals are first consolidated separately and then combined with priority on failure corrections, filtering duplicate, contradictory and example-specific suggestions (line 143; Algorithm 1 step 13, line 1278). | - | Description of how own rollouts are turned into skill edits; not a measurement. | §3.3 Backward Pass: Minibatch Reflection | 142 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | Epoch-wise slow update: at the end of an epoch the same training items are rolled out under the previous epoch's skill and the current skill and grouped into improvements, regressions, persistent failures and stable successes; the optimizer writes a longitudinal guidance block into a protected slow-update field, and this candidate still passes the validation gate. A separate optimizer-side meta skill summarizing which edit patterns helped, were rejected, or persisted is prepended to future optimizer prompts but not shipped with the target model (line 586). Default: 20 sampled tasks per epoch (line 869). | - | Description of what is stored across epochs (protected guidance block in the skill; optimizer-only meta skill) and how it is reused; not a measurement. | §3.6 Epoch-Wise Slow/Meta Update | 585 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Edit-level selection: the textual learning rate is the edit budget L_t, the maximum number of skill edits applied at step t; after aggregation the optimizer model ranks the merged edit pool by expected utility and keeps only the top L_t edits. | 6 | selection_rule | Candidate-level acceptance: a candidate skill is accepted only if its selection-split score is strictly greater than the current selection score, so ties are rejected; if it also exceeds the best score so far it becomes best_skill.md (line 148). ## s022 — VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.05395v1 · version read: arXiv 2606.05395v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2026-06-03
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | setting | Two robot platforms: a Clearpath Jackal ground robot controlled through velocity-control and object-detection APIs, and a PX4 quadrotor that executes velocity trajectories in the NED frame. GPT-5-nano is the skill model F_skill (generates and refines skills) and GPT-4o-mini is the planner F_plan (same line 209). The evaluation spans 11 temporal-logic specifications and 400 generated plans (line 104); global specifications are evaluated on all 400 plans and each skill's local contract only on the 40 plans generated from that skill (line 547). The 11 specifications (Jackal 1-5, PX4 6-11) are listed in Listing 2 (lines 552-586). | - | Description of the experimental setting; not a measurement. | §5 Empirical Evaluation, opening paragraph | 209 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Problem (lines 146-148): given atomic propositions AP, system commands S (e.g. APIs), global specifications G and a task prompt tau, construct a skill sk = (G, psi_sk, C_sk) that is (a) logically feasible, i.e. there exists an execution trace sigma with L_sk(sigma) /= G AND psi_sk, and (b) such that the generated plan satisfies the specifications under all possible executions, A_pi (x) M /= G AND psi_sk. Symbols (lines 121-144, Table 3): AP = {a_1..a_n} atomic propositions; sigma = sigma_0, sigma_1, ... an execution trace, sigma_t the execution state at time t; G = {phi_1..phi_m} global LTL specifications over AP that must always hold; psi_sk the skill's local rule (LTL) stating its intended behaviour or goal; C_sk = (L_sk, C^p_sk) the semantic contract, where L_sk: sigma_t -> 2^AP is the proposition-aligned labeling function giving the propositions that hold at time t and C^p_sk is a text-based plan template; F_skill generates sk = F_skill(tau, S, G); F_plan generates the plan pi = F_plan(C_sk, tau); A_pi = (S, S_0, T, L) is the transition system compiled from pi (states, initial states, transitions such as an API call or waypoint update, labels L(s_t) = L_sk(sigma_t)); M is described on line 144 as 'a predefined transition system representing the environment and system dynamics over all possible executions', but Table 3 (line 765) defines M as 'Universal transition system representing all possible transitions' and §4.1 constructs M as the universal transition system over 2^AP (lines 162-163); the plan-level check actually stated in §4.2 is A_pi /= G AND psi_sk without M (line 176); /= is used as 'satisfies' (line 161, 'satisfying the combined specification'); the product symbol (x) is not defined in words or in Table 3. The optimisation objective (lines 188-190) is C*_sk = argmin over C_sk of Loss(F_plan(C_sk, tau)), where the loss is the percentage of violated specifications over all specifications; the reported metric is Safety(pi) = (1/N) * sum_i 1[pi /= phi_i], the fraction of the N specifications satisfied by a generated plan (lines 218-220). | - | Formal problem statement and objective; not a measurement. The symbol M carries two definitions in the text (line 144 vs lines 162-163 and Table 3 line 765). | §3 Problem Formulation, 'Problem'; §4.2 'Semantic Contract Refinement'; §5 | 146 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | During optimisation the global specifications G are kept fixed while the skill's local rule psi_sk and semantic contract C_sk (labeling function L_sk plus plan template C^p_sk) are iteratively refined through verification feedback; foundation-model weights stay fixed. The authors say the evolving object is the skill representation itself, not a one-off plan, a flat planner prompt or hidden model parameters (line 100), and that optimisation works entirely at the prompt level with no parameter updates, gradient backpropagation or human supervision (line 207). The case studies show edits to the plan-template code (Jackal, lines 845-860; PX4 one-line change, lines 947-950). | - | Description of the editable object; not a measurement. | §4 Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills, opening paragraph | 155 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | The signal is formal verification of generated plans: the plan is compiled into an automaton in NuSMV via the labeling function (line 177, Algorithm 1), the model checker checks it against G and psi_sk, and the verifier returns y in {pass, fail(phi)} with phi in G or psi_sk (line 193). The outcome is converted into a textual gradient g, for example 'violate specification: G(person observed -> X stop)' or 'pass all specifications', which the authors treat as a discrete approximation of the loss gradient with respect to the contract (line 196). The loop is described as fully automated through verification feedback without a human in the loop (line 207). The abstract (line 62) says the counterexample trace is translated into the textual gradient; the formal definition on this line gives the gradient as the violated specification. | - | Feedback signal = model-checker verdict per specification (pass / fail with the violated specification), not execution reward, unit tests or an LLM judge; not a measurement. | §4.2 'Semantic Contract Refinement' | 195 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Update rule (line 199): C_sk^(k+1) = F_skill(C_sk^(k), g, tau), where k is the iteration number; the loop alternates Forward C_sk^(k) -> pi^(k) -> A_pi^(k) and Backward A_pi^(k) -> g^(k) -> C_sk^(k+1) (line 203), and the authors call this textual gradient descent in which F_skill performs the contract update (line 205). It is implemented by adapting LLM-AutoDiff with default parameters (line 206). What is kept is the refined skill contract, which guides future plan generation (line 103); for held-out prompts the frozen optimised skill is reused without further refinement (line 716). The learning material is the loop's own generated plans, treated as evidence for skill refinement (line 155), not executed robot trajectories. | - | Description of the update procedure; not a measurement. | §4.2 'Semantic Contract Refinement' | 201 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Skill-level gate (§4.1): the combined specification Phi_sk = (AND of all phi in G) AND psi_sk is checked with a model checker on a universal transition system M with S = 2^AP, S_0 = S, T = S x S and L(s) = s (lines 159-163), by verifying M /= NOT Phi_sk (line 165). If that property holds, every trace violates Phi_sk, the skill is infeasible and F_skill is re-queried to refine the local rule; otherwise the returned counterexample is a witness that the skill is feasible (line 167) and the skill goes on to plan-level optimisation (line 173). The text states no stopping, budget or keep/revert rule for plan-level refinement. Reported iteration counts are points at which results are given: optimised skills 'after 7 steps' in Fig. 5 (line 221) and VASO exceeding 90% safety 'within 7 steps' (line 223); in the Jackal case study the optimised skill satisfies all specifications 'After 10 iterations of refinement' (line 845); in the PX4 case study the refined skill satisfies all specifications 'After one iteration of skill optimization' (line 947). | - | Acceptance gate = model-checker feasibility of the local rule against the global specifications; for plan-level contract updates the text names no keep/revert rule beyond using LLM-AutoDiff with default parameters (line 206); not a measurement. No stopping criterion or iteration budget is stated for plan-level refinement. | §4.1 Skill-Level Verification and Local Rule Refinement | 166 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 14 | data_generation | The checker's interface is generated rather than hand-built: F_skill is queried to automatically generate the proposition-aligned labeling functions from APIs and specifications instead of manual engineering (line 231). Compared with handcrafted labeling functions, the automatic version is reported 'on-par' (line 232; Table 1 SS 96.8 vs 97.2, lines 262 and 253) and to give less than a 1% degradation in the final safety score across the optimisation process (line 988, author statement). Besides the labeling functions, F_skill also generates the skill's local rule psi_sk (lines 135, 152; prompt requirement line 422), which the verifier checks together with the user-given global specifications (lines 176, 193) and which is re-generated when infeasible (line 166). The in-domain and held-out task prompts are listed in App. B.1 (lines 656-715); the text does not say how they were written. | - | Description of what F_skill generates from APIs and specifications (the proposition mapping used by the verifier, and the local rule psi_sk); the global specifications are user-supplied; not a measurement. The '<1% degradation' is an author statement; Table 1 gives 97.2 vs 96.8 SS (0.4 points, calc.). | §5 'Practicality of Automatic Proposition Alignment' | 231 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 15 | limitations_stated | Stated limitations: (i) the proposition-aligned labeling function L_sk is AI-generated and unverified, so errors in the proposition mapping can invalidate formal guarantees (the plan-level guarantee is conditioned on correct proposition alignment, line 179; App. C gives a PX4 example where a mapping ignoring the vertical velocity passes a plan that actually violates G(linear_velocity < 1), lines 953-986); (ii) skills are verified under sequential, non-concurrent execution and the framework does not extend to overlapping or interleaved skill executions (line 280). Future work: uncertainty signals such as confidence calibration for labeling, and multi-agent settings (line 281). | - | Authors' own limitations; not a measurement. | §7 Limitations and Future Directions | 279 | primary | supported |

| 0 | problem_definition | Each task instance g is modeled as a finite-horizon POMDP M_g=(S,A,T,Omega,R,H): S latent state space, A action space, T transition kernel, Omega observation space, R task-specific reward function, H episode horizon. A TTL session on g is K consecutive episodes xi_g=(tau_1,...,tau_K), and after each episode the environment resets to its initial state, so any improvement must come from the agent. The session is scored by W-AUC(xi_g) = sum_k w_k*J(tau_k) / sum_k w_k*J_max(g), with linear weights w_k=k that weight later episodes more; tau_k is the trajectory of episode k, J(tau_k) its reward, J_max(g) the maximum achievable return for task g (Eq. 1, lines 138-150). | - | Definition of the per-session objective (reward-weighted learning-curve area normalized by the task's maximum return); not a measurement. | §3.1 Test-Time Learning Formulation, Eq. 1 | 150 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The paper separates the actor policy pi (behavior within an episode) from the self-improvement policy f, which after each episode maps the current actor and trajectory history H_k={tau_1,...,tau_k} to the next actor: pi_{k+1}=f(pi_k,H_k) (Eq. 2). In the prompt-based instantiation a frozen actor LLM pi_theta acts under system prompt rho, and a separate meta-agent LLM governed by meta-prompt phi writes rho_{k+1} ~ f_phi(./rho_k,H_k) (Eq. 3). Meta-training seeks phi* = argmax_phi E_{g~D_train}[W-AUC(xi_g^phi)] (Eq. 4), where D_train is the training-task distribution and xi_g^phi is the TTL session on task g run with meta-prompt phi. | - | Bi-level objective: inner loop = TTL session scored by W-AUC; outer loop = choice of meta-prompt phi maximizing expected W-AUC over training tasks; not a measurement. | §3.2-3.3, Eqs. 2-4 | 169 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | Two text components change, and no weights: within a session the actor's system prompt rho is rewritten between episodes by the meta-agent; across tasks, offline, the meta-prompt phi (the meta-agent's natural-language instructions, line 103) is the learnable component (line 167). Actor weights theta are frozen and all behavioral change is mediated through system-prompt rewriting (line 158); the outer loop is described as gradient-free search in prompt space yielding a text artifact (line 121). | - | Description of the modified components (actor system prompt per episode; meta-prompt per training run); not a measurement. | §3.2 Learnable Self-Improvement Policies, 'Actor.' | 160 | primary | supported |

Algorithm 1 applies rho_{k+1} <- Adapt(phi,{tau_1,...,tau_k}) for k<K (line 1359). | 4 | mechanism | Outer loop (offline meta-training) keeps a single expert meta-prompt phi*, initialized from a seed phi_0; each iteration samples one training task, runs a full TTL session with phi*, and a reflection module proposes a revised candidate (line 176). The reflection has two stages: first it extracts task-specific facts F_g from the session trajectory; then the reflection model uses F_g, the session xi_g and phi* to identify issues in the meta-agent's self-improvement strategy and write a revised meta-prompt. ## s027 — GenericAgent: A Token-Efficient Self-Evolving LLM Agent via Contextual Information Density Maximization (V1.0)

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.17091v1 · version read: arXiv 2604.17091v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v1 text also saved as sources/2604.17091-pdf.txt for the appendix cases missing from the HTML) · v1: 2026-04-18
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The objective is stated as a design principle rather than an optimisation formula. The paper's core view is that agent performance depends on how much decision-relevant information is introduced, maintained and updated within a limited context budget (line 143). It frames context engineering as a constrained optimisation that trades completeness against conciseness, with naturalness as a supporting constraint (line 174), and GA targets a budget of under 30k tokens (line 193). The only formula for the budget is Eq. 1 (lines 272-287): C_H = sum over messages m in the conversation history H of len(m), where len(m) is the character length of message m after JSON serialisation; B = alpha * W_tokens, where W_tokens is the configured token window and alpha ~ 3 chars/token is an empirical ratio that turns the token budget into a character budget. Compression or eviction is triggered when C_H > B. The authors note that alpha = 3 causes mildly early eviction for ASCII text (about 4 characters per token) and risks delayed eviction and context overflow for CJK text (1-2 tokens per character). The saved text gives no formula for 'information density' itself. | alpha ~ 3 chars/token | Problem statement and context-budget trigger rule; not a measurement. | §1 Introduction; §2.1 Design Principles; §2.1.4; §2.3.4 Eq. 1 | 272 | primary | supported |
| 1 | setting | GA is a general-purpose agent system for tasks in a local computing environment. It operates browsers, terminals, file systems, keyboard and mouse input, screen-based perception and mobile devices through configurable tool adapters, and is described as model-agnostic (line 199). The agent-system baselines are Claude Code, OpenClaw and Codex, with Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6, MiniMax M2.7 and GPT-5.4 as backbones (line 642). The LoCoMo study instead compares GA with Mem0 and A-MEM (embedding-based, text-embedding-3-small) and with OpenClaw (lines 749-750). The evaluations are: SOP-Bench, Lifelong AgentBench and RealFin-Benchmark (lines 645-647); a §4.2 tool-use benchmark on Claude Sonnet 4.6 with simple tool-generalization tasks (shown only as appendix substitution examples, Table 11) and five long-horizon tasks (lines 661, 665, 669); five repeated HuggingFace dataset-download runs on GPT-5.4 (line 707); a memory ablation on the SOP-Bench dangerous_goods subset with GPT-5.4 (lines 717-722); the first subset of LoCoMo with GPT-5.4, with Category 5 removed (lines 750-751); full prompt length after installing 20 skills (line 812); a nine-round GitHub research study run by GA alone and an eight-task web benchmark against OpenClaw, with Claude Opus 4.6 named for 'the comparative benchmark' (lines 834-838); and WebCanvas (12 sampled tasks), BrowseComp-ZH (10 sampled tasks) and 22 custom tasks, with Claude Opus 4.6 for both GA and OpenClaw (lines 953-958). | - | Description of the experimental setting; not a measurement. | §2.2 Overview; §4.1.1 Setup 'Baseline'; §§4.2-4.5 Setup | 642 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | GA keeps a fixed tool layer separate from an evolving knowledge layer (line 255). The tool interface stays the same during operation. All task-specific capabilities are stored in SOP files and reusable scripts, which the agent reads, creates and modifies with its own tools. Common subtasks are said to evolve into reusable scripts, which upgrades knowledge from plain-text instructions to executable code (line 257). GA does not modify the base model; it evolves by recording and updating the informational environment in which the model operates (line 190). Other state that evolves: the four-layer memory (L1 index, L2 facts, L3 SOPs, L4 raw session archive; lines 235-243), a skill tree with a usage counter per skill (lines 377-381), and a lightweight log of observed errors with their corrections, user preferences and verified success patterns, which is injected into the system prompt (line 441). | - | Description of the editable object; not a measurement. | §2.3.3 'What evolves: strategy, not tools' | 256 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Memory consolidation keeps experience only when tool execution succeeds. During consolidation the agent retains only information that has been strictly verified through successful tool execution; guesses, temporary intermediate states and failed decision branches are discarded under the 'No Execution, No Memory' rule (lines 262-263). For this step the text names no benchmark score, unit test, LLM judge or other external checker. Other channels use different signals. SOPs are also refined over multiple sessions by unspecified 'real-world feedback' (line 257). In autonomous exploration, even failed experiments are documented so that later planning avoids the same dead ends (line 440). The separate log of observed errors with corrections, user preferences and verified success patterns (line 441) currently relies on manual user curation (line 459). In the exploration loop, the scoring weights are adjusted using a skill's actual usage count u(t) within 30 days (lines 446-449). Benchmark graders appear only in §4, as evaluation metrics: automatic evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, and human review assisted by GPT-5.4 (line 960). | - | Acceptance signal for L2/L3 memory writes = successful tool execution, applied in the agent's own consolidation step (lines 262-263). The self-improvement log is curated manually by the user (line 459), and exploration reports keep failed experiments (line 440). Not a measurement. | §2.3.3 'How quality is controlled: selective consolidation' | 262 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | Storage: raw action traces go to L4, the raw session archive, and are not promoted automatically. Reusable L3 procedures are produced only by explicit consolidation steps, which are triggered at milestones such as completing a subgoal or recovering from a system error. After a task finishes, execution traces are compressed into structured long-term representations in shared memory (line 200). L3 SOPs hold workflows, preconditions, key steps, common failure cases and debugging or recovery strategies (line 240); L2 holds verified, stable facts (line 238). Reuse: by default only the meta-memory and the L1 index are injected, where L1 holds compact pointers, keyword mappings and a few hard constraints (line 236). The model follows the chain L1 -> L2/L3 through tool calls and prompt policy to read deeper content when it needs it (line 247). The evaluation describes three stages: natural-language execution, SOP distillation and code-based execution. GA's memory-management mechanisms trigger the transitions between them without manual intervention (lines 842-845). | - | Description of the consolidation and retrieval procedure; not a measurement. | §2.3.3 Self-Evolution Capability; §2.3.2; §4.4.1 'Evolution Stages' | 261 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Long-term memory uses a triggered commit. Information identified as potentially valuable goes through a validation stage that checks its usefulness and reusability before it is committed. Only verified information is written into L2 or L3, as small incremental updates, and the L1 index is updated to match (line 250). Admission to L2 requires validation through execution and proven reuse across tasks; transient states, one-time events and unverified hypotheses are excluded (line 238). A new L1 entry is added only when a genuinely new knowledge category appears (line 251). The text gives no numeric threshold for the validation check. It also says the self-improvement log currently relies on manual user curation (line 459). | - | Acceptance rule for memory writes; not a measurement. | §2.3.2 Hierarchical Memory Architecture | 249 | primary | supported |
| 6 | data_generation | Autonomous exploration generates its own practice tasks (§3.3). When there is no pending task list, a curriculum planner inspects the skill tree and scores candidate tasks with Eq. 2: S(t) = w_b*B(t) + w_d*D(t) + w_u*U(t) + w_i*I(t). Here t is a candidate task, B (breadth) rewards under-populated skill categories, D (depth) rewards frequently used skills, U (utility) is the estimated practical value and I (innovation) favours novel techniques or domains; each is scored from 1 to 10 (lines 397-406). Eq. 3 is B(t) = 10*max(0, 1 - /S_c//(S_bar+1)), where /S_c/ is the number of skills in the target category and S_bar is the mean skill count across categories. Eq. 4 is D(t) = 10*u(t)/(u_max+1), where u(t) is the usage count of the target skill and u_max is the maximum usage count across all skills. The LLM estimates U and I (lines 409-422). The initial weights are (w_b, w_d, w_u, w_i) = (0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2), and the task list must cover at least four skill categories. After each batch, the dominant weight is cut by 10% if S(t) > 8.0 but u(t) < 3 within 30 days, and raised by 10% if S(t) < 5.0 but u(t) > 5; the weights are then renormalised (lines 446-450). By default the trigger fires every six minutes (line 389). Each task is researched, prototyped and validated in a sandboxed temporary directory, and ends with a Markdown report that updates the skill tree (lines 429-439). The text describes no generated answer keys or tests. | (0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2) | Task-generation and weight-update rules; not a measurement. | §3.3 Autonomous Exploration Capability, Eqs. 2-4 | 423 | primary | supported |
| 7 | environment_knowledge | Environment knowledge is stored as natural-language SOPs, facts and scripts; the text describes no explicit state or transition model.
