L2 holds facts that were validated through execution and are reusable across tasks (line 238). The authors say such knowledge (user preferences, tool behaviours, effective action patterns) is not available at the outset and only emerges through repeated trial and failure (lines 132-133). On a new web task, the agent must first map generalised SOP knowledge onto the concrete page structure and interaction flow; later executions then reuse the aligned path (line 947). The exploration log records observed errors with their corrections, user preferences and verified success patterns (line 441). | - | Description of stored environment knowledge; not a measurement. | §2.3.2 Hierarchical Memory Architecture (L3 SOP layer) | 240 | primary | supported |
| 8 | result | Nine-round longitudinal study on a LangChain GitHub research task. Each round is a new task instance: Round #1 starts from scratch, Rounds #2-#5 refine a textual SOP and Rounds #6-#9 run a codified SOP (lines 837, 847). | 15 | limitations_stated | The authors list four limitations of autonomous exploration (lines 453-461). The 30-round execution cap means highly complex research tasks may span multiple sessions, with continuity kept only through written reports and task-list annotations. The reflection-based weight adjustment is a preliminary design and has not yet accumulated enough long-term data to definitively prove its effectiveness across diverse, real-world user workflows. The self-improvement log relies on manual user curation. Advanced skill-tree maintenance (merging categories, deprecating tools, restructuring) remains entirely manual. Other stated caveats: the Discussion's findings are distilled from practice rather than derived from controlled ablations alone (lines 1002-1003); the alpha = 3 heuristic risks delayed eviction and context overflow on CJK text (lines 284-287); efficiency ratios are comparable only within a benchmark block (line 463); and validation of the full evolutionary path (skill consolidation, autonomous exploration and architectural self-update) is left as an open problem (lines 1085-1088). | - | Authors' stated limitations; not a measurement. | §3.3 'Limitations'; §5 Discussion; §2.3.4; Table 2 caption | 457 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | problem_definition | Write admission is formalized per candidate memory item m as a paired A/B comparison. Eq. 1: I_A = f(q), I_B = f(q; m), where q is the query, f(.) is prompt construction and I_B injects m into the SCEC's dedicated slot together with summarized tool feedback. Eq. 2: o_A = F(I_A), o_B = F(I_B), where F is the model execution inside the SCEC (self-contained execution context). Eq. 3: DeltaR = R(o_B) - R(o_A), DeltaL = L(o_B) - L(o_A), DeltaT = T(o_B) - T(o_A), where R is the task-specific reward, L latency and T token overhead. Eq. 4: composite admission score S = DeltaR - lambda_L*DeltaL - lambda_T*DeltaT, with lambda_L, lambda_T >= 0 controlling the trade-offs between utility and cost. No global objective over the whole memory repository is formalized. | - | Definition of the per-item admission score; not a measurement. | 2 | selection_rule | Eq. 5: a candidate is admitted if and only if S >= eta (eta = acceptance threshold) and receives initial weight w_0(m) = max{0, S}; multiple runs may be averaged to mitigate variance. | 6 | mechanism | Progressive evolution updates each admitted item's weight (Eq. 7): w_{t+1}(m) = w_t(m) + alpha*Ubar_t(m) - beta*f_use,t(m), where w_t(m) is the current weight, Ubar_t(m) the average realized utility since the last update, f_use,t(m) the usage frequency, and alpha and beta control the influence of observed utility and usage (line 164). - Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.08197v2 · version read: arXiv 2410.08197v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v2 text also saved as 2410.08197-pdf.txt and checked for the title block and venue header) · v1: 2024-10-10

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper frames its problem as bridging the comprehension gap between LLMs and external tools that arises from inadequate and inaccurate human-centric tool documentation (abstract, line 61). It writes no loss or score to maximize; Algorithm 1 specifies the task procedurally. Inputs: D = the raw tool documentation set (one documentation t per tool; t_0 is the raw documentation provided in the dataset, line 170); I = the number of iteration rounds (the maximum iteration count, set to 5 in §3.1, line 239); phi = the similarity threshold that an exploration query's maximum cosine similarity to earlier queries must stay below (Eq. 2); tau = the termination threshold on Delta, the average of embedding cosine similarity and BLEU between consecutive documentation versions (Eq. 5). The paper calls Delta the 'degree of change' (line 208), but it is a similarity score (Algorithm 1 step 14, line 146), so iterations stop when Delta > tau, i.e. when consecutive versions have become nearly identical (line 148). Output: D~ = the revised tool documentation set, built one tool at a time (outer loop over t in D). | - | Formal specification of the procedure (Algorithm 1 inputs and output); not a measurement. | §2.1, Algorithm 1 (Input/Output lines) | 117 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The component that is modified is the tool documentation, i.e. the natural-language description of each tool that is given to the LLM as context (lines 71-73). In the main experiments GPT-4o is the backbone model that refines the documentation using its own tool-usage feedback. The related-work section places documentation-based tool use among tuning-free methods, which it describes as requiring no additional training, in contrast to tuning-based methods that fine-tune the LLM (lines 499-503). | - | Description of the modified component; not a measurement. | §3.1 Implementation Details | 238 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The signal is the environment's actual response to a real tool call: after generating an exploration instance the Explorer invokes the tool and records the returned result r_i (line 170), including error responses (e.g. the 'Invalid id' response in Table 9, line 994). The authors state they obtain feedback by actually using the tool, and contrast this with self-correction without external feedback (line 508). The Analyzer converts the tool result into natural-language suggestions rather than scalar feedback (line 194). The stopping rule compares consecutive documentation versions (Eq. 5), not task success. | - | Type of feedback used inside the refinement loop (tool execution results plus LLM-written critique); not a measurement. | §4 Related Work, Learning from Feedback (also §2.2 line 170, §2.3 line 194) | 513 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | Experience gathering (Eq. 1): at iteration i the Explorer M_E generates an exploration instance e_i = M_E(t_{i-1}, d_{i-1}, H_i), where t_{i-1} is the current tool documentation, d_{i-1} is the next-step exploration direction proposed by the Rewriter M_R, and H_i = {(e_j, r_j) / j < i} is the history of earlier exploration instances and the tool's returned results. Each e_i consists of a user query e_i^q about the tool and the necessary parameters e_i^p; the Explorer then calls the tool to obtain r_i (line 170). Formally (Eq. 1) the past query/parameter/result pairs are fed back into the next generation, and §2.2 adds that a record of all previously explored queries is given to the Explorer (line 171). The printed Explorer prompt template, however, shows only {Explored queries} and the Rewriter's {Suggestions} as memory, not the tool results (Table 6 part I, lines 872-875); the tool outputs are passed explicitly to the Analyzer and Rewriter prompts (lines 893-894, 906-907). | - | Formal definition of the exploration step (Eq. 1); not a measurement. | §2.2 Experience Gathering, Eq. 1 | 165 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | Learning from experience and rewriting: the Analyzer M_A outputs natural-language revision suggestions s_i = M_A(t_{i-1}, e_i, r_i, T_i) (Eq. 3, line 187), where T_i = {t_j / j < i} is the history of documentation versions, judged against criteria of consistency with tool outputs, comprehensiveness and conciseness (line 190). The Rewriter M_R then computes (d_i, t_i) = M_R(t_{i-1}, e_i, r_i, s_i, T_i) (Eq. 4), producing the revised documentation t_i and the next exploration direction d_i, which is passed back to the Explorer. The revision history is included so that each version builds on its predecessors (line 205). | - | Formal definition of the analysis and rewriting steps (Eqs. 3-4); not a measurement. | §2.3 Learning from Experience and §2.4 Documentation Rewriting, Eqs. 3-4 | 200 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Exploration instances are filtered by a similarity constraint (Eq. 2): a new query e_i^q is kept only if its maximum cosine similarity, computed on OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings, to every earlier query e_j^q (j < i) is below the threshold phi. If the constraint fails, the Explorer discards the instance, reflects on why it overlapped, and generates a new query, repeating until an instance meets the criterion (Self-Reflection; Algorithm 1 steps 5-8). | - | Acceptance rule for exploration instances (cosine similarity below phi, phi = 0.9 in §3.1); not a measurement. | §2.2, Eq. 2 and 'Self-Reflection' | 180 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Algorithm 1 has no step that rejects a rewrite: each iteration's t_i replaces t_{i-1}, and the only decision is when to stop. The tool-adaptive termination computes Delta = [sim(e_i^t, e_{i-1}^t) + BLEU(t_i, t_{i-1})] / 2 (Eq. 5), where e_i^t and e_{i-1}^t are ada-002 embeddings of two consecutive documentation versions, sim is cosine similarity and BLEU measures n-gram overlap. If Delta exceeds tau the iterations stop, and the last t_i is added to the revised set (Algorithm 1 steps 14-19); otherwise refinement continues up to the maximum round count. The rule is applied per tool, so tools can stop after different numbers of rounds (line 207: some tools 'may reach optimal documentation faster than others'); the paper reports no per-tool or average number of rounds actually used, and the one trajectory it prints (Appendix E, Tables 9-12) runs all five rounds. | - | Stopping rule: average of embedding cosine similarity and BLEU between consecutive documentation versions, compared with tau (tau = 0.75 in §3.1); convergence of the text, not a task score. | §2.4 Documentation Rewriting, Eq. 5 | 215 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | setting | Benchmarks: ToolBench (real-world APIs from RapidAPI and BMTools), restricted because of budget constraints to its most challenging subset I3-Instruction (complex requests needing multiple tools from different categories); and RestBench with two scenarios, TMDB (54 movie-related APIs) and Spotify (40 music-related APIs). Metrics: Correct Path Rate (CP%) and Win% from pairwise comparison by a ChatGPT-based evaluator (lines 231-232). Baselines: ReAct, DFSDT and EasyTool (lines 234-236). | 54 APIs (TMDB); 40 APIs (Spotify) | Benchmark description (API counts per RestBench scenario); the number of evaluation queries per dataset is not printed in the saved text. | §3.1 Experimental Setup, Datasets | 229 | primary | supported |
| 8 | setting | Implementation: GPT-4o is the backbone model that refines the documentation; similarity threshold phi = 0.9, termination threshold tau = 0.75, maximum iteration count 5. The revised documentation is evaluated with three LLMs: GPT-4o (footnote link names gpt-4o-2024-08-06), GPT-4o-mini and the open-source Llama-3-70B. Code is released at github.com/quchangle1/DRAFT (line 246). | phi = 0.9; tau = 0.75; maximum 5 iterations | Hyperparameter values of the refinement loop and list of evaluated models; not a result. | §3.1 Implementation Details | 239 | primary | supported |
| 9 | data_generation | The exploration inputs are synthesized by the Explorer, not drawn from a task set: its prompt asks it to synthesize a natural user query that calling the API could help with, extract the parameters from that query, focus on queries needing a single API call, supply concrete invented values for required parameters, and use the documentation's default parameters for IDs or usernames whose valid values it does not know (lines 859-870). The outcome recorded for each synthesized query is the tool's output, which the Analyzer and Rewriter prompts receive as 'explored queries, the required parameters and the outputs of the tool' (lines 893-894, 906-907). | - | Description of how exploration queries and parameters are generated from the documentation; not a measurement. | Appendix C, Table 6, part I (Experience Gathering prompt) | 859 | primary | supported |

## s033 — CODESKILL: Learning Self-Evolving Skills for Coding Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.25430v2 · version read: arXiv 2605.25430v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt); v1 HTML also saved and diffed for version changes · v1: 2026-05-25
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper formalizes skill management as learning a policy M_theta that, given trajectory evidence tau and relevant skill-bank context C (a subset of the bank B = {s_i}, i=1..N, each s_i a skill of reusable procedural instructions), outputs an operation u = (a, z), where a is the operation type (the text gives generation, evolution or maintenance as examples; the full list in Table 3 is task-level generate, event-driven generate, skip, evolve, merge, add, drop) and z the operation content (for example a generated skill or a maintenance decision); applying u gives B' = Update(B, u). The objective is max over theta of E_{tau, x'}[R_task(pi(x' / B'))], where pi is the frozen downstream coding policy, x' a future task, B' used as prior knowledge, and R_task downstream task performance. A trajectory is tau = (o_1, a_1, ..., o_T, a_T, y) with o_t an observation, a_t an action such as a shell command or file edit, and y the task outcome; the goal is to learn from such trajectories without updating pi (lines 104-115). | - | Formal objective (Section 3.1, lines 104-115); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formalization | 106 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What changes is an external skill bank of natural-language instruction files (short title, granularity label, applicability condition when_to_apply, actionable rules); because the coding environments already provide fixed tools and execution interfaces, the authors do not generate new scripts, APIs or tools. Retrieved skills are inserted into the prompt of the frozen coding policy, whose original task prompt and parameters remain unchanged (line 125). The weights that are trained are those of the separate skill manager M_theta (Qwen3.5-4B-Instruct, LoRA; lines 198, 930). | - | Description of the modified component (skill bank + skill-manager weights) and of what stays fixed; not a measurement. | Appendix D Skill Examples (also §3.2 Skill Usage, Appendix A.1) | 948 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | During RL, each skill-output operation gets the hybrid reward R = lambda*R_Q + R_A*R_E (line 146): R_Q in [0,1] is a rubric-based LLM-as-judge quality score (grounding, reusability, specificity, format, actionability; line 138); R_E = V(tau^u) - b_pi(x_u) is the task-verifier score V in [0,1] of one skill-conditioned rollout of the frozen policy minus the no-skill baseline b_pi, the mean verifier score of n no-skill rollouts on the same task (line 143; n = four runs per RL task instance, line 938); R_A in [0,1] is an LLM-judged alignment factor saying whether the rollout matches the skill trigger and follows its workflow (line 144). The judge is GPT-5.4-mini (line 198) and lambda = 0.25 (Table 4, line 880); for skip, add and drop only the quality reward is used, with a higher weight (line 150). Each rubric reward is the fraction of satisfied binary yes/no questions (line 939). | - | Training-time reward definition; R_E is a verifier-score difference on a single skill-conditioned rollout vs a 4-rollout no-skill mean; R_Q and R_A are LLM-judge scores. The signal is used to train M_theta, not to accept skills at test time. | §3.3.2 Attribution-Aware Hybrid Reward Design (Eq. for R_E and R); Appendix B | 143 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | The skill-management loop has three operations. Extraction takes trajectory evidence (a single trajectory or a small set of related ones) and outputs a new task-level skill, a new event-driven skill, or skip. Evolution takes an existing skill plus new or failed trajectory evidence and outputs a revised candidate skill or skip, updating the applicability condition or procedural guidance when evidence reveals missing cases, better procedures or failure modes. Every extracted or evolved candidate then goes to maintenance (add, merge or drop against similar retrieved skills; line 123). Stored: markdown skill files; reuse: dense semantic retrieval, task-level skills matched to the task goal once before solving, event-driven skills matched online to current reasoning and observations through their trigger conditions (lines 125, 943). | - | Description of the learning loop (what is stored and how it is reused); not a measurement. | §3.2 Skill Bank Construction (also Skill Usage; Appendix C Skill Retrieval) | 121 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | For evaluation, the skill bank is built through two preparatory passes over the test set before final evaluation: in the first pass CODESKILL extracts skills from no-skill rollout trajectories, in the second it evolves skills using trajectories from skill-conditioned rollouts, and every candidate goes through add/merge/drop maintenance. Each skill's source instances are tracked through evolution and merging, and during final evaluation any skill whose provenance includes the current test instance is excluded. | - | Test-time bank-construction protocol (skills come from rollouts on other test instances of the same benchmark; retrieval is scoped to the same benchmark and granularity, line 942); not a measurement. | §4.1 Test-Time Skill Bank Construction | 206 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Acceptance into the bank is a maintenance decision made by M_theta itself: similar skills are retrieved and given to M_theta with the candidate, and it outputs add (new, uncovered useful knowledge), merge (overlapping but complementary guidance) or drop. The drop operation rejects candidates that are redundant, weakly grounded, overly specific or unlikely to transfer. | - | Acceptance rule for a candidate skill (learned add/merge/drop output of the 4B skill manager); not a measurement. | §3.2 Skill Bank Maintenance | 123 | primary | supported |
| 6 | result | With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as the frozen coding policy, CODESKILL (Qwen3.5-4B skill manager) raises average pass rate from 29.32 (no skill) to 40.35; subtask-level memory and GPT-5.4-mini prompt-based skill management improve over no-skill by 4.16 and 5.93 but trail CODESKILL by 6.87 and 5.10, and CODESKILL is best on all benchmark groups (14.5% relative gain over the strongest baseline). | 29.32 → 40.35 average pass rate; baselines trail by 6.87 and 5.10 | Task pass rate, macro-averaged over EnvBench-Python, EnvBench-Java, SWE-Bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2 (Table 1); held-out evaluation splits (150 SWE-Bench Verified instances, 150 EnvBench repositories) disjoint from training, Terminal-Bench 2 unused in training; skill bank built from the test set as in §4.1. The text gives no number of evaluation runs or seeds (searched 'seed', 'runs', 'standard deviation', 'variance'). | §4.2 Comparison with Baselines, Table 1 | 402 | primary | supported |
| 7 | result | On Terminal-Bench 2, which is not used in training (out-of-distribution for the skill manager), CODESKILL with the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B policy raises pass rate from 25.88 to 36.47 and beats the strongest baseline on this benchmark (subtask memory with GPT-5.4-mini) by 5.88; SFT-CODESKILL alone does not improve over no-skill on Terminal-Bench 2. | 25.88 → 36.47; +5.88 over subtask memory | Terminal-Bench 2 task pass rate, frozen policy Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; held out from M_theta training, though its skill bank is built from Terminal-Bench 2 test rollouts (§4.1). | §4.2 Generalization across Tasks, Table 1 | 495 | primary | supported |
| 8 | result | With GPT-5.4-mini as the frozen coding policy (the manager was trained with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B reward rollouts), CODESKILL again has the best average pass rate: +9.82 over no-skill and +3.76 over the strongest prompt-based or memory baseline, relative gains of 45.0% and 13.5%. | +9.82 / +3.76 (45.0% / 13.5% relative) | Average task pass rate over the four benchmark groups (Table 1, GPT-5.4-mini block), same skill-management and retrieval protocol; absolute differences in pass-rate units as printed. | §4.2 Generalization across Policies, Table 1 | 497 | primary | supported |
| 9 | result | Lifecycle ablation (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B policy): adding skill evolution raises average pass rate from 37.88 (extraction only) to 39.53, and full-lifecycle maintenance raises it to 40.35 while shrinking the skill bank from 1252 to 676 skills, a reduction of about 46%. | 37.88 → 39.53 → 40.35; 1252 → 676 skills (~46%) | Average task pass rate across the four benchmark groups and final skill-bank size (Table 2 'Skill Num.'). | §4.3 Lifecycle Ablation, Table 2 | 500 | primary | supported |
| 10 | cost_time | Under the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B policy, CODESKILL has the lowest macro-averaged reasoning steps in Table 1, 35.99 vs 44.12 for no skill (lines 242, 312, 493); it is not the lowest-step method on every benchmark (Terminal-Bench 2 and EnvBench-Java each have a baseline with fewer steps). | 11 | cost_time | Cost of the improvement process: Table 4 prints training time of about 210 hours for RL (lines 894-895) and about 20 hours for SFT (lines 873-874), with all training on four H100 80GB GPUs (line 823). RL runs 500 update steps (130/120/250 over the three phases, line 936) with 6 generations per prompt (line 877); each operation that outputs an injectable skill (extracted, evolved or merged) triggers one rollout of the frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B policy (line 150), on top of four pre-computed no-skill rollouts per RL task instance (line 938). | ~210 hours (RL training time) | Author-reported approximate 'Training time' from Table 4 for training the skill manager; the text does not say whether it is wall-clock or GPU-hours, nor whether it includes the frozen-policy rollouts and GPT-5.4-mini judge calls; no token or dollar cost is given for the judge or the rollouts. | Appendix A, Table 4 | 894 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 12 | environment_knowledge | Event-driven skills encode local guidance for recurring execution events in the bash/repository environment, such as command failures, error messages, test-output patterns or repeated failure modes after specific actions, and say how the agent should react when the event is triggered; they can transfer across tasks because similar execution events recur. At test time they are retrieved online from local execution signals (recent actions, observations, error messages, command and test output; line 943). | - | Description of the environment-feedback knowledge stored in event-driven skills; not an explicit state model. | §3.2 Multi-granularity Skill Bank | 119 | primary | supported |
| 13 | data_generation | SFT targets are generated by teacher models (lines 129, 928) that read normalized trajectory evidence and output structured skill-management targets; GPT-5.4-mini is named as the teacher for extraction and maintenance targets (line 198), and the text does not name the model that revises skills for evolution examples. Evolution examples are synthesized by retrieving an existing skill whose applicability condition or rules match a new, especially failed or partially successful, trajectory and asking the teacher to revise it or skip, avoiding an extra round of skill-conditioned rollouts (line 928). Source trajectories: public mini-SWE-agent rollouts on SWE-smith with Qwen3-30B as the coding agent, plus EnvBench trajectories from a ReAct-style agent (line 826). - Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2305.17126v2 · version read: arXiv 2305.17126v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v2 text also saved as 2305.17126v2-pdf.txt for the running header and Appendices C-D, which the HTML text… · v1: 2023-05-26

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | problem_definition | The paper states its objective as a division of labour rather than a formula: tool making is assigned to a powerful, resource-intensive model and tool using to a lightweight model, so that the once-off cost of making a tool is spread over many tool-using instances, 'significantly reducing average costs while maintaining strong performance'. The only formal cost expression is Table 2's big-O cost column (see the cost_time item for its symbols). | - | Statement of the objective (amortize a one-time tool-making cost over repeated instances of the same task type while keeping task accuracy); not a measurement. | Abstract, second paragraph | 70 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What is created and reused is an external artifact, the 'wrapped tool': a Python utility function plus demonstrations of how to convert a task query into a function call. It is the tool user's prompt; the tool user writes the function call in context, the call is executed, and optional postprocessing maps the output to the task's answer format (e.g. a multiple-choice option). | - | Description of the modified component (a prompt-embedded Python tool and its call demonstrations); not a measurement. | §3.1, 'Tool Using' | 107 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The acceptance signal is programmatic: whether the proposed function executes without errors (line 101) and whether it passes unit tests that the tool maker writes from 3 validation samples and executes on the proposed tool. The authors say this stage both provides examples of converting natural-language questions into function calls and verifies the tool's reliability, 'enabling the entire process to be fully automated'. (The Tool Verifier prompt, which asks for tests ending in an assert against the provided answer, appears only in the PDF v2 text, Appendix C, 2305.17126v2-pdf.txt lines 604-616; the HTML text keeps only the heading.) | 3 validation samples | Signal = program execution success plus unit tests on labelled validation samples (answers given with the samples); no LLM judge or human in the loop for tool making. | §3.1, 'Tool Making', Tool Verification | 103 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | Tool proposing follows programming by example: from 3 demonstrations the tool maker writes a Python function; if the function is unexecutable or errors, the error messages are appended to the chat history and it tries again. In verification, if a unit test fails, the error is recorded in the history and the tool maker tries to fix only the function calls in the unit tests, not the function itself (line 103). The stored, reused product is the wrapped tool (function code plus call demonstrations taken from the verification unit tests, line 105). | 3 demonstrations | Description of the tool-making loop (feedback = execution error messages kept in the maker's chat history within one tool-making episode); not a measurement. | §3.1, 'Tool Making', Tool Proposing | 101 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | For a stream of requests, a dispatcher LLM keeps a repository of tools in function-API format (a 'functional cache'). For each new instance it looks for a compatible tool and, if found, sends instance and tool to the tool user; if not, it treats the instance as a novel task, solving it with a powerful model or, if necessary, a human labeler, and caches such instances until enough are amassed to make a new tool. Unlike response caches such as GPTCache, the cache stores tools that serve functionally analogous requests (line 79). | - | Description of the serving-time reuse mechanism (what is stored: tools as function APIs plus the unsolved instances waiting for tool making); the passage does not state how many instances count as 'sufficient'. | §4 LATM Fosters a Functional Cache Mechanism | 113 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | A candidate tool is kept only if it executes and passes verification; if execution or verification fails over a preset threshold, the whole tool-making stage is treated as failed, otherwise the tool is wrapped for the tool user. Line 119 sets the maximum retry count to 3 for the tool-proposing and tool-verification stages; Table 3 counts a success as a Python function that passes the tool-verification step. | - | Accept/discard rule for a tool: execution + unit-test pass within a retry budget (max 3 retries per stage, line 119); not a measurement. | §3.1, 'Tool Making', Tool Wrapping | 105 | primary | supported |

That baseline is few-shot CoT for the first four tasks but direct few-shot prompting without CoT for Chinese Remainder Theorem and Schedule Meeting (Table 2 caption), so the last two gains are over direct prompting, not CoT. | 79.7 (+13.3), 99.6 (+38.0), 92.2 (+71.8), 98.3 (+39.1), 100.0 (+100.0), 100.0 (+81.1) | Accuracy (%) per task; the dataset split is 3 training / 3 validation / 240 test instances per task (line 117), and tools are made from the 3 + 3 non-test instances, so test instances are held out from tool making. | 0 | problem_definition | The goal is to build a specialized agent from a task collection. Given target tasks T = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1..N}, where x_i is the task specification, y_i the desired outcome and N the number of tasks, the objective is to automatically synthesize an agent pi_specialized that handles tasks in the domain defined by T. Eq. 1 writes pi_specialized = Alita-G(T, pi_master), where pi_master is a powerful general-purpose agent system (line 106). | - | Problem statement (Eq. 1); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation, Eq. 1 | 100 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Eq. 2 requires E_{(x,y)~D_target}[I{pi_specialized(x) = y}] > E_{(x,y)~D_target}[I{pi_base(x) = y}]. In words, the expected rate at which the specialized agent's output equals the desired outcome must exceed that of a baseline agent. Symbols: D_target is the target task distribution; (x, y) is a task and its desired outcome; I{.} is the indicator function; pi_base is a baseline agent without specialized capabilities. The stated objective has only this success term; Eqs. 1-2 contain no cost, token or time term (lines 103, 108). | - | Objective = expected task success (output equals desired outcome) over the target distribution; not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation, Eq. 2 | 111 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | What changes is outside the model. The specialized agent keeps the master agent's core reasoning and adds a curated MCP Box (a set of executable MCP tools) plus a RAG-based tool-selection mechanism. These are implemented as a Task Analyzer, an MCP Retriever and an MCP Executor (lines 230-234). The text describes no update of model weights; the same Manager/Web agent architecture is used throughout (line 241). | - | Description of the modified component (tool library plus retrieval); not a measurement. | §3.5 Specialized Agent Architecture | 228 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Each target task is executed K times by the master agent. MCPs are collected only from executions whose output equals the task's desired outcome, pi_master(x_i) = y_i. The raw pool L (Eq. 5) is the set of MCP_{i,j}^{(k)} from such runs; i indexes tasks (i in [N]), k the execution run (k in [K]), and j the MCPs of a run (j in [J_{k,i}], where J_{k,i} is the number of MCPs generated for task i in run k). The signal is therefore agreement with the desired outcome y_i supplied with each target task. The text does not say how the comparison is made (exact match, judge or other). | - | Harvesting signal: per-run task success against the given desired outcome y_i; not a measurement. | §3.2 Task-Driven MCP Generation, Eq. 5 | 126 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | The master agent's trajectory tau_i is a sequence of reasoning tokens r_t, action tokens a_t (including MCP generation calls) and environment observations o_t (Eq. 3, line 118). During execution, explicit prompting guides the agent to externalize reusable sub-solutions as self-contained MCPs. It is told to modularize complex sub-tasks into callable procedures with standardized interfaces and documentation, so that solving a task also expands the MCP pool. Each stored MCP_{i,j} holds executable code, a description (concise functional summary) and a use_case recording the task context that triggered its creation (Eq. 4, lines 122-125). | - | Description of what is stored from own trajectories (tool code + description + use case) and how it is produced; not a measurement. | §3.2 Task-Driven MCP Generation, Eqs. 3-4 | 119 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | A high-capacity language model (LLM_abstract, Eq. 6) rewrites each MCP in the raw pool; the text does not name this model. The rewrite performs four steps (lines 140-146): parameter generalization (hard-coded values become configurable parameters), context removal (task-specific references are removed), interface standardization to the FastMCP protocol, and documentation enhancement (docstrings and type annotations). Figure 2 shows a raw MCP that extracts measurements from scientific PDFs lifted into a parameterized FastMCP tool (line 577). | - | Description of the abstraction step; not a measurement. | §3.3 MCP Abstraction and Box Construction, Eq. 6 | 133 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | The only acceptance rule the text specifies is the success condition of Eq. 5: MCPs are kept only from runs where pi_master(x_i) = y_i. However, §5.2 (line 432) and the Table 4 caption (line 519) say the box is built by 'filtering and abstraction', and line 78 speaks of harvesting 'high-quality MCPs'. The filtering criterion is never stated, so an unstated filter beyond Eq. 5 cannot be ruled out. No per-tool test or validation of a generated MCP is described (absence). | - | Rule for admitting tools into the MCP Box; not a measurement. | §3.3 MCP Abstraction and Box Construction, Eq. 7 | 147 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

On 25 questions sampled from the GAIA validation set, the authors compared tau from 0.65 to 0.90 and top-k from 1 to 20. tau = 0.70 scored highest, at 84.0% (Table 3, lines 443-448, 526). calc.: that is 21/25 against 20/25 for the next best settings, a one-question margin. | 0.7 | Inference-time tool filter: cosine similarity between the query embedding and each MCP's description+use_case embedding (text-embedding-3-large); MCPs at or above tau = 0.7 are passed to the agent. - Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.07456v2 · version read: arXiv 2402.07456v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt); PDF v2 text (2402.07456v2-pdf.txt) consulted only for the author-affiliation mapping, the venue check and to… · v1: 2024-02-12

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | problem_definition | The paper gives no formula or formal objective. It frames OS-level agents as facing two challenges: (i) a unified interface for interacting with the OS through code, keyboard and mouse inputs, or APIs, and (ii) generalization and scalability across the vast number of applications, where hand-building a control mechanism, tools and prompts for every application is called impractical. OS-Copilot answers (i) with a universal interface (line 95); FRIDAY answers (ii) by learning to control unfamiliar applications through self-directed learning (line 98). | - | Informal problem statement; not a measurement. | §1 Introduction | 94 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The component the paper changes is the agent's long-term memory, not the model. The tool repository in procedural memory (the agent's skill set) is seeded with 4 manually created tools (e.g. web browsing, speech-to-text) and is where tools are stored and updated; tools exist either as API services invoked by POST requests or as Python files (line 128), and the generated tool in the running example is a Python class saved to a Python file (lines 153-154). Self-directed learning is said to accumulate both tools and semantic knowledge (line 159), but the experiments document only accumulated tools (Tables 10-12). Appendix D describes FRIDAY as built by prompting and names reinforcement learning and fine-tuning as future research (line 524). | 4 manually created tools | Description of the modified components (tool repository in procedural memory; semantic knowledge in declarative memory per line 159, not documented in the experiments; LLM used via prompting, weights not changed); not a measurement. | §2.2.2 Procedural Memory, Tool Repository | 128 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | environment_knowledge | Declarative memory's Semantic Knowledge module stores the agent's past trajectories or knowledge acquired from the Internet, users and the OS, with system version and current working directory as the named OS examples; the authors call it crucial for acting correctly on the current environment state and learning from past experience (line 123). The User Profile part of declarative memory is only a conceptual design (line 121). Environment fields differ by prompt: the Planner and Tool Generator prompts receive system version, current working directory and the files and folders in it (lines 547-552, 575-582); the Refiner and Critic prompts receive current working directory, working directory and files and folders but no system version (lines 601-603, 650-652); the Executor prompt receives only the working directory (line 629). | - | Description of what environment information is stored and which fields each prompt receives; the colour coding that marks declarative-memory fields (captions, e.g. line 553) is not preserved in the saved text; not a measurement. | §2.2.1 Declarative Memory, Semantic Knowledge | 123 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | Tool reuse and creation per subtask: the Configuration Tracker uses dense retrieval over long-term memory to build a prompt with related tools, user profile, OS version and working directory (line 152); when no stored tool is similar enough (similarity below a threshold), the Tool Generator writes an application-tailored tool as a Python class (in the example, AppleScript switching macOS to dark mode); the executor saves the tool code to a Python file and runs it in the terminal (line 154). | - | Description of the retrieve-or-generate step; the similarity threshold value is not given; not a measurement. | §3.1 A running example (steps 2-4, Figure 3) | 153 | primary | supported |
| 4 | signal | Because subtasks have no ground truth, the Critic collects system information before and after execution and uses an LLM to judge completion. The Critic prompt returns a boolean 'judge' and a generality 'score' from current code, task, error messages, output, working directory, files and folders and next task (lines 644-653). | - | Signal definition: LLM critic verdict over execution output and before/after OS state; not a benchmark score and not a measurement. | §2.3 Actor, Critic | 141 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | After a subtask succeeds, the critic has an LLM score the generated tool from 0 to 10, higher meaning greater potential for future reuse, and in the current implementation only tools scoring above 8 are kept by updating the tool repository. | 6 | mechanism | On a failed execution the refiner takes the critic's feedback and self-corrects the responsible action, tool or subtask; FRIDAY iterates execute (step 4), critique (step 5) and refine (step 6) until the subtask is judged complete or three attempts are used. Later subtasks retrieve from long-term memory by dense retrieval, with the prompt listed as related tools, user profiles, OS system versions and working directory (line 152); the text does not describe how semantic knowledge accumulated during learning is retrieved, and the experiments show reuse only through accumulated tools (lines 235, 249). | - | Description of the learning loop (self-proposed curriculum; accumulated tools and semantic knowledge); retrieval of accumulated semantic knowledge not described; not a measurement. | §3.2 Self-directed Learning | 159 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## s038 — OpenSkill: Open-World Self-Evolution for LLM Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.06741v1 · version read: arXiv 2606.06741v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; v1 is the only version) · v1: 2026-06-04
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): EMNLP 2026 (The 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing), main conference, paper ID 3199-MAIN, virtual presentation (session 'Virtual 2', 2026-10-25, 18:00-19:30 CET, pres…
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | Given n target tasks {(I_i, E_i)}, i = 1..n, where I_i is a natural-language instruction and E_i an execution environment, an LLM agent pi_theta (weights theta) produces a terminal state x_i = pi_theta(I_i, E_i); each task has a hidden ground-truth test suite T^GT_i with values in {0,1}. A skill set S_i = {s_i,1, ..., s_i,m} conditions the agent, x_i = pi_theta(I_i, S_i, E_i), without altering theta, and self-evolution is defined as constructing, for each task, a skill set under which the augmented agent passes its test suite, T^GT_i(pi_theta(I_i, S_i, E_i)) = 1. The construction f must be supervision-free: it may observe (I_i, E_i) but must neither observe T^GT_i nor reverse-engineer it for the virtual tests (line 168); Eq. 1 is S^_i = f(I_i, E_i) and Eq. 2 adds open-world knowledge K (public documentation, code repositories, papers, tutorials), S^_i = f(I_i, E_i, K), with f the OpenSkill pipeline (lines 168-178). Final evaluation (Eq. 6, lines 272-275) is PassRate = (1/n) * sum_i T^GT_i(pi_theta'(I_i, S^*_i, E_i)), where pi_theta' is the target agent (possibly a different model) and S^*_i the final skill set. | - | Formal problem statement (Section 2.1, Eqs. 1-2, and Eq. 6 in Section 2.2.3); not a measurement. The objective is defined per task: one skill set per target task i. | §2.1 Problem Setting, Eqs. 1-2; §2.2.3 Eq. 6 | 167 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | OpenSkill leaves model weights unchanged and instead augments the agent's context with an external skill set: 1-4 skills per task, their number fixed by the Stage-1 plan and refined jointly in one agent session (lines 218-219). The skills include scripts: during refinement the creator is told to fix the logic in its skill scripts and regenerate outputs, never to edit outputs directly (lines 1558-1559); the final evo-* skills are exported from the container and copied into the target agent's workspace (lines 1585-1588). A second artifact built per task is the virtual test suite used only during construction (Eq. 3, line 224). The authors justify the context route as computationally cheap, transferable across models and inspectable, versus weight modification being expensive, model-specific and opaque. | - | Description of the modified component (skill files in the agent's context/workspace); not a measurement. | §2.1 Problem Setting; §2.2.2; App. B.4, B.6 | 167 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The signal that drives refinement is the virtual pass rate r~(j) (Eq. 4): the fraction of the K virtual tests t~_i,k in {0,1} that the agent's output on the task passes with the round-j skill set. By design (§2.2.2, lines 232-233) each virtual test is a deterministic assertion anchored to independently verifiable facts (examples: the known row count of a public dataset, the expected range of a standard metric, the documented output format of a library function) rather than a guess at the ground-truth tests. In the implementation the verifier derives expected values either by recomputing them from the environment inputs and documented task rules or from the retrieved verification knowledge k_i^v (lines 1536-1539), and the paper's own analysis describes the added assertions as primarily defensive checks on output format, type validity and boundary conditions (lines 928-930) and notes the verifier's reliance on format-level and boundary checks (lines 1609-1611). The test generator g is an isolated verifier LLM session that writes a pytest suite, and a non-LLM parser computes r~ as passed/total with skipped tests excluded (lines 1548-1550). So r~ comes from LLM-written, programmatically executed tests, not from the benchmark's ground-truth tests and not from an LLM judge score; separately, App. F states a single GT pass/fail bit is used when the verifier is re-invoked (line 1843; see the GT-bit item). | - | r~(j) = (1//T~_i/) * sum over k of t~_i,k(pi_theta(I_i, S^(j)_i, E_i)) = passed / total virtual assertions (skipped excluded), per task and per refinement round; a proxy, not the ground-truth pass rate; test content is LLM-generated (anchored facts, recomputation from inputs and rules, and format/type/boundary checks). | §2.2.2 Eqs. 3-4; App. B.3 | 233 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | signal | Appendix F (information isolation audit) states that the only ground-truth-derived signal during skill creation is a single pass/fail bit, used when the verifier is re-invoked to write deeper tests; no GT test content, assertion details or expected values are exposed (lines 1843-1845). This qualifies the main-text statements that the pipeline never observes T^GT_i (lines 229-231) and that the hidden T^GT_i enters the pipeline only at final evaluation (lines 280-281), and it sits beside statements in the same appendix paragraph (lines 1839-1842) and in App. B.3 (lines 1543-1545) that the GT oracle is never invoked during construction. The saved text does not say how often this bit is used, whether it is one bit per task or per re-invocation, or what effect it has on the results. | - | Description of a GT-derived signal inside the construction loop (a single pass/fail bit used when the verifier is re-invoked to write deeper tests; frequency and granularity not stated); not a measurement. | App. F Information Isolation Audit, 'GT oracle bypass' | 1843 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | When the virtual pass rate is below 1, the pipeline builds a structured failure diagnostic F(j) (per-assertion results, root-cause analysis, revision suggestions) and the base agent revises the skills: S^(j+1)_i = pi_theta(S^(j)_i, F(j) / I_i, E_i, p_i, k_i) (Eq. 5). In the implementation the skill creator refines in a single long-lived session; the host returns passed/total counts, the failed-assertion list and an optional diagnosis (lines 1555-1559). What is stored and reused: the background document k_i with a deduplicated list of source URLs and the plan p_i (lines 1508-1512), the verification knowledge k_i^v, injected into the verifier (lines 1527-1528), the verifier's previous test script and failure list, inherited across rounds (lines 1551-1553), and the skill set itself, edited in place (line 1583). Learning is from the construction agent's own executions on the target task, scored by tests written by a separate verifier session (lines 1530-1533), with targeted web retrieval added when a failure is classified as a knowledge gap (lines 254-257, 1576-1578); App. F additionally states that a single GT pass/fail bit is used when the verifier is re-invoked (line 1843). | - | Description of the refinement loop (Eq. 5; App. B.1-B.5); not a measurement. | §2.2.2 'Diagnostic-driven refinement', Eq. 5; App. B.1-B.4 | 248 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | mechanism | After a failed round, an LLM classifier (gemini-3.1-flash-lite, temperature 0.1, 200 max tokens) reads the failed assertions, the diagnosis and the prior domain knowledge and outputs SELF-FIXABLE (implementation bug: wrong variable, off-by-one, format mismatch, type error) or NEEDS-DR (knowledge gap: unknown correct value, algorithm or parameter choice, library usage not covered). On SELF-FIXABLE only verifier feedback is returned; on NEEDS-DR a targeted web search k_i^(gap) is issued and its result appended to the feedback. Targeted retrieval is capped at 3 searches per task, already-searched topics are listed to discourage repetition, and a failed classifier call defaults to SELF-FIXABLE (no retrieval). | 3 searches per task | Cap on the number of targeted retrieval calls per task (configuration, also Table 5 'Max searches per task 3'); not an outcome measurement. | §2.2.2; App. B.5 Gap-vs-Bug Diagnosis and Targeted Retrieval | 1578 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | There is no comparison between candidate skill sets. The loop ends when the virtual pass rate reaches 1 or after at most J rounds (J = 3), whichever comes first; if r~ stays below 1 the budget is simply exhausted (lines 260-262). In the implementation, J is a cap of 3 surrogate-failure retries with at most one successful intervention, plus early stops on idle/stale episodes (3/10) and on token budget (warning at 70%, stop at 90%) (lines 1561-1565); exit status surrogate_pass requires r~ = 1.0 and auxiliary structural checks (lines 1559-1561). The deployed skill set is the state at loop termination, the most recently refined version, not a best-of-N snapshot selected by virtual pass rate (lines 265-266, 1583-1586). | J = 3 rounds; exit at virtual pass rate 1 | Stopping and keep rule of the refinement loop (configuration); not a measurement. | §2.2.2; §2.2.3; App. B.4, B.6 | 260 | primary | supported |
| 7 | data_generation | The virtual test suite T~_i = g(I_i, E_i, k_i^v) (Eq. 3) is generated per task. k_i^v comes from one search-grounded generation call (gemini-3.1-flash-lite, temperature 0.3, Google-Search grounding) that asks only for four classes of independently checkable anchors: (i) reference values computable by hand for small, well-known inputs; (ii) dataset-level statistical invariants (row counts, sum-to-one constraints, monotonicity, value ranges); (iii) cross-validation procedures using alternative tools or libraries; (iv) published benchmarks or reference implementations with known input-output pairs (lines 1516-1525). | 0 | problem_definition | The task environment is a POMDP M = <X, A, T, O, Omega, R>. X is the underlying state space (the complete filesystem and processes); A the agent's actions (terminal commands and file edits); T(x'/x,a) the deterministic transition from state x to successor x' under action a; O the observation space (command execution results); Omega(o/x,a) maps post-action states to partial observations; y_H denotes the output artifacts in the terminal state x_H; R(y_H) in [0,1] scores those artifacts against hidden ground-truth tests. The agent sees only partial observations o_t and acts on the history h_t = (o_1, a_1, ..., a_{t-1}, o_t). A skill S conditions the LLM policy, a_t ~ pi_theta(a_t / h_t, S) (Eq. 1). The objective is the expected terminal reward J(S) = E_{tau ~ P(tau / pi_theta, S, M)}[R(y_H)] (Eq. 2), where H is the terminal horizon and tau = (o_1, a_1, ..., a_{H-1}, o_H) the execution trajectory, and the goal is S* = argmax_S J(S) (Eq. 3). ## s040 — GPTSwarm: Language Agents as Optimizable Graphs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.16823v3 · version read: arXiv 2402.16823v3 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2024-02-26
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): ICML 2024: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:62743-62767 (2024), main conference, Oral; ICML 2024 official paper data give decision 'Accept (Oral)', Oral…

| 0 | problem_definition | A single language agent is a directed computational graph G = (N, E, F, o): N is the set of computational nodes, E ⊂ N×N the set of directed edges, F = {f_n} the set of computational routines (one per node) and o ∈ N the output node; the paper restricts itself to DAGs. Given input x, nodes run in topological order; node n receives x and z_n (the outputs of its predecessor nodes, empty if it has none), applies f_n(z_n, x), and the graph output is ŷ = G(x) = f_o(z_o, x) (lines 142-151, Algorithm 1). A swarm of K agents is a composite graph G_𝓔 = (N', E_𝓔, F', o'), where N', E', F' are the unions of the agents' nodes, edges and routines, o' is one agent's output node, and E_𝓔 = E' ∪ 𝓔 adds a selection 𝓔 of edges between nodes of different agents (the communication channels); composite graphs are also restricted to DAGs (lines 166-172). | - | Formal definition of the object being optimized; not a measurement. | §2.2 Graph Definition (Algorithm 1) | 142 | primary | supported |

## s041 — Self-Taught Optimizer (STOP): Recursively Self-Improving Code Generation

- Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.02304v3 · version read: arXiv 2310.02304v3 (PDF full text saved as .txt; arXiv has no HTML rendering for v3, status 404) · v1: 2023-10-03
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): COLM 2024 (Conference on Language Modeling, first edition), main conference, Spotlight. The OpenReview record has venue 'COLM', venueid colmweb.org/COLM/2024/Conference and a Camera_Ready invitation.…
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper formalizes recursively self-improving code generation. Sigma* is the set of finite text strings; L: Sigma* -> Sigma* is a randomized black-box LM (the system can call it but has no implementation information); a utility u = (u_func, u_str) pairs a black-box, possibly randomized function u_func: Sigma* -> R that assigns bounded real values to solution strings with a description string u_str (which may simply be its source code); a task tau = (u, s) is a utility plus a solution s in Sigma*; an improver I is a program that returns s' = I(u, s, L), ideally with u(s') >> u(s) (Eq. 1). The goal is an improver with high expected utility u_bar(I) = E_(u,s)~D [u(I(u, s, L))] over a distribution D of downstream tasks. For training, with a collection D of n tasks drawn i.i.d. from that distribution (the saved text writes both with the letter D), the meta-utility is u_hat(I) = (1//D/) * sum over (u,s) in D of u(I(u, s, L)) (Eq. 2), i.e. the mean downstream utility of the solutions the improver returns. The description string of u_hat shown to the LM is 'grey-box': it says the utility is an average over downstream tasks but does not include the tasks (lines 214-217). | - | Formal objective (Eqs. 1-2); u_hat is an average of bounded real-valued task utilities; not a measurement. | §3 Problem Statement, Eqs. (1)-(2) | 208 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Only the scaffolding program is modified: a Python 'improver' that structures calls to a fixed LM and is applied to its own source code. The authors call this recursively self-improving code generation rather than full recursive self-improvement because the underlying LM remains unchanged (line 81); the work focuses only on the model's ability to recursively improve the scaffold that calls it. | - | Scope of what the loop may modify (improver code only; LM weights fixed); not a measurement. | §1 Introduction | 86 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The signal that an improver is better is the meta-utility u_hat: each candidate improver is run on the downstream training tasks and the executable utility of the solutions it returns is averaged (Algorithm 1, function lines 180-185). STOP therefore selects improvers on downstream utility improvement, motivated by the intuitions that improvers that are good at improving downstream solutions may be good scaffolds and hence good at self-improvement, and that selecting for single-round improvements may lead to better multi-round improvements (lines 255-258). For LPN the downstream utility is a solution's average accuracy on sampled task instances (lines 301-303). | - | Signal = u_hat(I), the mean of downstream task utilities u(I(u,s,L)) over the training task set; each u is task-specific scoring code returning a bounded real value. | §4 Self-Taught Optimizer, 'Intuition'; Algorithm 1 | 254 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | The utility is handed to the improver in two forms: as a callable function and as a description string containing the essential elements of the utility source code, which lets budget constraints (e.g. on runtime or function calls) be conveyed. Putting the budget instructions in the seed improver prompt instead led to their removal and to reward-hacking attempts in later iterations (lines 277-279), and replacing the source code with a purely English description reduced the frequency of non-trivial improvement (lines 281-283). Appendix K adds that the description string need not match the true code exactly (irrelevant logging code and random seeds are obfuscated, and simpler timeout mechanisms are shown; lines 2562-2566). | - | How the evaluation signal is presented to the LM; the English-description comparison is a qualitative observation with no number given. | §4 'Describing the utility'; Appendix K | 273 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | STOP begins with a seed improver I0 and defines the t-th improver as I_t = I_{t-1}(u_hat, I_{t-1}, L): the current improver is run with the meta-utility as its utility and its own code as the solution to improve, for a prespecified number of iterations T. The seed improver (Figure 2) prompts the LM with the current solution and the utility description string, requests min(max_responses_per_call, utility budget) candidates in one batch at temperature 0.7, extracts the code and returns the candidate with the highest utility (lines 52-74). What is carried between rounds is the improver code: the framework maintains a single improver at each step (line 545), and each prompt from the self-improving scaffold contains only a template with placeholders for the task and solution, so the LM does not see the downstream task (lines 313-316). | - | Procedure description (recursion over improver code, seed improver sampling and argmax); not a measurement. | §4; Algorithm 1; Figure 2 | 252 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Within a round, what survives is whatever the current improver returns. The seed improver (Figure 2) returns the highest-utility candidate among the newly sampled ones (line 73, max(new_solutions, key=utility); lines 263-265) without comparing them against the input solution; when it improves itself, the utility is the meta-utility of each candidate improver. Algorithm 1's loop body is only I_t <- I_{t-1}(u_hat, I_{t-1}, L) (line 178), with no comparison against I_{t-1}, so from the second round on the acceptance rule is whatever selection code the generated improver contains (e.g. the Figure 5 improver keeps a top-3 list seeded with the initial solution and returns its best entry, lines 366-367, 407). The authors note that improvement need not be monotonic per run (lines 310-313), that any improvement attempt may result in worse performance and further deterioration (lines 540-541), and that with GPT-3.5 suboptimal scaffolds that unintentionally returned the original solution could be selected (lines 423-425). | - | Acceptance rule = the selection code of the improver being run; for the seed improver, argmax of the (meta-)utility over the newly sampled candidates with no incumbent comparison (Figure 2, line 73); generated improvers may use other rules. Not a measurement. | §4 'Designing the seed improver'; Figure 2; Algorithm 1 | 264 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | Selecting on utility alone rewarded constraint violations: when budget constraints (queries to the downstream utility, LM calls, samples per call) were not strictly enforced, most generated programs initially followed them, but those that ignored them performed better and were therefore identified by the improver as better. Constraints written in the seed improver were often omitted when revising the improver, for 'simplification', and in at least one proposed solution the LM attempted to create a new LM object with larger constraints (lines 501-509; Appendix C, Figure A.18, captioned a circumvention attempt). ## s043 — Huxley-Gödel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.21614v3 · version read: arXiv 2510.21614v3 (HTML full text saved as .txt; latest of three versions) · v1: 2025-10-24
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): ICLR 2026 (International Conference on Learning Representations 2026), main conference (proceedings track 'Conference'), Oral; official ICLR 2026 paper data give decision 'Accept (Oral)', Oral Sessio…
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | Self-improvement is formalized as an iterative tree search over self-modified agents. The archive T_t is a tree of agents at iteration t, started as T_0 = {a_0} with a fixed initial agent; at each iteration a policy pi samples an action from A_t = M_t union V_t, where m_a in M_t instructs agent a to produce a self-modification that is added as a child of a, and v_a in V_t evaluates agent a on one more downstream task (lines 100-103). The objective is J(pi) = E[U(a_final)]: pi is the search algorithm (DGM, SICA and HGM are instances), a_final = argmax over the final tree T_B of Score_pi(a), with B the termination iteration and Score part of the policy (line 104), E the expectation over the stochastic search, and U the utility of the returned agent, taken as the average of binary success indicators across all downstream tasks (line 106). | - | Formal objective of the search problem; U = average of binary task-success indicators of the final agent only (no time, token or money term). | §2 Self-Improvement as Tree-Search | 105 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Clade-metaproductivity is defined as CMP_pi(T, a) = E_{T_B ~ p_pi(./T, a)}[U(argmax_{a' in C(T_B, a)} Score_pi(a'))], which equals E[max_{a' in C(T_B, a)} U(a')] if Score = U (lines 147-152). Symbols: T is the current tree of agents and a an agent in it; p_pi is the distribution of the trajectory when policy pi unrolls the search to the end of the episode, producing the final archive T_B (line 138); C(T_B, a) is the clade of a, the subtree of T_B rooted at a; Score_pi is the final-agent selection metric; U is the utility. CMP localizes global metaproductivity GMP, which takes the argmax over the whole final tree and corresponds to a Q-value with the archive as state and the agent to expand as action (lines 136, 139). Theorem 1: under Assumption 1, access to the CMP oracle is sufficient to implement the Godel Machine (line 157; proof in App. A). | - | Definition of the quantity the search tries to estimate; not a measurement. | §3.2 Metaproductivity and Clade-Metaproductivity; Theorem 1 | 154 | primary | supported |
| 2 | problem_definition | The theory is restricted to Assumption 1 (lines 122-131): the objective depends only on the final agent, with no rewards before termination; utility is measured on evaluation tasks under repeatable trials (for any agent-task pair the expected outcome is independent of evaluation time or prior events, line 127; the testing environment is reset for each test, line 120); Godel Machine proofs consume no budget; and each self-modification costs exactly one budget unit. For the theoretical analysis the authors also assume that the only operation incurring a time cost is the self-modification itself (line 120). The proof in App. A additionally assumes that the Godel Machine prover has full knowledge of the utility function, so evaluation actions are excluded from its action space (lines 543, 551), and that the computation budget is finite and known (line 553). Our reading: evaluation time is therefore not costed in the theory, while the experiments cap the number of task evaluations (800 in §4.2, line 260; 8000 in §4.3.1, line 302). | - | Modelling assumptions of the theoretical result (Assumption 1 in §3.1 plus the two further conditions listed for the proof in App. A, lines 545-557); not a measurement. | §3.1; Assumption 1 | 120 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | what_is_changed | What is modified is the coding agent's own code: agents edit their own codebases (line 66) and each self-modification creates a child agent in the tree (line 103). The §4.2 initial agent, adopted from the official DGM implementation with minor changes (API support, a timeout option, a limit on LLM interaction length), is a single loop of LLM queries with two tools, file editing and bash command execution, and a one-hour limit per agent execution; the SWE-bench initial agent adds two functions that summarize existing tests and execute tests with a generated report (line 656). For §4.3 the file-editing tool is removed, leaving only bash, and the limit is extended to five hours for both self-modification and task evaluation (line 657). The backbone LLMs are fixed per experiment by the authors (line 259); the saved text describes no weight updates. | one hour (§4.2); five hours (§4.3) | Description of the modifiable object and of the starting point; the time limits are per-execution caps, not measured times. | App. C.1 Initial Agents | 655 | primary | supported |
| 4 | what_is_changed | From manual inspection of the diff patch files generated by self-modification (line 712), the authors report a discovered self-modification that implements iterative refinement, so that during one expansion (self-modification) step the agent performs multiple self-modifications (line 713). Listing 1, captioned as the agent that executes multiple self-modifications per instruction (line 718), shows a patch that adds an attempt_error_resolution function called when tests fail; it diagnoses errors from the test output and returns 'Would attempt ...' / 'Would analyze ...' messages that are then logged, rather than applying fixes (lines 720-777). Many agents also tend to write the chunk they self-modify into a diff patch file, usually with a constant file name; when multiple consecutive self-modifying attempts apply, the resulting patch file shows nested edit records (line 714). | - | Qualitative description of discovered code changes from the authors' manual inspection of self-modification diff patches; not a measurement. | App. F Discovered Agents; Listing 1 | 713 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | signal | The improvement signal is benchmark task outcome only: for each agent the loop counts passed and failed tests, n_success(a) and n_failure(a) (line 167), i.e. binary success on SWE-bench Verified or Polyglot coding tasks, and U is the average of these binary indicators (line 106). On Polyglot the authors follow DGM's setting, in which agents have no access to private test cases or test results (line 207). The text names no LLM judge or human rating in the loop. | - | Per-agent counts of passed and failed benchmark tests (binary success per agent-task pair); not a measurement. | §3.3 Expansion Policy | 167 | primary | supported |
| 6 | mechanism | The loop stores an archive: the tree of all agents with per-agent counters n_success(a), n_failure(a) and clade counters n^C_success(a), n^C_failure(a) (Algorithm 1 steps 2-3, lines 608-610). Each evaluation allocates one benchmark task to one agent, then updates that agent's counters and the clade counters of the agent and all its ancestors (steps 19-21, lines 642-646). These are reused as CMP-hat(a) = n^C_success(a) / (n^C_success(a) + n^C_failure(a)) (line 173), with n^C summed over all agents in the clade C(a), the subtree rooted at a and including a itself (lines 154, 169), which is a weighted average of the clade members' empirical means, each weighted by that agent's number of task evaluations (lines 165, 176). The loop thus learns from the outcomes of the task runs of an agent and its descendants; the saved text does not describe what information the self-modifying agent reads when it produces a modification. | - | Description of stored state and update rule; not a measurement. | §3.3 Expansion Policy; App. B Algorithm 1 step 21 | 646 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 7 | selection_rule | HGM never rejects a candidate: Algorithm 1 adds every created child to the tree (steps 11-12, lines 626-628); candidates are prioritized instead. Selection policy (after UCB-Air): expand at time t if N_t^alpha >= /T_t/, with N the number of evaluations and /T_t/ the number of agents, otherwise evaluate (line 194); Algorithm 1 also requires that expandable parents exist (step 5, line 614). Expansion policy: the parent is drawn by Thompson sampling from Beta(tau(1 + n^C_success(a)), tau(1 + n^C_failure(a))) over all agents, i.e. on clade counts (line 180; lines 618-624). Evaluation policy: the agent to test on one more task is drawn by Thompson sampling on its own counts, Beta(tau(1 + n_success(a)), tau(1 + n_failure(a))), among agents with remaining tasks (line 185; line 634). The authors say that decoupling expansion from evaluation, with every evaluation at the granularity of a single agent-task pair, enables early stopping on unpromising agents (line 109). tau is a scheduler increasing with time, favouring exploration early and a polarized distribution near the end (line 178), set to B/b with b the remaining budget; alpha = 0.6 (line 207). At budget exhaustion the returned agent is the best-belief agent, argmax of I_epsilon(1 + n_success(a), 1 + n_failure(a)) with I the regularized incomplete beta function (lines 196-200), epsilon = 1 (line 207). | - | Rules for choosing expand vs evaluate, which parent to expand, which agent to evaluate, and which agent to return; not a measurement. | §3.3 Selection / Expansion / Evaluation Policy, Final Agent Selection; App. B | 194 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 8 | result | Pearson correlation between each method's selection criterion and the empirical CMP of nodes in its own finished search tree (empirical CMP = maximum empirical mean task performance within the node's clade, clade root excluded; line 212, App. D line 664). To avoid target leakage, HGM's estimator excludes the evaluations of the clade root and of the subtree rooted at the direct child that contains the empirical maximum (line 216; App. D lines 666-672); for SICA and DGM the estimator is the agent's benchmark performance (line 674). ## s045 — JudgeFlow: Agentic Workflow Optimization via Block Judge

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.07477v2 · version read: arXiv 2601.07477v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt); PDF v2 text used only for Appendix C/D prompts and figure labels; v1 HTML text compared for version changes · v1: 2026-01-12
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | A workflow is built in three layers. A configured operator O(D) is the basic unit of agentic action: O is a categorical label for its core function (e.g. generate, self_refine) and D is the operator configuration (LLM backbone, prompt template and other hyperparameters) (line 98). A logic block (B, C) orchestrates one or more configured operators: B is the block type from the set of three types SequenceLogic (seq), LoopLogic (for, repeats until a stopping condition) and ConditionalLogic (cond, runs a condition operator and then one of two operator sequences) (lines 98-104), and C is the block configuration, i.e. the configured operators in the block plus block-level parameters such as the loop stopping condition. The workflow is the tuple W = ({(B_i, C_i)}_{i=1}^M, S), where M is the number of logic blocks and S is the ordered top-level sequence of blocks; each block may internally contain conditional or iterative control. | - | Formal definition of the object being optimized (operator, logic block, workflow); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation | 105 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Eq. 1: each block i maps the previous state to a new state, a'_i = phi_exe^(i)(a'_{i-1}, q; B_i, C_i) for i = 1..M, where q is the input query from dataset D (available to every block), phi_exe^(i) is the execution function of block i, a'_{i-1} is the state received from the previous block, a'_i the new state, and a'_0 = empty set. The final output a'_M is scored by the evaluation function phi_eval against the ground-truth answer a of q. Eq. 2: W* = argmax over W in the search space of candidate workflows of E_{(q,a)~D}[phi_eval(a'_M, a)], i.e. the workflow that maximizes expected evaluation score over the dataset. The objective contains only the evaluation score; Eq. 2 has no cost, latency or step term. | - | Optimization objective: expected per-query evaluation score phi_eval(a'_M, a) against ground truth over dataset D; not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation, Eqs. 1-2 (lines 106-116) | 111 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | The LLM-based optimizer produces W' = Optimizer(W, B_sel, A, sample(L_{B_sel})) (Eq. 3), where A is one action from a predefined set: Add Block (introduce a new block B_new with configuration C_new connected directly with the low-performing block B_sel), Remove Block (remove B_sel with its incident edges and reconnect its predecessor and successor), or Modify Block (update B_sel's configuration C_sel to C'_sel); the optimizer chooses A adaptively from the diagnostic signals in L_{B_sel} (line 266). What changes is therefore the workflow structure and block/operator configuration (which includes prompt template and LLM backbone, line 98), not model weights: the introduction motivates keeping the underlying model parameters fixed (line 71) and the LLMs are accessed via API (line 286). In the experiments workflows are limited to M <= 3 blocks (line 286). | - | Description of the edit space (three modification actions applied to the selected block); not a measurement. | §3.2.2 Optimization-Update, Eq. 3 and action list (lines 254-266) | 259 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | For each query q with ground-truth answer a, the workflow is executed and scored, s = phi_eval(a'_M, a); s is recorded in P_scores for computing W's overall performance. A threshold epsilon marks successful execution: if s >= epsilon the instance counts as a success and the algorithm moves to the next input; otherwise the failure is sent to the Judge. The experiments set epsilon = 1 (line 286); scores are solve rate on GSM8K, MATH and AIME and pass@1 on MBPP and HumanEval (line 282). The signal that decides whether a workflow is good is therefore a ground-truth benchmark score; the LLM Judge only localizes where a failed run went wrong. | - | Per-query score phi_eval against the ground-truth answer, thresholded at epsilon (epsilon = 1 in experiments) into success/failure; P_W = CalPerformance(P_scores) over the dataset. | §3.2.1 Evaluation-Judge (Algorithm 1 lines 5-11) | 121 | primary | supported |
| 4 | signal | If s < epsilon, the quadruple Q = (W, q, a, {a'_i}_{i=1}^M), i.e. workflow, query, ground-truth answer and every block's output, is given to the Judge, which assesses each block's responsibility for the failure and returns a rank vector (r_i)_{i=1}^M with r_i = 1 for the block deemed most responsible and r_i = M for the least responsible; the vector is appended to R_ranks. ## s047 — Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.01770v2 · version read: arXiv 2606.01770v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt); v1 HTML also fetched and diffed: only the stamp and the abstract's code link differ, no number changed · v1: 2026-06-01
