- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | Tasks arrive as an open-ended stream x_1, x_2, ..., x_T with x_t ~ P_t, where P_t is the task distribution at time t and each x_t has a fixed ground truth y(x_t). The agent sees the history H_t = {(x_i, r_i, tau_i)} for i = 1..t-1, where r_i is the (optionally available) realized reward on task x_i and tau_i is the agent's solving trajectory (actions, intermediate observations, tool calls). A harness C = phi(H_t) with /C/ <= K is a bounded representation (prompts, skills, memory, tools) with capacity budget K; phi is the evolver, the agentic system that turns history into the harness. The solver acts by a_t ~ pi(a / x_t, C_t), where pi is the LLM-induced sampling distribution over actions given the task and harness (line 109). Utility V(C, x_t) = E_{a_t ~ pi(./x_t, C)}[r(a_t, y(x_t))], the expected reward of the harness-conditioned solver (Eq. 1, line 115). Full-history utility V(H_t, x_t) = sup over /C/ <= K of V(C, x_t) (line 119). Regret(phi, x_t) = V(H_t, x_t) - V(phi(H_t), x_t) >= 0 (Eq. 2, line 122). C*_Phi(x_t) is the best harness any evolver in class Phi could build if allowed to condition on x_t at solve time (Eq. 3, lines 129-133). Proposition 1: E_{x_t}[Regret(phi, x_t)] = L_evo(Phi) + L_adapt(phi) (Eq. 4, line 137), with evolution loss L_evo = E[V(H_t, x_t) - V(C*_Phi(x_t), x_t)] (the evolver class's capability gap) and adaptation loss L_adapt = E[V(C*_Phi(x_t), x_t) - V(phi(H_t), x_t)] (the loss from committing to one harness before seeing x_t) (Eqs. 5-6, lines 143-151). The utility in Eqs. 1-6 is expected task reward only; no cost, token, step or latency term appears in the formulation. | - | Formal objective (reward-based regret over a task stream); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation; §3.2 Analytical Framework, Eqs. 1-6 | 109 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The model weights stay fixed (no training or fine-tuning, line 487); what changes is the harness in the solver's workspace, which is a git repository. The evolver builds regime-specific git branches (e.g., branch/crypto-classical, branch/binary-reversing), each with its own prompt, skills and tool registry (line 164); the Builder edits prompts/system.md, tools/ (evolved tool scripts) and infra/ (evolved infrastructure) (lines 1446-1449). All three benchmarks start from zero seed skills, tools and memory entries; seed prompts are 27 (PolyBench), 24 (CTF-Dojo) and 114 (FutureX, with an infrastructure scaffold) lines (Table 4, lines 573-598). At solve time a router agent (Sonnet 4.6, Table 3 line 505) reads each branch's workspace via git show and picks one branch, which the solver checks out (line 164); its prompt routes to a specialized branch with confidence >= 0.7 only if exactly one branch matches strongly, otherwise to main (lines 1394-1397), although on the routing subsets the router never used the main fallback (line 1005). In a designed replay analysis in which one branch is seeded per task category, the tree is evolved over the stream and every task is replayed through every branch (lines 305, 316), the Oracle-minus-Naive gap (the paper's empirical L_adapt) is +37.5 pp Pass@1 on CTF-Dojo, +8.8 pp CWR on PolyBench and +6.9 pp on FutureX (not significant after correction); Adapt-minus-Naive is +17.5, +2.7 and -5.2 (Table 11, lines 1071, 1101-1108; 40/80/58 replay tasks). The paper describes Adapt both as category-based routing (§4.5, line 316) and as the LLM router's actual choice on the nav run (Appendix G, lines 1003, 1072). | - | Description of the editable surface and the solve-time selection operator; the routing numbers are Pass@1 (%) or CWR (%) means on replay subsets (40/80/58 tasks) of a designed tree seeded with one branch per task category (Table 11; lines 305, 316, 1003); Oracle and Worst are post-hoc bounds (line 703); Adapt's definition differs between §4.5 and Appendix G. | §3.4 Solve-Time Adaptation via Harness-Tree Routing; Appendix B Table 4; Appendix J builder and router prompts | 164 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | The evolver's outcome signal is the benchmark's own ground truth, released to the evolver only after resolution: a temporal-reveal gate surfaces a task's evaluation signal to the evolver only after its resolution date (line 159); each task stores a release timestamp and, when available, a resolution timestamp, and evolution cycles receive the trajectory immediately but outcome feedback only after the task has resolved, so unresolved tasks stay unlabeled history (line 699). ## s049 — The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators

- Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.26294v2 · version read: arXiv 2606.26294v2 (PDF text saved as .txt; arXiv HTML for v2 returned 404) · v1: 2026-06-24
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | Self-improvement is formalized as tree search over a growing archive T_t of agent nodes seeded with T_0 = {a_0}: at each step t the search either modifies a node a (adding the edited copy as a child of a) or evaluates a node on one task, recording a binary outcome o in {0,1}; S_a and F_a count the successes and failures node a accumulates; when the evaluation budget B is exhausted the highest-scoring node is returned. The search utility is clade metaproductivity CMP(a) = n^C_success(a) / (n^C_success(a) + n^C_failure(a)) in [0,1], where the clade C(a) is the subtree rooted at a and n^C_success(a), n^C_failure(a) pool the successes and failures of all nodes in C(a); nodes are picked for expansion or evaluation by Thompson sampling over these clade-level outcomes. The final agent is chosen by the epsilon-best-belief score BB_eps(a) = I^-1_eps(1 + S_a, 1 + F_a), with eps in (0,1) a confidence level and I^-1_eps the inverse regularized incomplete Beta function, i.e. the eps-quantile of the Beta posterior over S_a and F_a (a conservative utility estimate). In RQGM (§3.2, lines 228-253) each node is a workspace of K roles R = {r_1..r_K}, each role r with task pool D_r; p_{r,d,j}(a) is node a's expected binary success rate on task d in D_r under epoch vector j = (j_1..j_M), one epoch index per evaluator-dependent slot (M <= K); the per-role rate is p_{r,j}(a) = (1//D_r/) sum over d in D_r of p_{r,d,j}(a), and the agent utility is U_j(a) = (1//R/) sum over r in R of p_{r,j}(a), both in [0,1], so all utilities are epoch-local. | - | Formal problem statement and utility definitions (Eq. for CMP, BB_eps, p_{r,j}, U_j); not a measurement. | §3.1 Preliminaries: Self-Improvement as Tree Search; §3.2 Search Space, 'Utility definition' | 212 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Each archive node is a shared, evolvable workspace of task agents and learned evaluators plus a meta-agent that oversees and can modify the workspace; the meta-agent and role-agent code are editable and roles may re-use each other's code; only the scoring and orchestration harness is fixed (line 237), and the fixed search configuration of Table 3 is not exposed to the meta-agent (line 1047). The verbatim meta-agent instruction allows modifying any part of the codebase, including the meta-agent's own loop, prompts, tool surface and the task-agent harness (lines 1148-1150); Table 4 exposes runtime settings such as output tokens per call (initial 32,768), timeouts, coder tool calls per task (initial <= 16) and meta-agent tool calls per turn (<= 40) (lines 1069-1079). Every task agent starts from a shared minimal template with no role-specific code, described as one LLM call (line 1123); the coder is the exception, the one role with tool access in the initial configuration (bash, editor and model delegation, at most 16 tool calls per task; lines 1133-1134). Across roles the search's most common move rewrites a vague one-line instruction into a specific, criterion-bearing rubric (lines 1293-1294). | - | Description of the editable search space (Table 4 surface editable, Table 3 configuration fixed); not a measurement. | §3.2 Search Space, 'Multi-agent architecture' (also App. C.5, Table 4, App. E) | 237 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | signal | Each domain pairs a generator role with a learned evaluator role and a ground-truth anchor (lines 338-346): paper writing with paper review, anchored to APReS accept/reject decisions; proof writing with proof grading, anchored to IMO-GradingBench human grades, where a proof counts as accepted only when the epoch's frozen grader awards full credit (7 of 7); coding uses two anchors, the coding agent anchored to executable Polyglot tests and a co-evolved code reviewer anchored to CRAVE (accepted/rejected pull requests) that scores each Polyglot patch at generation time. Because Polyglot is built around multi-turn agent editing, the paper calls this agent-as-a-judge reviewer a much cheaper and complementary surrogate objective (lines 417-419): cheaper than multi-turn coding-agent execution because the reviewer is queried once (lines 24, 112-113), and complementary to test execution (line 112). During search, evaluator-dependent task agents (writer, prover) are scored by their epoch-local frozen evaluator (Fig. 2 caption, lines 199-201; lines 238-241). | - | Sources of the binary outcome per role: execution tests (Polyglot), human-label anchors for evaluators (APReS decisions, IMO-GradingBench grades, CRAVE PR labels), and a frozen LLM evaluator for generator roles without a benchmark; not a measurement. | §4 Experimental Design, 'Domains and ground-truth anchors' | 344 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | RQGM separates feedback that creates nodes from evidence that selects them: training results of each node and its ancestors are shown to the meta-agent to guide self-modification but never influence search utility; node selection uses only the validation split, and final performance is reported on a separate held-out test split (3 train samples per node, Table 3). The reported endpoints are the specialist (highest best-belief on one target utility) and the generalist (highest average best-belief across active utilities) (lines 352-353). ## s050 — Group-Evolving Agents: Open-Ended Self-Improvement via Experience Sharing

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.04837v1 · version read: arXiv 2602.04837v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v1 text consulted only for the title block) · v1: 2026-02-04
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | problem_definition | The paper frames open-ended self-improvement as evolution in which a group of agents, not a single agent, is the unit of evolution. GEA keeps an archive A of all discovered agents; each iteration (1) selects K parent agents from the archive with a Performance-Novelty criterion and (2) lets the parent group jointly produce an offspring group of the same size K through experience sharing across the parents (lines 81-82). Algorithm 2 takes the parent group G = {a_1, ..., a_K}, the archive A and a coding benchmark T as input and returns the offspring group G' (/G'/ = K) and the updated archive (lines 147-149). The paper states no single objective function; its only formulas (Eq. 1-3) define parent selection (see the selection_rule item for every symbol). | - | Problem formalization (archive, parent group, offspring group, two stages per iteration); not a measurement. | §3 Method, opening paragraph; Algorithm 2 | 80 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What is modified is the agent's own implementation (framework code), not a prompt store: each agent's reflection module analyzes the shared traces and produces evolution directives targeting its workflow, tool usage or prompting strategies; the evolution module turns the directives into framework-level patches, which are applied to the agent (Algorithm 2: Reflect, Evolve, ApplyPatch). Line 126 says evolution proceeds through iterative modifications of the agent's implementation. | - | Description of the modified component; not a measurement. | §3.2 Open-Ended Group Evolution | 219 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | Appendix Table 3 lists the lineage patches of the top-3 GEA agents on SWE-bench Verified with a Delta Score each. For the Top-1 agent: docutils_debug +0.10, modified core agent logic +0.10, updated tests logic +0.22, add snippet_extract tool +0.10, then three edit-tool updates (+0.01, +0.05, +0.02; lines 697-702). The caption states that the performance-improving patches primarily enhance workflows and tool usage rather than model-specific prompting strategies (line 728). | +0.10 (docutils_debug); +0.22 (Updated tests logic) | Delta Score per patch along the agent's lineage as printed in Table 3; the text does not define the scale or the task set behind Delta Score beyond 'on SWE-bench Verified' in the caption. | Appendix A.2 Case Study, Table 3 | 688 | primary | supported |

The authors adopt staging to mitigate the cost of evaluating every evolved agent on the full benchmarks (line 223). Unlike Polyglot, where evolution is conducted 'exclusively' on a 10-task set (line 227, which contrasts this with SWE-bench Verified), the text names no held-out split for SWE-bench Verified: the full-Verified evaluation of the top-2 agents is not described as disjoint from the tasks used during evolution. | 10 tasks; 50-task Verified-Mini; top-2 to full set | Success rate of an agent on the staged SWE-bench subsets (10-task sanity set, 50-task Verified-Mini, full Verified for the top-2 agents). | 5 | mechanism | For each parent agent the loop collects four evolutionary traces (lines 209-216): the code-modification patches already applied to its framework; a predicted task patch it generated for a randomly sampled unsolved task; that task's execution logs, including the complete tool-invocation history and workflow; and the task's evaluation outcome, which the authors say exposes failure modes and directions for framework-level improvement. The traces of all parents are pooled (S = union of T_j, Algorithm 2) and given as shared input to every parent, so each agent reflects on its own and the other members' failures and patches while diverging through adaptations to its own codebase (line 218). The DGM baseline differs in that the reflection module receives only the agent's own traces (line 242). | - | Description of what experience is stored and how it is reused; not a measurement. | §3.2 Open-Ended Group Evolution; Algorithm 2 | 218 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Parent selection ranks every archive agent by score(i) = alpha_i * sqrt(nov(i)) (Eq. 3) and takes the top-K. ## s052 — Curious Causality-Seeking Agents in Open-ended Worlds (arXiv listing title for 2506.23068: 'Curious Causality-Seeking Agents Learn Meta Causal World')

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.23068v3 · version read: arXiv 2506.23068v3 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2025-06-29
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): NeurIPS 2025 (poster), main conference: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38, Main Conference Track; DOI 10.52202/085713-5145
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | Definition 3 formalizes the world model as a Meta-Causal Graph MG = {G_u}_{u in U}. Symbols: X = {X_i}_{i in [p]} are the p environment state variables (e.g. 'door open'); U is a set of latent meta states; each G_u is a causal subgraph (a DAG over the p variables) that is active in meta state u; M_u is the binary causality skeleton matrix of G_u, with M_u[i,j] = 1 meaning variable i is a parent of variable j in G_u; C: X -> U is the state-to-meta-state mapping that assigns each observation x its active meta state u = C(x). (MG, C) is a Meta-Causal Graph if (1) a ground-truth mapping C exists and (2) M_u differs from M_u' for every u != u'. The underlying MG is assumed invariant; identifying it takes two steps: identify the latent meta states, then identify each meta state's causal subgraph (line 147). | - | Formal definition of the object to be learned; not a measurement. | §3.1 Meta-Causal Graph, Definition 3 (lines 136-147) | 139 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The training objective is L = L_MLE + lambda_sparse * L_sparse + lambda_mask * L_mask + lambda_quantization * L_quantization (line 276). L_MLE = -log P(X_j^{t+1} / Pa_{G_u}(X_j)) is the negative log-likelihood of the next value of variable X_j given its parents in the subgraph of the active meta state u (line 271); L_sparse = //M_hat_theta//_1 is the L1 norm of the causal-skeleton probability matrix, added to favour parsimonious causal structures (line 273); L_mask is the mask-refinement loss from intervention verification (line 224); L_quantization = //sg(E_phi(X)) - z_u//^2 + beta * //sg(z_u) - E_phi(X)//^2, where sg is the stop-gradient operator, E_phi the encoder and z_u the codebook embedding; the paper calls the first term the reconstruction loss and the second the commitment loss (lines 1531-1533). Algorithm 1 lists lambda_sparse, lambda_mask and lambda_quantization as input hyperparameters (line 508); beta (line 1531) and the lambda_1, lambda_2 and tau inside L_mask (lines 224-226) are not listed there, and the saved text gives no values for any of these weights. | - | Loss function definition; not a measurement. | §4.3 Transition Probability Learning (lines 269-276); Appendix E.1 (lines 1529-1533) | 274 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | What is learned is the agent's world model: an encoder maps concatenated state-action pairs (x_t, a_t) to a latent vector z_e, which is vector-quantized (VQ-VAE) to the nearest codebook entry z_u, one entry per meta state u; each codebook entry defines a distribution over causal structures from which the skeleton matrix M_{C(X_t)} is sampled (line 245). Appendix E.1 adds that a decoder D: R^d -> [0,1]^{p x p} outputs edge probabilities M_hat_u, sampled with Gumbel-Softmax for end-to-end gradient learning (line 1528); Algorithm 1 initializes and updates encoder parameters phi, decoder parameters theta and embeddings (line 510). Note: §4.2 says the encoder takes state-action pairs (line 244), whereas Appendix E.1 defines E: X -> R^d on the observed state x (line 1525). | - | Description of the trained components (network weights, codebook, edge-probability decoder); not a measurement. | §4.2 Representation Learning (lines 242-246); Appendix E.1 (lines 1524-1528) | 245 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Interventions are chosen by a curiosity reward R_t. The default in the main results is edge entropy, I^edge_t = sum over i,j in [p] of H(M_hat_{C(X_t)}[i,j]), where M_hat_{C(X_t)}[i,j] in [0,1] is the posterior probability of an edge from variable i to j in the current meta state C(X_t) and H is Shannon entropy; the authors say this term prioritizes interventions on the most uncertain parts of the causal graph. Three alternatives were tried: prediction uncertainty H[p_theta(x_{t+1} / x_t, a_t)], feature discrepancy //E(x_{t+1}) - E_theta(x_hat_{t+1})//^2, and predictive negative log-likelihood -log p_theta(x_{t+1} / x_t, a_t); the text says the other forms yield comparable behaviors (Table 9, lines 212-213). | - | Intrinsic reward definition (entropy of edge-probability estimates); not a measurement. | §4.1 Curiosity Reward (lines 190-213) | 197 | primary | supported |
| 4 | signal | Intervention verification: after curiosity-guided interventions do(X_i = x'_i), the agent observes the resulting changes in the other variables and estimates the causal effect Delta_ij = log P(X_j^{t+1} / X^t, do(X_i = x'_i)) - log P(X_j^{t+1} / X^t) (line 220). These effects enter the mask-refinement loss L_mask = -lambda_1 * sum over pairs with /Delta_ij/ > tau of log M_hat_ij + lambda_2 * sum over pairs with /Delta_ij/ < tau of log M_hat_ij, where tau >= 0 controls sensitivity (lines 224-226): pairs whose measured interventional effect exceeds tau are pushed toward an edge, the rest away from one. The signal is thus the environment's observed response to the agent's own interventions. | - | Signal = estimated interventional effect Delta_ij (difference of log-probabilities of the next value of X_j with and without the intervention), thresholded at tau; not a measurement. | §4.1 Intervention Verification (lines 214-226) | 216 | primary | supported |
| 5 | mechanism | Algorithm 1 loops until convergence: assign each state embedding to its nearest meta state u; decode the skeleton-probability matrix M_hat_u and sample M_u with Gumbel-Softmax; select the intervention do(X_i = x'_i) that maximizes the curiosity reward R_t; perform it and record the resulting state transitions; estimate Delta_ij and update the mask via L_mask; predict X_j^{t+1} from its parent set and update the world model via L_MLE; apply sparsity via L_sparse; update the codebook via L_quantization. It returns the learned causal subgraphs G_u, the world-model parameters and the embeddings. What is kept from experience is therefore the codebook (meta states), the per-meta-state edge probabilities and the transition model; §4.3 describes training as alternating among interventional exploration, subgraph updating, world-model learning and codebook refinement (line 278). | - | Procedure description; not a measurement. | §4.3, Algorithm 1 (lines 506-534) | 522 | primary | supported |
| 6 | mechanism | In Appendix D.2 the authors state that the MCG framework does not implement Gödel-Machine-style code-level self-rewriting, but that it self-improves its knowledge structure: the agent collects new data under curiosity rewards and, upon prediction failures or high uncertainty, dynamically refines and expands its set of causal subgraphs and meta-state mappings, which they call self-correction and knowledge-level self-evolution. | - | Authors' conceptual characterization in an appendix; not a measurement. | Appendix D.2 Gödel Machines and Meta-Causal Graphs | 1521 | primary | supported |
| 7 | selection_rule | Adaptive Codebook Fusion keeps the meta-state set minimal: during training, codebook entries that encode similar latent embeddings and produce comparable decoded causal skeleton matrices are automatically merged. | 8 | selection_rule | The authors' theory argues that the correct meta-state partition is the one with the sparsest skeletons. Under Assumption 1 (a single graph learned from data pooled across several subgraphs has, for each variable, the union of their parent sets; lines 155-158), the proof of Theorem 1 (A.3, lines 942-975) states that a partition merging two distinct true meta states yields the element-wise OR of their skeletons, which the authors state has a strictly larger L1 norm (edge count) than each constituent, and hence a larger expected L1 norm than the true partition. A.1 summarizes this as: any departure from swap-label equivalence 'leads to higher L1 norm of causal skeleton matrices and thus contradicts the optimality principle underlying our framework' (line 926). Theorem 2, also under Assumption 1, states that if the learned mapping has more clusters than there are true meta states, it is observationally equivalent to the true mapping (lines 168-170). The agent must discover the latent meta states (root-node colours), learn each subgraph through interventional exploration, and generalize to unseen state configurations (line 1245). With a codebook of 2 meta states the model learns two distinct causal patterns corresponding to them. With 4, some codes correspond to similar causal graphs (Patterns 1 and 3), while a code with a significantly different graph (Pattern 4) occurs less frequently (line 573; shown only in Figure 3, environment not named, no numbers). ## s055 — Planning to Explore: Curiosity-Driven Planning for LLM Test Generation

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.05159v1 · version read: arXiv 2604.05159v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2026-04-06
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper frames iterative test generation as a heuristic approximation of Bayesian exploration of an unknown environment: the agent interacts with a program whose internal branch reachability is initially unknown; at each step it generates a test (action), executes it and observes which branches are reached (observation). The objective is to choose tests so that cumulative branch coverage, which the paper treats as its measure of knowledge about the program, grows as quickly as possible. | - | Objective definition, not a measurement. Cumulative branch coverage = cumulative number of unique branches executed across all test scripts (§4 Metrics, line 184). | §3 Method, 'Test Generation inspired by Bayesian Exploration' | 111 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | Formal objective (Eq. 1-2, instantiated in Table 1). Eq. 1: expected information gain g~(a/h) = I(O; Theta / h, a), the mutual information between the unknown parameter Theta (Table 1: the program's branch reachability structure) and the observation O (Table 1: branches hit by executing the plan), conditioned on the history h = (a1,o1)...(at,ot) (Table 1: sequence of (test, coverage result) pairs) and the action a (Table 1: a test plan of S scripts). Eq. 2: curiosity Q-value q(h,a) = g~(a/h) + gamma * E_{o/h,a}[v(hao)], where v(h) = max_a q(h,a) is the curiosity value of history h, v(hao) is the value of the history after taking a and observing o, gamma is a discount factor, and the expectation is over the observation o given h and a. Table 1 maps the prior p(Theta) to 'no branches observed', the posterior p(Theta/h) to the coverage map C_t (sufficient statistic after t executions), and 'corridor' to validation gates and setup sequences. The authors note that information gain is additive only in expectation and so cannot be substituted directly as a reward in standard RL (line 148). | - | Formal definitions (Eq. 1, Eq. 2, Table 1, lines 112-153); not a measurement. | §3 Method, Eq. 1-2 and Table 1 | 153 | primary | supported |
| 2 | what_is_changed | The modified components sit outside the model, in the prompt and the candidate-selection step of the test-generation loop. CovGreedy adds the coverage map C_t to the generation prompt: a structured text block reporting branches discovered, recent discovery rate, stagnation warnings and the most informative prior tests. CovQValue (line 180) additionally generates K=3 trajectory plans of S=3 sequential test scripts, each with a different diversity hint (e.g. main functionality, error handling, interactions), and executes the plan with the highest LLM-estimated Q-value (gamma = 0.5). The same model is used for generation, Q-value scoring and greedy selection within a run (line 182). | - | Description of the method's components (prompt content, number of candidates, selection step); not a measurement. | §4 Experiments, 'Strategies' | 178 | primary | supported |
| 3 | signal | Two signals drive the loop. (i) Environment feedback: each executed test reveals which branches are reached (line 111), and the reached branches update the coverage map (line 155). Tests run in Docker: a single image with all 9 packages for RepoExploreBench (line 474) and repository-specific SWE-bench Docker testbeds for TestGenEval Lite (line 167); the text names the coverage tooling (Python's standard branch coverage tooling) only for RepoExploreBench (Appendix A, line 474). (ii) Before execution, candidate plans are ranked by the same LLM's own estimates of immediate new branches and future reachability (line 161), i.e. an LLM self-estimate, not an execution check. Pass rate (fraction of generated scripts that execute without error) is reported as a secondary metric (line 184). | - | Signal definition; observation = set of branches reached by executing a test; not a measurement. | §3 Method, 'Test Generation inspired by Bayesian Exploration' | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | What is stored and reused: the coverage map, i.e. the set of branches observed across all test executions, accumulated as C_t = C_{t-1} ∪ B(a_t) (line 155; Algorithm 1 writes C <- C ∪ Branches(o_s) after each executed script, line 518), plus the test history h of (test, observation) pairs (Algorithm 1, line 520). The map is fed back to the LLM as structured text; in CovQValue the LLM conditions on it only at the start of each plan round, because a selected plan is executed open-loop without intermediate feedback (line 160) and the text counts one coverage-map update per round, 8 per target (line 186). Each round the LLM generates plans conditioned on the source file P, C, h and a diversity hint (line 493). The authors describe the map as a deterministic proxy of the posterior that does not encode a full probability distribution over unseen branches (line 155). Algorithm 1 initializes an empty coverage map and history for each input source file (lines 476-485). | - | Description of the stored state and its update rule; not a measurement. | §3 Method, 'Coverage Maps as Exploration State'; Appendix B Algorithm 1 | 155 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | selection_rule | For each of the K candidate plans, the LLM is given the plan and the current coverage map and predicts two values on a 0-50 scale: expected new branches g^ and additional branches made reachable for future tests v^; Q = g^ + gamma * v^ (gamma = 0.5 in the main experiments, line 180). The plan with the highest Q among the K candidates is executed; only the ranking matters, not the absolute scale. - Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.14728v1 · version read: arXiv 2506.14728v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v1 text saved as sources/2506.14728-pdf.txt for cross-checking only) · v1: 2025-06-17

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | problem_definition | Eq. 2 (line 136) states the objective as max over B ⊂ L of E_(x,y)~D [ I{ π_S(x; B) = y } ], under the constraint of Eq. 1, ∇_θ π_S = 0 (no gradient update to the student, lines 129-131). Symbols (lines 127-141): D = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1..N} are supervision pairs (input, ground-truth answer); π_T is the teacher agent; π_S is the student agent with a small language model; θ appears only as the gradient subscript in Eq. 1 and is not defined in the text (the natural reading is the student's parameters); L is the space of all teacher-agent-generated MCPs; B is the MCP-Box distilled from L; π_S(x; B) is the student's behaviour on input x augmented with guidance from the MCP-Box; I{·} is 1 if the student's output matches the ground truth. So the stated objective is the student's expected accuracy against the ground truth on D, maximized over subsets of teacher-made MCPs; the formula contains no cost, token or time term. The procedure actually described (§3.2-3.4, lines 155-190) never evaluates candidate boxes against this objective: the box is built in one LLM-prompted pass and mounted whole. | - | Formal objective (expected indicator of a correct student answer); not a measurement. | §3.1 Problem Formulation, Eqs. 1-2 | 128 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | what_is_changed | The component that changes is the student agent's tool library, which sits outside the model. At inference time the entire MCP-Box B is mounted into the student's tool interface on the SmolAgents framework. Each consolidated MCP is a callable tool with a standardized input/output interface (e.g., @mcp.tool() in the FastMCP runtime). The student policy is frozen and receives no gradient updates (line 188). At each step all tools in B are exposed as callable modules; the student decides which tool to invoke (if any), fills in the arguments and receives a return value o_t that updates its context (line 189). Neither the teacher nor the student is fine-tuned (line 95). | - | Description of the modified component (tool interface of the student agent); not a measurement. | §3.4 Student Inference with the MCP-Box | 187 | primary | supported |
| 2 | mechanism | The MCPs are mined from the teacher's trajectories, not the student's. For each training input x_i, the teacher π_T interacts with an environment E and produces a trajectory τ_i = (r_1, a_1, o_1, ..., r_{L_i}, a_{L_i}, o_{L_i}) of reasoning tokens r_t, action tokens a_t (e.g., tool calls, MCP generation) and environment observations o_t (Eq. 3, lines 143-148). The teacher is prompted to emit structured, self-contained MCPs separately from its reasoning. One trajectory can yield several MCPs, MCP_{i,j} = the MCP generated at step j for example i, one per distinct subtask (lines 149-154). The teacher has three modules: a Manager Agent, a Basic Image Captioner and an MCP Creation Module (line 193). The Manager decomposes the task, decides whether external tools are needed and, if so, delegates MCP creation (line 195). The MCP Creation Module runs brainstorming, open-source searching, script generation and virtual-environment execution, which validates and executes the scripts (line 199). What is kept and reused is the MCP code; per the Figure 1 caption, the student inherits capabilities without gradient updates or trajectory replay (line 71). | - | Description of how teacher trajectories yield MCP code snippets; not a measurement. | §3.2 MCP Creation; §3.5.1 Teacher Agent | 149 | primary | supported |
| 3 | mechanism | All MCPs collected from successful teacher trajectories go to a high-capacity instruction-tuned LLM (e.g., Claude-Sonnet-4), which builds the MCP-Box in three prompted steps. (1) Abstraction rewrites each raw MCP_{i,j} into a concise, task-agnostic, parameterized form: it removes example-specific phrases and makes up to three critical parameters configurable (Eq. 4, lines 159-164). (2) Clustering groups the abstracted MCPs by functionality with a code-level clustering prompt, giving clusters such as 'image utils' or 'numeric analysis' (Eq. 5, lines 166-171). (3) Consolidation merges each cluster into one general-purpose tool with unified parameters, validation and documentation; each output is a FastMCP-compatible Python file (Eq. 6, lines 173-178). The box is B = {(MCP_k^final, cluster_name_k)}_{k=1..K} (Eq. 7, lines 179-184). | - | Description of the LLM-prompted construction pipeline; not a measurement. | §3.3 MCP-Box Construction, Eqs. 4-7 | 157 | primary | supported |
| 4 | signal | Material is admitted to distillation when the teacher's final answer matches the dataset's ground-truth label: only trajectories where π_T(x_i) = y_i on the labelled supervision pairs are used. The second check is that the snippet is syntactically correct and executable (same line), and the teacher's MCP Creation Module validates scripts by executing them in a virtual environment (line 199). The construction steps described (§3.2-3.3) contain no step that scores the MCP-Box or its consolidated tools on student performance. | - | Admission signal = ground-truth answer match of the teacher trajectory, plus syntax/executability of the MCP snippet; not a measurement. | §3.2 MCP Creation | 155 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | A raw MCP_{i,j} enters the temporary pool L only if it comes from a successful teacher trajectory and the snippet is syntactically correct and executable. The authors call the resulting pool 'rich but noisy'; abstraction, clustering and consolidation then reduce it to the MCP-Box. The final box is mounted whole, without retrieval, reranking or parameter selection (line 187), and 'No external scoring, selection, or retrieval is required' at inference (line 190). The procedure is a single pass: no accept/revert loop over candidate boxes is described. | - | Acceptance rule for raw MCPs (teacher success + syntactic correctness + executability); not a measurement. | §3.2 MCP Creation | 155 | primary | supported |
| 6 | mechanism | In the authors' explanation, the MCP-Box acts as an external library of executable protocols, distilled from teacher trajectories and abstracted for reuse. The student can skip low-level code generation but still decides whether to call a tool, which MCP to use and how to fill in the arguments. No policy gradients or planning heuristics are transferred. The benefit comes from restricting the tool-calling space to functional, verified options, which the authors say reduces generation complexity. This is an explanation; the paper reports no ablation or measurement that isolates it. | - | Authors' causal explanation of the gains; not a measurement. | §4.2 'Why MCP Distillation works.' | 337 | primary | supported |
| 7 | setting | Student agents use three models the paper calls small instruction-tuned language models: GPT-3.5-turbo, Qwen-8B and LLaMA3.1-8B (line 216). The Qwen model is named 'Qwen-8B' at lines 216, 262, 312 and 334-335, and 'Qwen3-8B' in Tables 1-2 and in the prose at lines 88, 98, 123, 201 and 309. In the teacher agent, the Manager Agent runs on Claude-Sonnet-4 and the MCP Creation Module on GPT-4o; all models are frozen (lines 216-217). A student has only a Manager Agent and a Basic Image Captioner (line 201). The captioner turns images into text because many of the text-only models used cannot take image input (line 197). Compared settings (lines 218-220): student before distillation; agents with pre-defined tools in the Octotools framework; student after distillation; the teacher; and Octotools with GPT-4o. The student before and after distillation, the student with pre-defined tools and the teacher are then evaluated 'on the same dataset'. | 0 | problem_definition | Each assistant decision is formalized as Eq. 1, o_t ~ pi_theta(o_t / s_t, R_t, f_t^i). Here o_t is the assistant's output at time step t, pi_theta is the assistant's policy, s_t is the current state, R_t is the reward signal (the reward score for task performance) at t, and f_t^i is the checker's feedback in the i-th iteration. The stated objective is for the assistant agent A to maximize the expected reward R over successive iterations (line 105); refinement ends when the checker validates the output or an iteration limit N is reached (line 122). | - | Formal problem statement (Eq. 1, §3.1.2); not a measurement. | 1 | problem_definition | The 'evolutionary goals' are Eq. 6, G^{t+1} = (A^{t+1}, D^{t+1}) with D^{t+1} = argmin over D_t in Delta of the sum over i in I_t of L_D(D_t; f_t^i, pi_theta^t). G^{t+1} is the new evolutionary objective, A^{t+1} the updated memory optimization mechanisms, and D^{t+1} in Delta the model's self-adjustments 'to make the RL algorithm converge' (line 153). The policy update is Eq. 7, theta^{t+1} = theta^t + alpha * grad_theta[lambda_A L_A(theta^t, A^{t+1}) + lambda_D L_D(theta^t, D^{t+1})]. L_A and L_D are MSE losses for memory optimization and self-adjustment, and lambda_A, lambda_D >= 0 are weights (line 158). alpha is not defined anywhere in the saved text. Delta and the index set I_t are not defined as used in Eq. 6: the text uses I_t elsewhere for 'the information received at time t' (line 179) and Delta(S_i) for the mixed-strategy simplex in the proof (line 909), and neither is tied to Eq. 6. The prose names the update function psi while Eq. 7 writes phi, and Eq. 7 takes a '+alpha * gradient' step on an MSE loss without explaining the sign. | - | Formal update rule (Eqs. 6-7); not a measurement. The saved text reports no training run, loss values or hyperparameters (alpha, lambda_A, lambda_D) for this update. | §3.1.3 Evolutionary Goals and Directions, Eqs. 6-7 | 158 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | The contribution list says the reflection mechanism works without any additional training and lets agents use historical information better. 'Linguistic optimization' turns I_t into I_t* with strength S* > S (Eq. 11). Under Eq. 12 and the conditions listed after it, I_t* is kept in short-term memory if R(I_t*, tau) >= theta_1, discarded if R < theta_2, and transferred to long-term memory if theta_2 <= R < theta_1, with theta_1 > theta_2 predefined. | 0 | problem_definition | Section 3 formalizes the problem with two definitions and a retrieval task statement. Agent (Definition 2): an LLM agent A: P -> alpha is controlled by verbal prompts P and outputs an action sequence alpha = [alpha_1, ..., alpha_L]; each action is a tuple (f in T, i in I_f, o in O_f), i.e. a tool function f from the tool space T, its specified input(s) i, and a designated variable o that receives the output(s); later actions may use earlier outputs, and the final action alpha_L renders the task result. Tools (Definition 1, line 107): T = {f_k: I_fk -> O_fk / k = 1, 2, ...}, where each implemented function f_k maps its input I_fk to its output O_fk (e.g. a search-index API, an encoder, a classifier). Retrieval task (line 117): given a user query q, identify or generate a ranked list of relevant entities E from the entity space of a knowledge base; each query has a set of ground-truth answers Y used to compute prediction quality. | - | Formal definitions (Definitions 1-2 and the retrieval task statement, §3); not a measurement. | §3 Problem Formulation, Definition 2 (also Definition 1, line 107; retrieval task, line 117) | 108 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What the loop changes is the actor LLM's prompt: the instructions generated by the comparator LLM are appended to the initial prompts to update the actor. The authors contrast the method with fine-tuning approaches, saying it needs only a small subset of training data and tool descriptions (line 105). | - | Description of the modified component (prompt instructions and the regenerated action sequence); not a measurement. | §4.2, Step 2 (also §4.1, line 156) | 161 | primary | supported |

Two thresholds l and h with 0 < h <= l < 1 bound the groups: a query whose metric (e.g. Recall) is above l is positive, below h negative; the lower bound may be adapted to keep enough negatives; a mini-batch of b queries is drawn at random with b/2 positive and b/2 negative. The experiments use Recall@20 or Accuracy for this split, with l = h = 0.5 and b = 20 on all datasets (line 200). | 0 < h <= l < 1; b/2 positive + b/2 negative per mini-batch | Per-query evaluation metric computed against ground-truth answers (Recall@20 or Accuracy per line 200), thresholded into positive/negative groups. | 4 | mechanism | Step 2, contrastive reasoning: the comparator contrasts the positive and negative groups by their key characteristics, attributes the performance gap to specific tool usage within the solution, and suggests general modifications; the resulting instructions are appended to the actor's prompt. | 0 | problem_definition | The paper formalizes Agent S as a retrieval-and-generation pipeline rather than an optimization objective. Q = LLM(T_u, O_0): T_u is the task from the user, O_0 the initial environment observation (annotated accessibility tree plus screenshot) from the ACI, and Q an observation-aware query in a 'How to do X' format. K_web = Retrieve(Web, Q) is external knowledge from online web search (Perplexica); E_{n_u} = Retrieve(M_n, Q) is a similar full-task experience summary from the Manager's narrative memory M_n, retrieved by query-embedding similarity; K_fused = LLM(M_n(Q), K_web) is the fused guideline. From K_fused the Manager's Subtask Planner produces a topologically sorted queue of subtasks s_0..s_n, each with context C_{s_i}. Each Worker w_i retrieves subtask experience E_{s_i} = Retrieve(M_e, <T_u, s_i, C_{s_i}>) from episodic memory M_e. ## s060 — CRAFT: Customizing LLMs by Creating and Retrieving from Specialized Toolsets

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2309.17428v2 · version read: arXiv 2309.17428v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt) · v1: 2023-09-29
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): International Conference on Learning Representations 2024 (ICLR 2024), main conference, poster (decision 'Accept (poster)'; OpenReview G0vdDSt9XM)
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | CRAFT states no single objective to optimize. It builds a toolset from a source dataset, either a general instruction dataset or a training set of problem-answer pairs (line 128), in four steps: Generation, Abstraction, Verification (the step heading says Validation, line 149) and Deduplication (line 129). The only formula in tool creation is the min-max problem-sampling rule Q <- Q U argTopK_min( max_{q_s in Q} sim(q_r, q_s) / q_r in R_i ). Here Q is the set of sampled problems, initialized with n random samples from the source dataset, and R_i is the set of remaining problems after the i-th iteration, initialized as the rest (line 136). q_r is a remaining problem and q_s an already-sampled problem; the similarity of q_r to Q is its highest similarity to any member of Q (line 137). argTopK_min returns the indices of the k smallest values, where k is the number of problems added per iteration (set to 100), and sim(.) is the cosine similarity of SimCSE sentence vectors. Each iteration therefore adds the k remaining problems least similar to Q, to diversify the toolset (lines 138-139). | k = 100 | Formal definition of the problem-sampling step (k = problems added per iteration); not a measurement. | §2.1 Tool Creation, Generation | 139 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | What changes is an external, task-specific toolset of executable Python functions. Each function is an abstracted solution with a general name and a docstring. The toolset is built offline (line 184) and retrieved per problem, and the retrieved snippets are inserted into the backbone LLM's prompt so that its generated code can call them (lines 180-181). The backbone is not fine-tuned; the authors call CRAFT training-free and plug-and-play (line 191). The final toolsets hold 525 (VQA), 181 (tabular) and 282 (math) tools. Louvain community detection groups them into 195, 23 and 234 classes, and their average cyclomatic complexity is 2.64, 2.07 and 1.34 (Table 4, lines 529-540; line 550). Against the sampled source problems (2,000 VQA and 500 for the other tasks, lines 895, 897), that is 26%, 36% and 56% retained (calc., assuming 500 per task and that Table 4 counts the final toolsets). | - | Description of the modified component. Toolset counts are tool and class counts from Table 4 (classes = Louvain communities); retention shares are calc.; not a performance measurement. | §2.2 Tool Retrieval (end); §2 Summary and Discussion; §4.5 Table 4 | 180 | primary | supported |
| 2 | signal | The signal during creation is execution plus answer match. For each sampled problem a specific Python solution is generated: §2.1 says GPT-4 is instructed to write it (line 140), while for VQA Appendix B says ViperGPT is employed to generate the specific code solutions (line 896); the text does not reconcile the two. Solutions that run without bugs and produce the correct output are kept, and everything else is discarded (line 142). The source data are problem-answer pairs (lines 128, 134). For VQA, Appendix C.2 also contains an LLM-judge prompt titled 'Evaluate the Specific Generation for VQA'. It asks whether a predicted answer means the same as the reference answer and expects Yes or No (lines 913-919); the main text does not say at which step it is applied. No unit tests are described. Human inspection of problematic tools is mentioned only as a possibility (line 195). There is no benchmark-score feedback loop over the toolset. | - | Filter criterion: the generated code executes without error and its output is correct for the source problem; not a measurement. | §2.1 Tool Creation, Generation; Appendix C.2 | 142 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | The system learns from solved problems by rewriting them, not by storing trajectories. GPT-4 is told to replace problem-specific variable names with general ones (e.g. cat -> animal, desk -> object). It also turns hard-coded textual inputs of internal calls into tool arguments (e.g. df["date"] -> df[column_name], with column_name passed in by the tool user). Finally it assigns a general function name and a docstring (line 147). Each tool is stored as the abstracted code plus the triple (original problem q_i, function name f_i, docstring d_i), which retrieval uses later (lines 163-167). For VQA, Appendix B says ViperGPT is used to generate the specific code solutions (line 896), while §2.1 says GPT-4 is instructed to write them (line 140). | - | Description of the abstraction step and of what is stored per tool; not a measurement. | §2.1 Tool Creation, Abstraction; §2.2; Appendix B | 147 | primary | supported |
| 4 | selection_rule | After abstraction, each tool is validated on the problem it came from. GPT-4 gets the abstract function and must solve the original problem by supplying arguments to it; tools that fail to derive the correct answer are discarded (lines 151-153). With the pre-abstraction filter (line 142), a tool therefore passes two correctness checks, both on its own source problem. No test on other problems is described. | - | Accept/discard rule for abstracted tools: a correct answer on the original source problem when GPT-4 calls the tool; not a measurement. | §2.1 Tool Creation, Validation | 153 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | Deduplication groups tools that share both the function name and the number of input arguments (lines 156-157). For each group with more than one tool, GPT-4 is prompted to decide on the most comprehensive, widely applicable tool (line 158). The Appendix C.4 prompt asks for the number of the most generic tool as a one-token answer (lines 1282-1299). The stated aim is to reduce redundancy and confusion from tools with the same name (line 155). | - | Keep rule within a duplicate group (same name and argument count): GPT-4's choice of the most general tool; not a measurement. | §2.1 Tool Creation, Deduplication; Appendix C.4 | 158 | primary | supported |
| 6 | mechanism | Tools are reused at inference in four stages. First, the evaluated LLM writes candidate function names f_t and docstrings d_t for the target problem q_t (line 162). Second, CRAFT searches the toolset T three ways. Eq. 1 is T_{q_t} = argTopK_max( sim(q_i, q_t) / t_i in T ), where t_i is a stored tool, q_i its source problem, sim a SimCSE sentence similarity, argTopK_max the indices of the k largest values, and T_{q_t} the k tools retrieved by problem matching (lines 171-176). T_{f_t} and T_{d_t} are obtained the same way by matching names and docstrings (line 177), with k = 10 for q_t, 5 for f_t and 10 for d_t (lines 899-900). Third, the three lists are pooled and ranked by frequency, and the three most frequent tools are kept by majority vote. Tools that appear only once are dropped; if nothing remains, the LLM writes code without task-specific tools (lines 178-179). Fourth, the retrieved code goes into the prompt, and the retrieved functions plus the LLM-generated solution are executed to obtain the prediction (lines 180-182). | - | Retrieval procedure and its hyperparameters (k per view, three tools kept); not a measurement. | §2.2 Tool Retrieval, Eq. 1; Appendix B Tool Retrieval | 178 | primary | supported |

The vanilla tool baseline (ViperGPT for VQA, Program-of-Thoughts otherwise) scores 35.0 / 36.9, 15.4 / 24.7, 15.6 / 23.0, 80.6 and 58.2 (lines 296-304). | 0 | problem_definition | The paper gives no formula. It states the optimisation problem in words: a teleprompter is an optimizer that takes a DSPy program, a training set and a metric and returns a new optimized program; teleprompters optimize all modules in the pipeline to maximize a metric (line 148). The program is Python code that composes modules, each declared with a signature, i.e. a tuple of input fields and output fields plus an optional instruction (line 151). The training set may be a handful of examples, may contain only inputs, and in practice carries labels at most for the program's final output, not for intermediate steps (line 227). | - | Problem statement (inputs: program, training set, metric; output: optimized program; objective: maximize the metric); not a measurement. | §3.3 Teleprompters can automate prompting for arbitrary pipelines | 226 | primary | supported |
| 1 | what_is_changed | Each LM call that implements a signature has parameters: (1) which LM to call, (2) the prompt instructions and the string prefix of each signature field, and (3) the demonstrations used as few-shot prompts for frozen LMs or as training data for finetuning; the authors focus mainly on automatically generating and selecting demonstrations. §4 Stage 1 repeats that this iteration of DSPy focuses on demonstrations, while naming instructions and field descriptions as possible candidate parameters (line 276). The pipeline itself is written by the developer, who declares the modules and connects them in any control flow (line 99). Of the three stages that typical teleprompters go through (line 274), only Stage 3 modifies the program's control flow; ensembles are named as one of its simplest forms and are the form used in the case studies (line 285). Among the teleprompters the paper describes, BootstrapFinetune is the one that changes model weights: it uses the demonstrations to update each predictor's LM weights (line 281). | - | Description of the tunable parameters of a module and of which compiler stage changes what; not a measurement. | §3.2 Parameterized & templated Modules, 'Parameterization' | 199 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

In the experiments the ensemble takes the top-7 candidate programs of a bootstrapping compiler run with majority voting (line 445). In the Appendix E.1 pseudocode each Predict call's trace entry (predictor, inputs, outputs) from a passing example is stored as a demonstration Example in that predictor's demonstration list (lines 2310-2318); Predict later formats its prompt with these demonstrations (line 168), or BootstrapFinetune uses them as finetuning data (line 281). The teacher can itself be a compiled program, e.g. bootstrap×2 uses the optimized bootstrap program as teacher (lines 438-441). | - | What is stored: per-module input/output pairs (trace entries of each Predict call) from the teacher program's runs on training inputs that pass the metric; the teacher is by default the zero-shot program being compiled, but can be another program (the compiled bootstrap program for bootstrap×2, line 441; a llama2-13b-chat multihop ensemble for the T5 compile, line 620). - Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.02085v6 · version read: arXiv 2508.02085v6 (PDF full text saved as 2508.02085v6-pdf.txt, used for all anchors; HTML v6 full text 2508.02085v6.txt also read). Versions v1 2025-08-04 th… · v1: 2025-08-04

- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The environment is a tuple E = (T, S, A, P, R): T is the space of all tasks that need multi-step reasoning; S is the state space, each state s capturing progress toward solving a task; A is the agent's action space (information gathering or direct task execution); P: S x A -> S is the transition dynamics; R: S x T -> real numbers is the reward function scoring a state for a task. A trajectory is tau = (s0, a0, ..., si, ai, ..., sn), with s0 the initial state, ai the action at step i, sn the final state and s(i+1) = P(si, ai); it is generated by a policy pi: S x T -> A, and its quality is the final reward R(tau, t) = R(sn, t). | - | Formal problem setup; not a measurement. | §3 Preliminaries and Problem Setup (lines 136-153) | 139 | primary | supported |
| 1 | problem_definition | The stated objective is a policy pi* = argmax over pi of E_{t~T}[R(tau^pi(t), t)]: pi is the policy, t a task drawn from the task space T, tau^pi(t) the trajectory policy pi generates for task t, and R the final-state reward defined in §3. The method itself (§4.1; Eq. 11, lines 333-336) returns, for one given task t, the trajectory tau* in the final pool Gamma_K with the highest internal Reward(tau, t) of Eq. 8 (weighted TaskCompletion = rule-based AutoEval + lambda * LLM-based ExpertEval, ReasoningQuality and Efficiency), not the trajectory with the highest §3 reward R. | - | Objective definition; not a measurement. | §3 'Objective of SE-Agent' (lines 154-157); Eq. 11 (lines 333-336) | 156 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | What is changed is the pool of candidate trajectories for a given task t. SE-Agent first builds Gamma0 = Gamma0^plan union Gamma0^mutate, where each planned trajectory is Plan(theta_p, t) with theta_p the planning parameters and strategies (Eq. 1) and each mutated one is Mutate(tau_p^plan, delta_m) with delta_m the degree and nature of mutation (Eq. 2); it then repeatedly applies revision, recombination and refinement to produce generations Gamma_k. SE-Agent is presented as a plug-and-play module inside existing agent frameworks and is built on SWE-Agent in the experiments (lines 385-386). Appendix A prints LLM prompts for the five planning strategies, reflection/revision, crossover, transfer and restructuring; no mutation prompt is printed (and the Implementation Details, lines 387-398, do not mention mutation), selection is a rule over reward scores and dissimilarity (Eq. 10), and the A.3 'TaskCompletion' prompt is a verbatim repeat of the restructuring prompt. No model-training procedure is described (searched 'train', 'fine-tun'); the text's statement that pilot trajectories 'generate references for imitation learning of the SE-Agent' (line 194) is not followed by any training step. | - | Description of the object being optimized (per-task trajectory pool); not a measurement. | §4.1 Overview; §4.2.1 Eqs. 1-2 (lines 239-257); §5.1 Baselines | 202 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | Revision learns from the agent's own earlier attempt on the same issue. A 'Find the Critical Step' prompt asks for the single most influential decision step (JSON: step, action, reasoning, impact); a 'Conclude Features' prompt analyzes the first attempt's patch and returns JSON fields such as approach_summary, modified_files, key_changes, strategy, the specific technique to avoid, files or functions not to modify the same way, assumptions, components not touched and a different perspective. The Revision prompt fills these fields in and asks for a fundamentally different approach to the same problem that avoids the first solution's techniques, challenges its assumptions and still aims for a patch that passes all tests. | - | Prompt content (what is extracted from a prior trajectory and how it is reused within the same task); not a measurement. | Appendix A.1.2 Reflection and Revision (lines 788-888); Eqs. 3-4 (lines 259-264) | 877 | primary | supported |
| 4 | mechanism | Recombination applies three prompt-based operators to the trajectory pool: Crossover(tau_j1, tau_j2, alpha) combines high-performing segments of two trajectories (alpha sets crossover points and combination strategy, Eq. 5); Transfer(tau_j1, {tau_j2, tau_j3, ...}, beta) moves strategies from successful trajectories into a weaker target trajectory (beta controls the transfer, Eq. 6); Restructure(Gamma_k, gamma) rebuilds a trajectory from a global analysis of the whole pool (gamma is aggregated pool information, Eq. 7). The prompts return new trajectories as JSON step lists, and the Restructuring prompt asks the model to identify redundant reasoning paths and filter out ineffective or repetitive steps (line 971). | - | Operator definitions and prompt content; not a measurement. | §4.3 Recombination Operation, Eqs. 5-7 (lines 271-289); Appendix A.2 (lines 891-1002) | 280 | primary | supported |
| 5 | signal | Candidates are scored by an internal reward Reward(tau, t) = w1*TaskCompletion(tau, t) + w2*ReasoningQuality(tau) + w3*Efficiency(tau) (Eq. 8). TaskCompletion uses structural validation (non-empty patch files, sufficient code-editing steps, a reasonable trajectory length); ReasoningQuality scores logical coherence, depth and robustness; Efficiency scores computational efficiency in reasoning steps and resource use; w1-w3 are hyperparameters whose values are not printed. Eq. 9 sets TaskCompletion = AutoEval + lambda*ExpertEval, where AutoEval is rule-based structural validation, ExpertEval is an LLM-based evaluation of solution quality and lambda weights it (lines 305-307). The developer-written unit tests are named in §5.1 as the benchmark's check of patch correctness (line 352), not as a reward term. | - | Definition of the in-loop selection signal (weighted sum of rule-based checks, LLM judge and an efficiency score); weights not reported; not a measurement. | §4.4.1 Evaluation Function, Eqs. 8-9 (lines 293-307) | 298 | primary | supported |
| 6 | selection_rule | Each generation is Gamma_(k+1) = Select(Gamma_k union Gamma'_k union Gamma_k^new, o) (Eq. 10): the top-performing trajectories by reward score are kept, with o the number of elites, while trajectory dissimilarity metrics keep distinct reasoning approaches represented. Evolution stops after a predefined number of cycles or when convergence criteria are met; the text gives, as an example only ('e.g.'), the improvement in maximum reward falling below a threshold epsilon for consecutive iterations, and does not say which criterion was used in the experiments. The output is tau* = argmax over the final pool Gamma_K of Reward(tau, t) (Eq. 11, lines 331-336). The values of o, epsilon, the cycle count and the dissimilarity metric are not printed. | - | Selection and stopping rule based on the internal reward of Eq. 8; not a measurement. | §4.4.2 Selection and Convergence, Eqs. 10-11 | 313 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

SE-Agent's Pass@5 ranges from 35.2% (Llama) to 63.6% (Claude-3.7-Sonnet). | Pass@1 SWE-Agent / SWE-Search / SE-Agent: 31.6 / 39.4 / 54.8; 18.8 / 23.4 / 38.8; 15.4 / 21.8 / 32.6; 22.4 / 32.6 / 40.4; 40.6 / 47.4 / 61.2 % | Pass@1 = percentage of issues resolved on the first attempt; Pass@5 = percentage for which a correct solution is identified within five attempts (§5.1, lines 355-360); correctness by developer-written unit tests (line 352). | 1 | problem_definition | SICA ranks agents by a utility (Eq. 1): U = w_score*p_score + w_cost*(1 - min(1, p_cost/$10)) + w_time*(1 - min(1, p_time/300 s)), where U is the base utility, p_score in [0,1] is the normalised benchmark performance score, p_time is the wall-clock time in seconds, p_cost is the dollar cost, and w_score, w_cost, w_time are weights set to 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25; $10 per problem is the cap on the worst cost and 300 s is the timeout after which the agent is cancelled (lines 184-196). Eq. 2: U_final = U(1 - tau) if the run timed out, otherwise U, with timeout penalty tau = 0.5, to give partial credit for work done before the timeout (lines 197-203). Algorithm 1 takes evaluation benchmarks B = {b_j : j = 1..m} and an iteration count n and outputs the improved agent system A_n (lines 275-288). | w_score 0.5, w_cost 0.25, w_time 0.25; cost cap $10 per problem; timeout 300 s | Objective definition. Half the weight is benchmark score and half is efficiency: cost and wall-clock time enter as linear credit for staying under the $10 and 300 s caps. The weights are the authors' settings, not measurements. | §3 Methods, Eq. 1-2 | 193 | primary | supported |
| 2 | selection_rule | In each iteration SICA takes the best-performing agent in the archive so far as the meta-agent, which is instructed to look through the archive, identify an improvement and implement it (lines 179-181). Because no weights are updated, the numerical utility is used only to pick the next meta-agent and the base agent for the next iteration (lines 204-206). ## s064 — WebCoach: Self-Evolving Web Agents with Cross-Session Memory Guidance

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2511.12997v2 · version read: arXiv 2511.12997v2 (HTML full text saved as .txt; Appendix A worked-example text is in the raw HTML but not in the saved .txt). v1 (2025-11-17) not read. · v1: 2025-11-17
- Source class: institutional supplement · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): ICLR 2026 Workshop on Memory for LLM-Based Agentic Systems (MemAgents), workshop paper in Poster and Discussion Session 1. This is not the ICLR main conference.
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 16 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | problem_definition | The paper motivates the problem as wasted steps across sessions: web agents revisit the same links, stall at login gates or trigger CAPTCHAs across sessions (line 81); the next sentence of the same paragraph (line 82) adds that agents rarely remember mistakes or successes beyond the current task. The paper states no objective function; the goal is stated in words as letting agents learn from their own trajectories without retraining the base policy (line 84). | - | Problem statement (motivation); not a measurement. | §1 Introduction | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | problem_definition | The problem setup defines no objective, state space or reward function. The formal object on the input side is the logged trajectory: after every environment step the actor writes a structured log of the partial trajectory T_{1:t} = {(o_i, a_i, r_i)}_{i=1..t}, where T_{1:t} is the trajectory from step 1 to the current step t, o_i the observation at step i, a_i the action at step i and r_i the reward at step i (line 98). Line 96 describes these as intermediate rewards that are not necessarily a numerical score but self-evaluations on the status of task completion. The Condenser is said to be agnostic to the log schema (browser-use, Nova-Act or any other framework, line 99). The other formally defined objects are the stored record <embedding, summary_text, meta> (line 118) and the cosine retrieval score (line 126). | - | Definition of the input record; not a measurement. | §2.1 WebCondenser, 'Input.' | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | what_is_changed | Nothing inside the actor model is changed: when the Coach decides to intervene, its advice JSON is appended synchronously to the actor's message history as a system message before the next action selection, which requires no change to the actor's policy network (lines 143-144); no gradients are backpropagated and the actor's internal policy remains untouched (line 140). Apart from these injected system messages the default browser-use system prompt is used without modification (lines 169-170). In the dynamic EMS configuration what changes over time is the content of the External Memory Store, into which each main agent iteratively writes its own completed trajectories (lines 175, 282), and hence the advice injected into the actor's context; in the two frozen EMS configurations the memory is initialized with GPT-4o trajectories (lines 278-280) and labelled 'Frozen' in Table 1. | - | Description of the modified component (actor context via injected system messages; external memory store); not a measurement. | §2.3 Coach, 'Injection mechanism.' | 143 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | mechanism | A small LLM (at most 8B, line 101) converts each raw trace into a fixed schema: summary_text of 3-5 sentences (line 103), a 1536-d OpenAI embedding of the summary (line 105), final_success true/false/null (null = still running, line 107), and fail_modes or success_workflows. If a complete trajectory satisfied all conditions of the user query, the Condenser should highlight the workflows that led to success; otherwise it should summarize the errors or challenges behind the failed attempt (line 109). The text does not name the Condenser model used in the runs: line 283 states the authors' belief that Qwen3-8B is sufficiently capable to act as condenser and coach in the zero-shot setting; the coach is GPT-4o in configuration 2 and Qwen3-8B in configurations 3 and 4 (lines 278-282). | - | Description of the stored record (what is written from each trajectory); not a measurement. | §2.1 WebCondenser, 'Processing.' (schema lines 101-109) | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | mechanism | Reuse is by retrieval: each EMS record stores <embedding, summary_text, meta> with meta = episode_id, domain / URL root, user goal, model name, total steps and timestamp (lines 117-120). The store is a FAISS vector database with HNSW-128 indexing; retrieved candidates are ranked by similarity to the current context embedding via a normalized dot product. Given the Condenser embedding e_t of the current partial trace, EMS returns the top-K past experiences by score(e_t, e_i) = e_t^T e_i / (//e_t//_2 //e_i//_2) (lines 124-126), where e_i is the stored embedding of past episode i, i.e. cosine similarity. The Coach receives the current partial-trace summary plus the top-K (K=5) EMS summaries at each call (lines 135-137). | - | Description of the retrieval rule (cosine similarity, top-K with K=5); not a measurement. | §2.2 External Memory Store, 'Retrieval.' (Eq. at line 126) | 122 | primary | supported |
| 5 | selection_rule | What is kept online: partial episodes are streamed to the Coach for real-time decisions but not stored; only completed episodes that reach a natural stopping point are written to memory, and these include both successes and failures (lines 112-113, 175). The stated purpose is to keep finalized examples and avoid storing noise or transient decision states. No quality or success filter on online writing is described: the routing rule is completion only. Separately, for a cold start the EMS 'can be seeded with high-quality episodes from previously trained web agents' (line 129), and the frozen EMS configurations are initialized with GPT-4o trajectories whose selection is not stated (lines 278-280). | - | Write rule of the memory (store = completed episodes, success or failure); not a measurement. | §2.1 WebCondenser, 'Routing.' | 112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 6 | selection_rule | When advice is used: the Coach LLM is instructed to intervene when it predicts a high failure probability (looping, CAPTCHA, HTTP 4xx) or when a faster path exists in memory; otherwise it returns "intervene": false (line 143). §2.3 says the Coach is 'explicitly trained or prompted' to stay silent otherwise (line 140) and is an 8B LLM (line 131); in the experiments the coach is Qwen3-8B or GPT-4o (lines 278-282), and the authors decided against DPO fine-tuning of Qwen3 and used it zero-shot (line 283). | - | Decision rule for injecting advice; judged by the Coach LLM, not by a test or score; not a measurement. | §2.3 Coach, 'Injection mechanism.' | 142 | primary | supported |
| 7 | signal | The per-step signal logged by the actor is described as intermediate rewards that are not necessarily numerical scores but self-evaluations on the status of task completion; the Condenser LLM (<=8B, line 101) turns these traces into a summary, an embedding and metadata such as whether the task was completed successfully (lines 96, 107). The Coach then uses both the content and the success/failure outcome labels of past experiences to ground its advice (line 133). The saved text therefore derives the stored success label from the Condenser's reading of the actor's logged trace; it does not state whether the task-success check used for reporting (browser-use's evaluation of the final state, line 152) feeds into that label or is kept out of it. | - | Source of the success/failure label attached to stored episodes (Condenser LLM output from the actor's logged trace, which includes self-evaluations); the text does not state whether the reporting evaluator's verdict is used; not a measurement. | §2.1 WebCondenser | 96 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 8 | signal | Benchmark success is judged by browser-use's own evaluation capability, which checks the resulting state of the agent's last action against the initial user query and determines whether the task succeeded. The sentence does not name the model or procedure used for this check. | - | Task-success criterion for all reported success rates (browser-use evaluation of final state vs user query); not a measurement. | §3.1 Data | 152 | primary | supported |
| 9 | setting | Four configurations on WebVoyager with base models Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-32B and Skywork-r1v3-38B plus a GPT-4o ceiling baseline: (1) baseline without coaching, (2) frozen EMS initialized with GPT-4o trajectories with GPT-4o as coach, (3) a frozen EMS also initialized with GPT-4o trajectories, with Qwen3-8B as coach (the text does not say it is the identical store), (4) dynamic EMS where each main agent iteratively writes its own trajectories into the store, coached by Qwen3-8B (lines 275-282). In the dynamic EMS configuration memory is built during, and evaluated on, the same 643-task pass, starting from an empty database (lines 274, 282, 288); for the frozen EMS configurations the text says only that memory is initialized with GPT-4o trajectories, without stating on which tasks they were collected (lines 278-280). | 13 | cost_time | The authors acknowledge that average completion time rises because of the extra inference of the Coach and Condenser, and state that dynamic EMS adds about 150 seconds of average runtime relative to baseline while reducing redundant actions by 1-2 steps per episode; they argue the overhead is transient because HNSW search stays efficient as the EMS grows. Calc. from Table 1 (dynamic vs baseline): Skywork-38B 215 -> 395 s (+180 s, x1.84) and 10.7 -> 10.2 steps; Qwen-VL-32B 201 -> 367 s (+166 s) and 13.3 -> 11.9 steps; Qwen-VL-7B 144 -> 200 s (+56 s) and 16.4 -> 17.4 steps. Only the 32B model shows a step reduction in the 1-2 range, and wall-clock per task rises for every model. | ~150 seconds added; 1–2 steps fewer | Average completion time per task in seconds (wall-clock, including Coach and Condenser inference) and average action steps per task, dynamic EMS vs no-coaching baseline, WebVoyager 643 tasks, one run each.
